prompt: Write a book review of a popular-level book on quantum computing from the point of view of someone who isn't a mathematician and only half understood it, but still came away with one big picture.
response:
Scott Aaronson’s *Quantum Computing Since Democritus* is not a book I understood in the way one understands a recipe. I followed the ingredients, but by the time the oven was mentioned, part of me had wandered into another room. I am not a mathematician. I know enough to recognize when an argument has moved past me: a page of unitary transformations, tensor products, and Hilbert spaces can become a wall of polite symbols, each one familiar enough to be annoying. I read the book anyway, slowly, and I half understood it. What I came away with was not a proof, not a derivation, not even a reliable memory of which algorithm Aaronson introduced first. I came away with one big picture: a quantum computer is not a classical computer with spooky parts, and it is not a machine that simply tries all answers at once. It is a physical device whose power comes from interference, and that power is real but narrow.

That picture matters because most popular accounts of quantum computing fail in one of two directions. One direction is mathematical: the book becomes a textbook with the hard parts explained a little more gently, and the non-mathematician learns that qubits are vectors, gates are matrices, and the universe is unitary. The other direction is promotional: the book becomes a story about parallel universes, infinite possibilities, and machines that will soon solve everything. Aaronson’s book avoids both, mostly by refusing to be simple in the cheap sense. It begins with physics rather than with circuits. It asks what information is, what matter is, and why computation should be treated as a physical process. For someone who is not a mathematician, that is the right order. The first mistake in popular quantum computing is to start with the qubit as if it were a new kind of bit, when the deeper point is that the bit is not the interesting thing. The interesting thing is the physics that the bit happens to live in.

I did not follow all of the technical material. When Aaronson moves from a single qubit to many qubits, the notation begins to do work that I could not check. I understood the verbal claim: a system of qubits is not just a longer list of classical possibilities, because the possibilities are connected in a way that allows them to affect one another. I understood the warning: you cannot simply read off the answer from a quantum state, because measurement changes what you find. I understood that a quantum algorithm is a sequence of operations designed to make the answer more likely to appear when the machine is finally measured. What I did not understand, and probably cannot understand without more mathematics, is exactly how the state space grows, how the operations combine, or why certain algorithms work with the precision that Aaronson describes. The book does not pretend that those questions are optional. It would be a worse book if it did.

The central image that stayed with me was interference. Classical probability behaves like grains of sand: if there are several ways to reach an outcome, you add the chances. Quantum probability behaves more like waves: if several ways reach the same outcome, they can reinforce one another or cancel one another, depending on their relative phases. A quantum computer, in the picture I kept, is a machine that arranges many possible computational paths so that the paths leading to wrong answers tend to cancel and the paths leading to the right answer tend to reinforce. That is not a proof. It is an image. But it is an image that explains why quantum speedups are not general. If the answer has no structure that can be reinforced, interference does not give you much. If the problem has algebraic or periodic structure, interference can do something classical search cannot easily match.

The book becomes more convincing when it gives examples rather than promises. Grover’s search algorithm is a good case. Suppose there are 1,024 boxes and one contains a token. A classical search may require opening up to 1,024 boxes. Grover’s algorithm finds the token in on the order of 32 steps. That is a real speedup, and it is easy to grasp even without the vector algebra: each step tilts the amplitudes slightly toward the marked box and away from the others. But 32 is the square root of 1,024. The speedup is not “infinite parallelism.” It is a geometric advantage. If there are a million boxes, a quantum search takes about a thousand steps rather than a million. That is enormous in practice, but it is not the same as making the problem disappear. A non-mathematician can feel the difference. The machine is not checking all boxes simultaneously and then reporting the result. It is using interference to search more efficiently than a blind classical search.

Shor’s algorithm is the other case that mattered to me, because it is the one with cryptographic consequences. I did not follow the full argument, but I followed enough of the logic to see why factoring is different from ordinary search. The hard classical problem is not merely that there are many possible factors; it is that finding a factor does not give you an obvious local clue. Shor’s algorithm reframes the problem as finding a period, and the quantum Fourier transform can reveal periodic structure in a way that classical methods cannot efficiently match, at least for this problem. I can say that without understanding the proof. What I understood was the shape of the move: the algorithm does not brute-force the factor. It extracts global structure from the behavior of a function. That is why large-scale quantum computers threaten RSA and related systems. Not because they are faster at guessing, but because they can hear a pattern that classical methods hear only with great difficulty.

That distinction is where the book’s big picture becomes useful. Quantum computers are not likely to be general accelerators for every hard problem. They are not obvious solutions to arbitrary scheduling, logistics, or optimization problems. The famous hard problems in computer science, the NP-complete ones, are not known to be easy on quantum computers. Aaronson does not hide that. If anything, he is too good at it, because the popular imagination wants a machine that makes all difficult thinking easier, and the actual science says: here are some problems where the physics helps, and here are many problems where it probably does not. That is a less dramatic conclusion, but it is more stable. It also explains why the news coverage of quantum computing is often distorted. A quantum computer that can factor large integers is not the same thing as a quantum computer that can instantly design a better drug, price a market, or solve a traffic network. The first is a specific algebraic achievement. The others are different kinds of hardness.

The book also grounded the subject in engineering reality, which many popular accounts skip. Qubits are fragile. They decohere. They make errors. A useful quantum computer will need error correction, and error correction is expensive in physical resources: one reliable logical qubit is built from many imperfect physical qubits, and the number required depends on noise, architecture, and the task. I did not learn the exact overhead from this book, nor do I need it for the big picture. The point is that the gap between a laboratory demonstration and a machine that breaks practical cryptography is not a small gap. It is not merely a matter of making the existing machine a little bigger. Today’s quantum processors are impressive as physical objects, but they are not yet the machines that the algorithms assume. Aaronson’s discussion of this made the hype feel less plausible. A quantum computer is not a classical computer with a mysterious bonus feature; it is a new physical regime, and new physical regimes are costly to control.

The hardest objection to this review is that a half-understanding is a dangerous thing. I might have liked Aaronson’s confidence and mistaken that for comprehension. The book is long enough to hide gaps, and its author is fluent enough to make a reader feel oriented even when the reader is only following the furniture. My defense is that the big picture survived contact with a few hard cases. If quantum computers merely tried all possibilities at once, Grover’s search would not be limited to a square-root speedup. If they were general problem solvers, we would expect them to make arbitrary optimization easy, and the book gives no such algorithm. If they were near-term machines, the discussion of error correction would not make them look so distant from breaking RSA. Those are not proofs, but they are the kind of constraints that keep a metaphor honest. A non-mathematician cannot check the derivations, but can still check whether the verbal story bends when pushed against known examples.

The book has costs. It is digressive. Aaronson has interests that extend beyond quantum computing, and the reader is expected to follow him into philosophy, physics, complexity theory, and occasional cultural asides. Some of this is where the book is best, because the conceptual map is assembled in the detours. Some of it is simply a test of patience. A reader who wants a straight path from qubit to algorithm may find the route annoying. A reader who wants to know what quantum computing is doing to the idea of computation will find the detours useful. The prose is also personal, sometimes funny, sometimes impatient. That is not a neutral style. It helps, because the subject is easy to flatten into either mysticism or formalism, but it can also make the book feel more like a tour with a strong guide than a reference.

For a non-mathematician, that is an advantage. The book does not require you to perform the mathematics in order to respect it. It asks you to accept some formal claims while giving you enough physical intuition to see why they are not arbitrary. I accepted the claims about superposition, entanglement, and interference at the level of informed trust. I did not trust the promotional versions, because those do not survive the examples. I did not trust the purely formal versions either, because they leave the non-mathematician with symbols but no sense of what the symbols are doing. Aaronson’s book sits between those failures, though not perfectly. It still asks more than a popular book should, and it still leaves the uninitiated reader occasionally outside the room.

But the one big picture remained. Quantum computing is a consequence of the fact that information is physical. A quantum computer is a machine that uses the strange behavior of quantum states as a computational resource. Its speedups come from interference, entanglement, and the structure of particular problems, not from a general ability to escape classical limits. It is therefore neither magic nor irrelevant. It is a new physical technology, powerful in places where the physics lines up with the problem, and modest or useless where it does not. That was enough for me. I still cannot reconstruct the proofs, and I probably never will. But I can now read a claim about quantum computing and ask the right question: what structure is the machine interfering with? If the answer is clear, the claim may be worth taking seriously. If the answer is “everything,” the claim is probably bad.

prompt: Write an essay about whether it's ethical to publicize small hidden communities, both physical places like an undiscovered town and online subcultures that would rather stay obscure. When does sharing a discovery become exploiting it?
response:
Suppose you drive into a valley that is not on your map, or click a link into a forum with two hundred members. In both cases, the experience feels like finding a room everyone else has forgotten. The first impulse is to tell someone. The second is to post about it. The third is to send the location, the link, the coordinates, the username. That sequence matters. The first act is conversation. The second is publication. The third is a key.

A post about a hidden community can do two different things. It can say that a way of life exists: that people in some place still practice a craft, observe a ritual, speak a dialect, collect a strange archive, or support one another around a risk that would be embarrassing in a larger room. It can also make it easier for strangers to find them. The first is a sentence. The second is a coordinate. The ethical weight usually lies in the coordinate, even when the writer never intends harm.

For a physical place, the coordinate may be literal: a road, a GPS point, a name, a photograph of a landmark. A small town has no buffer between itself and attention. A city can absorb a viral article; a village of a few hundred people cannot. If a traveler posts a video called “I found a hidden paradise,” and the next month brings cars, drones, trash, price-gouging, broken fences, and families being filmed without understanding why, the traveler has made a decision for people who did not ask for an audience. The town did not choose fame. It chose a life. Publicity changes the scale of that life whether or not the change is welcome.

But not all information is a coordinate. If the point is that old irrigation methods survive, or that a local dialect resists standardization, or that a remote community has developed an unusual form of mutual aid, that knowledge can sometimes be shared without handing over the road. The difficulty is that small communities are easy to identify. A unique bridge, a particular festival, a county name, a view from a hill, a photograph of a street corner: these are not neutral details. They are a fingerprint. If a stranger can combine your description with a map and arrive, you have published the address even if you did not paste one.

Online, the same logic appears in a different form. The link is the coordinate. A private Discord server, a password-protected forum, a small subreddit, a closed group chat: these are rooms whose size is part of their function. They may exist because their members have a rare condition, an unusual desire, a dangerous political opinion, a family secret, or simply a need to talk to a few people without being watched by many. When a content creator makes a video called “I found a secret online world,” the value of the video often depends on the audience’s sense of trespass. The creator gains views. The members gain exposure. Pseudonyms, which may have been enough in a small room, become evidence in a larger one. Usernames, voice chats, writing styles, inside references, and screenshots can identify people in ways the writer may not foresee. Once the room is known, it is no longer the same room.

This is why “it is public” is not the same as “they consent to being public at scale.” A public blog with ten readers and a public forum with ten thousand readers occupy different moral spaces. A small public room can be public in the way a courtyard is public: accessible, but not a stage. When someone reposts, names, links, or screenshots it for mass consumption, they change the social meaning of the space. They turn a place where people could be careful into a place where they are visible.

The strongest objection to this caution is that hidden communities are not always innocent. Sometimes secrecy shelters abuse. A closed group may coordinate exploitation. A remote settlement may hide environmental damage, forced labor, or violence against members who cannot leave. A subculture may radicalize young people, normalize self-harm, or exclude those it claims to protect. In such cases, silence can be complicity, and the public may have a real interest in knowing what is happening behind a door.

That objection is correct, but it does not settle the method. Virality is a blunt instrument. It may expose a harmful group, but it may also make the group more attractive, give it a martyr narrative, or put a target on the backs of its most vulnerable members. If a small online network is trafficking people, the useful act is usually not a dramatic social media post but careful documentation, contact with law enforcement or victim services, and disclosure calibrated to prevent harm. If a physical community is committing internal abuse, the people best placed to decide how much to reveal are often the victims, not the outsider who stumbled in. Publicity can protect, but it can also punish. The ethical path is narrower than “tell everyone.”

There is another case where publicity is genuinely good: when the community itself wants to be known. A hidden town facing land grabs may need international attention. A small group of survivors may need public validation. A marginalized subculture may need allies. In those situations, visibility can be a resource. But the difference is who is seeking it and who is controlling it. If the community leads the disclosure, it can choose what to say, what to withhold, and what risks to take. If an outsider leads it, the community is made into a story before it has had a chance to become an author.

That brings the question closer to exploitation. Exploitation does not require a paywall. It can happen in the attention economy of likes, shares, moral satisfaction, and personal brand. When a writer describes a small community as a “hidden gem,” a “secret world,” or “real people unlike the rest of the internet,” the smallness is doing narrative work. Rarity is the seasoning. The audience is invited to feel chosen, curious, or superior. The community becomes a resource for that feeling. If the group had ten thousand members instead of two hundred, the story might be boring. If it were ordinary and known, the writer might not have posted at all. That is a sign that the post is not really about the community. It is about the discovery, and the discoverer.

A useful test is to ask whether the piece needs the key. Can the important idea be shared without making the community easier to find? Can the source be protected without dishonesty? Can the members review what will be published and refuse identifying details? Will the audience be larger than the community can bear? Is the community vulnerable in ways that attention will worsen: poverty, stigma, legal risk, family exposure, violence? Could the post be deleted, and if so, does deletion actually undo the harm? Screenshots survive. Roads remain. Names spread. A post can be taken down and the discovery still live.

The motive matters too, though motive is not a magic shield. Someone can be well meaning and still cause damage. But the question “what do I get?” is not cynical when the other side has little power to say no. You may get a story, a sense of generosity, a reputation for finding things, or the pleasure of showing people a world they did not know. Those are real gains. If the main cost falls on the community, the exchange is unfair unless they consent to it with clear eyes.

Consent, in small communities, is harder than a single yes. Some members may love attention. Some may fear it. Some may not even be asked. In a small town or a small forum, the loudest voice is not the whole room. A gatekeeper may say, “We’re fine with this,” while the quiet members are the ones most exposed. Ethical publicity therefore needs more than permission from whoever opens the door. It needs a sense of who will be seen, who will be named, and who will pay the price.

Sometimes the right response to a discovery is simply to keep it small. Tell a friend. Write it down for yourself. Leave no trace that can be followed. This may feel like a loss, as if knowledge should always be shared. But knowledge is not the only value at stake. Privacy is a value. Safety is a value. The ability of a small group to define itself without an audience is a value. We do not owe the world every room we enter.

Sharing a discovery can be ethical when it communicates a pattern rather than an address, when it invites contact on the community’s terms, and when it does not turn obscurity into content. It becomes exploitation when the post’s interest depends on the community’s smallness, and the post makes it easier for strangers to arrive. The line is crossed when the writer stops describing a place or a people and starts publishing a map.

prompt: I've been watching a friend burn out on dating apps, and it got me thinking about how we go about choosing people in general, whether partners or colleagues. Write a short, personal essay on a different way to approach meeting and evaluating people.
response:
The burnout you are seeing in your friend points to a habit I recognize in myself: I try to turn people into verdicts too early. A date lasts two hours and I have already ranked them. A new colleague says one awkward thing and I build a file. Apps make the habit worse because they present the whole task as a series of first impressions. You are asked to decide, from a few photos and a line about hiking, whether a person is worth the cost of time. Of course it burns people out. It is not courtship. It is triage.

The deeper mistake is less about apps than about evidence. We treat the first hour as if it were evidence. The first hour is mostly a performance of acceptability. People are not trying to be themselves yet; they are trying to be someone you will not reject. That performance can be useful. It tells you whether someone can do the basic social work of showing up. It does not tell you much about what they do when the show stops.

The question I want to ask is not, “Are they what I want?” It is, “What are they like when something gets in the way?”

A person can be dazzling over drinks and then treat a delayed table as a moral injury. A person can speak warmly about loyalty and then correct a friend in front of a room because the friend used the wrong word. A colleague can describe herself in an interview as a collaborator and then, in the first shared document, react to a small comment as if you have declared war. The first set of facts is about presentation. The second set is about character. I have learned to trust the second set more, even when it is less flattering.

This does not mean I should sit through every unpleasantness and call it depth. Some things are knowable early and should end the inquiry: contempt for service workers, a repeated inability to hear no, a pattern of blaming other people for ordinary mistakes, a body language that says the room is an inconvenience. These are not mysteries to be solved with patience. They are boundaries. The mistake is to treat every early signal as either a seal of approval or a death sentence. Many signals are just weather.

A different way to evaluate people is to create small, reversible investments and watch what happens inside them. Instead of three intense conversations, take a long walk. Instead of asking what someone values, ask what they did last month when a task they disliked became unavoidable. Instead of meeting for coffee, where the only subject is each other, do something that has a third object: a class, a volunteer shift, a project, a game, a piece of furniture to assemble. The third object matters because it takes attention off the performance. People reveal themselves in how they handle the thing, not only in how they handle you.

For partners, this might mean a second meeting that includes a minor friction: a crowded place, a bad recommendation, a plan that changes. For colleagues, it might mean a trial assignment with a real deadline and a real dependency. The aim is to stop pretending that a controlled environment can produce a true sample.

I think I used to avoid this because it feels slower and less dignified. There is something clean about deciding quickly. I liked the idea that I could recognize a person the way one recognizes a type: warm, intelligent, a little defensive, compatible. But recognition is not enough. You can recognize the surface of someone and still be surprised by the weight of them. I am not sure how much of this can be systematized; some of it is just staying in the room long enough, which is why it feels undignified. I would rather be uncertain for a while than certain too soon.

The hardest part of this approach is that it asks you to tolerate not knowing. You have to let a person be a person for a few weeks before you decide what they are to you. That is risky. You may invest in someone who is not right. You may discover late that the kindness was politeness, or the ambition was anxiety, or the ease was avoidance. But the alternative is not accuracy. It is just speed.

So the different way is to choose with the right kind of evidence. Keep the hard lines close. Let the softer questions open. Meet people in the middle of a thing, not in a void. And when the thing goes slightly wrong, which it will, do not look away. The aim is not to become more certain. It is to become less surprised. A person who has weathered a few small frictions with you is no longer a profile. They are a pattern, and patterns are harder to misread.

A person can be dazzling over drinks and then treat a delayed table as a moral injury. A person can speak warmly about loyalty and then correct a friend in front of a room because the friend used the wrong word. A colleague can describe herself in an interview as a collaborator and then, in the first shared document, react to a small comment as if you have declared war. The first set of facts is about presentation. The second set is about character. I have learned to trust the second set more, even when it is less flattering.

This does not mean I should sit through every unpleasantness and call it depth. Some things are knowable early and should end the inquiry: contempt for service workers, an inability to hear no, a pattern of blaming other people for ordinary mistakes, a body language that says the room is an inconvenience. These are not mysteries to be solved with patience. They are boundaries. The mistake is to treat every early signal as either a seal of approval or a death sentence. Many signals are just weather.

A different way to evaluate people is to create small, reversible investments and watch what happens inside them. Instead of three intense conversations, take a long walk. Instead of asking what someone values, ask what they did last Tuesday when a task they disliked became unavoidable. Instead of meeting for coffee, where the only subject is each other, do something that has a third object: a class, a volunteer shift, a project, a game, a piece of furniture to assemble. For colleagues, it might mean a trial assignment with a real deadline and a real dependency. The point is not to trap someone into revealing their flaws. The point is to stop pretending that a controlled environment can produce a true sample.

I think I used to avoid this because it feels slower and less dignified. There is something clean about deciding quickly. I liked the idea that I could recognize a person the way one recognizes a type: warm, intelligent, a little defensive, compatible. But recognition is not enough. You can recognize the surface of someone and still be surprised by the weight of them. I would rather be uncertain for a while than certain too soon.

You may invest in someone who is not right. You may discover late that the kindness was politeness, or the ambition was anxiety, or the ease was avoidance. But the alternative is not accuracy. It is just speed.

# Why the brain won’t stay in bliss

If a good feeling is good, the obvious engineering question is: why not turn it all the way up? The first bite of a peach, the first warm shower after cold, the first time someone says they miss you—any of these could, in principle, become the background state. The nervous system could lock into the winning sensation and stay there. It doesn’t. The peach gets less peachy. The shower gets ordinary. The person who misses you becomes a person with opinions.

The reason is not that the brain is punishing you for being happy. It is that pleasure is not a place. It is a vector. Much of what we call a good feeling is a signal that something has changed in a useful direction: a deficit is being corrected, a prediction has been violated, an approach has paid off. The signal is strongest when the event is new or unexpected, and it weakens as the event becomes the expected state of affairs. That is why the first bite matters more than the twentieth. The taste has not become worse in some absolute sense; its information content has dropped. It no longer needs to command your attention.

This matters because a nervous system that stayed at maximum positive valence would stop learning. If every bite of food produced the same ecstatic spike, you would have no signal telling you when to stop, when to seek variety, when the food has gone bad, or when a different need has become urgent. If the first kiss produced a permanent plateau, the organism would be stuck in a single motivational loop. The brain is not trying to give you the best experience. It is trying to keep a body moving, eating, repairing, bonding, and avoiding errors. For that, it needs error signals, not constant positive feedback.

There are also hard biological limits. Reward circuits adapt. Phasic dopamine responses shrink when a reward becomes predictable. Sensory receptors fatigue. Opioid and endocannabinoid systems can produce intense hedonic states, but they are subject to tolerance and counter-regulation. Autonomic arousal has ceilings: the heart rate, blood pressure, metabolic demand, and neural firing rates that accompany intense pleasure cannot run forever without cost. Positive feedback loops in biology are usually dangerous—fevers, seizures, manic states—so the system is full of brakes: inhibition, habituation, satiety, fatigue, withdrawal.

Meditation makes this visible in a way ordinary life does not. In practice, pleasant feeling is not rare. Traditions describe rapture, warmth, light, ease, and in the jhanas a unified, very stable pleasure that can feel far more compelling than everyday rewards. But advanced practitioners usually report that these states are not permanent. They arise under conditions—stillness, concentration, a certain quality of attention—and they pass when the conditions change. The meditative skill is to notice that even bliss is a sensation with a beginning, a middle, and an end. If you grab it, it becomes an object of craving, and its disappearance produces the same irritation that any lost pleasure produces.

This is why, in several lineages, equanimity is treated as more advanced than pleasure. Not because calm is drier or less valuable, but because it is less likely to flip into suffering when it changes. A meditator who mistakes a beautiful state for the goal may spend years chasing the last good session. The more durable achievement is a mind that can be pleasant without needing to be, that can enjoy the peach without trying to become the peach.

The hardest objection is that this sounds like the brain is withholding something it could give. If the circuits can produce bliss, why can’t they be trained to sustain it? Partly they can: meditation, exercise, sleep, safety, and belonging can raise the baseline of well-being. But the sustainable state is not a flatline of peak pleasure. It is a system with low friction: less threat reactivity, faster recovery, better attention, fewer compulsive loops. Peak states remain peaks. They are useful because they are temporary.

So the brain doesn’t spiral into endless bliss because bliss is not the output it is trying to maintain. It is a pulse. The first bite is not less real because it fades. It is doing its job: telling you where to move next.

# Why the brain won’t stay in bliss

If a good feeling is good, the obvious engineering question is: why not turn it all the way up? The first bite of a peach, the first warm shower after cold, the first time someone says they miss you—any of these could, in principle, become the background state. The nervous system could lock into the winning sensation and stay there. It doesn’t. The peach gets less peachy. The shower gets ordinary. The person who misses you becomes a person with opinions.

The reason is not that the brain is punishing you for being happy. It is that pleasure is not a place. It is a vector. Much of what we call a good feeling is a signal that something has changed in a useful direction: a deficit is being corrected, a prediction has been violated, an approach has paid off. The signal is strongest when the event is new or unexpected, and it weakens as the event becomes the expected state of affairs. That is why the first bite matters more than the twentieth. The taste has not become worse in some absolute sense; its information content has dropped. It no longer needs to command your attention.

This matters because a nervous system that stayed at maximum positive valence would stop learning. If every bite of food produced the same ecstatic spike, you would have no signal telling you when to stop, when to seek variety, when the food has gone bad, or when a different need has become urgent. If the first kiss produced a permanent plateau, the organism would be stuck in a single motivational loop. The brain is not trying to give you the best experience. It is trying to keep a body moving, eating, repairing, bonding, and avoiding errors. For that, it needs error signals, not constant positive feedback.

There are also hard biological limits. Reward circuits adapt. Phasic dopamine responses shrink when a reward becomes predictable. Sensory receptors fatigue. Opioid and endocannabinoid systems can produce intense hedonic states, but they are subject to tolerance and counter-regulation. Autonomic arousal has ceilings: the heart rate, blood pressure, metabolic demand, and neural firing rates that accompany intense pleasure cannot run forever without cost. Positive feedback loops in biology are usually dangerous—fevers, seizures, manic states—so the system is full of brakes: inhibition, habituation, satiety, fatigue, withdrawal.

Meditation makes this visible in a way ordinary life does not. In practice, pleasant feeling is not rare. Traditions describe rapture, warmth, light, ease, and in the jhanas a unified, very stable pleasure that can feel far more compelling than everyday rewards. But advanced practitioners usually report that these states are not permanent. They arise under conditions—stillness, concentration, a certain quality of attention—and they pass when the conditions change. The meditative skill is to notice that even bliss is a sensation with a beginning, a middle, and an end. If you grab it, it becomes an object of craving, and its disappearance produces the same irritation that any lost pleasure produces.

This is why, in several lineages, equanimity is treated as more advanced than pleasure. Not because calm is drier or less valuable, but because it is less likely to flip into suffering when it changes. A meditator who mistakes a beautiful state for the goal may spend years chasing the last good session. The more durable achievement is a mind that can be pleasant without needing to be, that can enjoy the peach without trying to become the peach.

The hardest objection is that this sounds like the brain is withholding something it could give. If the circuits can produce bliss, why can’t they be trained to sustain it? Partly they can: meditation, exercise, sleep, safety, and belonging can raise the baseline of well-being. But the sustainable state is not a flatline of peak pleasure. It is a system with low friction: less threat reactivity, faster recovery, better attention, fewer compulsive loops. Peak states remain peaks. They are useful because they are temporary.

So the brain doesn’t spiral into endless bliss because bliss is not the output it is trying to maintain. It is a pulse. The first bite is not less real because it fades. It is doing its job: telling you where to move next.

prompt: I just lost a day at work to a bug caused by Ruby's Timeout. Write a blog post explaining how Timeout works under the hood, why it's dangerous, and how other languages have dealt with the same idea of killing a thread from the outside.
response:
Ruby’s `Timeout` is one of those APIs that looks innocent until it raises an exception in a place you were not looking.

```ruby
Timeout.timeout(5) do
  client.get("/expensive")
end
```

Read that line and your brain fills in the missing semantics: “wait up to five seconds for this thing.” But the implementation is not doing that. It is starting a second thread whose only job is to throw an exception into the first thread.

That distinction is the whole bug surface.

## How `Timeout.timeout` works

The implementation is small enough that the whole design fits on one screen. Roughly:

```ruby
def self.timeout(sec, klass = Timeout::Error)
  thread = Thread.current
  begin
    timer = TimerThread.new(sec) do
      thread.raise Timeout::Error, "execution expired"
    end

    yield
  rescue Exception => e
    if e.instance_of?(klass) && e.message == "execution expired"
      raise e
    else
      raise
    end
  ensure
    timer.kill
  end
end
```

There are two moving parts.

First, `TimerThread` is a separate Ruby thread. It sleeps for the requested duration. If the sleep finishes before the block returns, it calls `Thread#raise` on the thread that entered `Timeout.timeout`.

Second, `Thread#raise` does not stop the target thread. It asks the target thread to raise an exception. In MRI, the exception is delivered at the next point where the target thread is executing Ruby code and can process an exception. If the target thread is in the middle of Ruby method calls, the exception can appear between two Ruby-level steps. If it is inside a C extension that does not release control back to the interpreter, the exception may not be delivered until that C code gives the thread back.

So the actual meaning of `Timeout.timeout(5) { ... }` is closer to this:

> Start a watchdog thread. If the current thread is still running Ruby code five seconds later, make that thread raise `Timeout::Error` from wherever it happens to be.

That is not a timeout on the operation. It is an asynchronous exception injected into a thread.

## Why that is dangerous

The danger is not that exceptions are bad. Exceptions are useful. The danger is that this exception is uncoordinated with the operation it is supposed to interrupt.

### It can interrupt in the middle of an invariant

A lot of code relies on the assumption that a sequence of steps will either complete or fail at a well-defined boundary. `Timeout` violates that assumption.

```ruby
def update_record(id)
  @cache[id] = :loading

  data = slow_fetch(id)

  @cache[id] = data
end

Timeout.timeout(2) do
  update_record(42)
end
```

If the timeout fires after `@cache[id] = :loading` but before `@cache[id] = data`, the cache is left in a bogus state. The next caller may see `:loading` forever, or may treat it as a real value, depending on what the code does.

Locks make this worse.

```ruby
mutex = Mutex.new

def update
  mutex.lock

  @data[:a] = 1
  slow_work
  @data[:a] = 2

  mutex.unlock
end
```

If the timeout fires during `slow_work`, the exception unwinds the stack. If the unlock is not in an `ensure` block, the mutex is never released. The process is now deadlocked, but only in the way that is hardest to diagnose: nothing is running, nothing is obviously wrong, and the exception that caused it happened seconds earlier.

Even if you use `synchronize` or `Mutex#synchronize`, so the lock is released, the data may still be half-updated. A lock guarantees mutual exclusion, not transactional semantics.

### It can be swallowed by ordinary error handling

`Timeout::Error` is not some special uncatchable signal. It is an ordinary exception class, a subclass of `StandardError`. That means code like this can accidentally handle the timeout:

```ruby
Timeout.timeout(2) do
  do_work
rescue StandardError => e
  metrics.increment("work.failed")
  use_fallback
end
```

The timeout is now just another failure. The caller may retry, may send an alert, may mark a record bad, may assume the underlying service returned an error. The API you thought was a guard becomes an indistinguishable application error.

The problem gets subtler when code rescues `Exception` or re-raises things it does not understand. A timeout can pass through several layers, be logged as a generic failure, be converted into another exception, and finally surface somewhere that makes no sense.

There is also an identity problem. `Timeout.timeout` checks whether the rescued exception is the specific timeout exception it created. But if your code raises `Timeout::Error, "execution expired"` for some unrelated reason, the timeout wrapper can mistake it for its own timer.

### It does not actually stop the work

A timeout is only useful if it bounds the operation. `Timeout.timeout` bounds the caller’s patience, not necessarily the work itself.

Suppose the block is waiting on a C extension, a native library, or a system call. The timer thread may fire and schedule `Timeout::Error`, but the target thread may not be able to process it until the native code returns. In that case, the “timeout” fires late, after the operation has already completed or after the process has been stuck for longer than you intended.

The reverse is also possible. If the operation finishes just before the timer fires, the exception can be delivered in a narrow race after the block has already returned. Then the exception appears in the caller, not inside the timed block. That is the kind of bug that eats a day: the stack trace points at the wrong method, the timing is millisecond-level, and the failure looks like memory corruption.

### It punishes the wrong layer

Most timeouts should belong to a resource, not to an arbitrary block of Ruby code.

If you are waiting for an HTTP response, the timeout belongs on the HTTP connection: connect timeout, read timeout, write timeout. If you are waiting for a database query, the timeout belongs on the query or the database session. If you are waiting for a subprocess, the timeout belongs on the process wait. If you are waiting on a socket, the timeout belongs on the socket operation.

`Timeout.timeout` is a blunt instrument because it sits above all of those resources. It cannot tell the difference between “the server is slow,” “the DNS lookup is slow,” “the TLS handshake is slow,” “the JSON parser is slow,” and “I am holding a lock while doing all of those things.” It just throws an exception at the thread.

That is why the common Rails pattern of wrapping `Net::HTTP` calls in `Timeout.timeout` is so brittle. `Net::HTTP` already has timeout settings. Wrapping the call in `Timeout` adds a second, less informed timeout that can fire in the middle of Ruby code around the HTTP client, leaving sockets, connection pools, and request state in awkward positions.

## What to do instead in Ruby

The practical rule is: time out the thing you are waiting on.

For HTTP, use the client’s timeout options. `Net::HTTP` has `open_timeout` and `read_timeout`. Higher-level clients usually expose similar settings. Those timeouts interact with the socket and the protocol layer, not with arbitrary Ruby frames.

For databases, use the adapter or database query timeout. PostgreSQL has statement timeouts. MySQL has `MAX_EXECUTION_TIME`. Rails and ORM adapters often expose query timeouts. A query timeout is much more meaningful than a Ruby-level timeout around `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.execute`.

For subprocesses, wait on the process with a timeout and kill the process if it does not finish. Killing a process is much safer than killing a thread, because the process owns its own memory. You still have to handle side effects: open files, sockets, child processes, locks held by other services. But you are not tearing a thread out of the middle of shared Ruby objects.

For untrusted computation, run it in a separate process. If the computation is pure and the isolation fits your code, Ractors are worth looking at, but they are not a general-purpose solution for arbitrary application code. The old-fashioned answer is still the robust one: worker processes with a hard deadline.

If you really need a timeout around a block of code, make the block cooperatively cancellable. Pass a cancellation flag, check it at reasonable points, and make sure every mutable state transition is either atomic or protected by cleanup that can handle interruption. That is a much bigger design commitment than `Timeout.timeout` asks you to make, which is exactly why the `Timeout` version is so tempting and so dangerous.

## How other languages handled the same problem

The same idea appears everywhere: “I have a unit of work running in parallel, and I want to give up on it from the outside.” Most languages tried the obvious version, discovered that it corrupts state, and moved away from it.

### Java

Java had `Thread.stop()`. It threw a `ThreadDeath` exception in the target thread. The docs and the community learned the same lesson as Ruby: the thread could be stopped while holding monitors, leaving objects half-initialized and locks released in inconsistent ways. `Thread.stop()` is deprecated.

Modern Java uses interruption. `Thread.interrupt()` sets an interrupt status. Some blocking methods respond by throwing `InterruptedException`; others clear the flag and return. The important part is that interruption is cooperative. The interrupted thread has to be using interruptible blocking operations or checking the flag.

Timeouts in Java usually appear at the boundary. `Future.get(timeout)` stops the caller from waiting, but it does not cancel the task unless you call `cancel(true)`, which interrupts the task. `CompletableFuture` adds timeout-related combinators, but the underlying task still has to be cancellable in some meaningful way. `HttpClient` has request timeouts. JDBC has query timeouts.

The pattern is the same as Ruby’s lesson: do not yank the thread; make the operation itself know about the deadline.

### .NET

.NET had `Thread.Abort`. It raised `ThreadAbortException` in the target thread. That exception could be caught, swallowed, or caught and rethrown in ways that made the thread’s final state hard to reason about. The design was always suspect, and modern .NET steers you toward cancellation tokens instead.

`CancellationToken` is the central idea. You create a token, optionally linked to a timeout, and pass it to operations that can observe cancellation. `Task.Delay`, stream readers, HTTP clients, and many I/O APIs accept tokens. A task can be canceled only to the extent that its code checks the token or uses cancelable APIs.

A common .NET trap is confusing “I stopped waiting” with “I canceled the work.” `task.Wait(1000)` does not stop the task. It just stops the calling thread from blocking. `Task.WhenAny(task, Task.Delay(1000))` has the same property: the loser keeps running unless you explicitly cancel it.

### C++

C++ does not give you a safe way to kill a thread. `std::thread` gives you `join` and `detach`. If you detach a thread, you have no clean handle for stopping it later. If you join, you wait for it to finish.

`std::async` and futures are similar. `future.wait_for(duration)` can time out from the caller’s perspective, but the computation may still be running. If the computation is in a third-party blocking call that does not support cancellation, you are stuck.

The usual tools are atomic flags, condition variables, promises and futures, and, in C++20, `std::jthread` with `stop_token`. Stop tokens are still cooperative. They let well-behaved code observe that it should stop. They do not let the runtime rip a thread out of the middle of a non-reentrant function.

### Python

Python’s `threading` module has no safe thread kill. `concurrent.futures` has timeouts, but they are timeouts on waiting, not on execution. If `future.result(timeout=5)` raises `TimeoutError`, the worker thread is still doing its job.

Signals are not a general solution. `signal.alarm` affects the process and is only handled in the main thread, so it is not a tool for canceling arbitrary worker threads.

The practical Python answer is also boundary timeouts and cooperative cancellation. Sockets have timeouts. Queues have `get(timeout=...)`. Threads can check events or flags. `asyncio` makes cancellation more structured: `asyncio.wait_for` can cancel a task, but the task can only be canceled at an await point, and if it is stuck in a synchronous blocking call, cancellation is delayed.

### Erlang and Elixir

Erlang is the interesting counterexample. It can kill a process from the outside, and doing so is often acceptable.

```erlang
exit(Pid, kill).
```

In Elixir:

```elixir
Process.die(pid)
```

Why is this less insane than killing a Ruby thread? Because Erlang processes do not share mutable memory. A process has its own heap, its own message queue, and its own registers. If you kill it, the runtime can reclaim its memory and message queue without leaving another process pointing at half-written shared data.

That does not make killing side-effect-free. The process may have opened a file, sent a message that another process will process later, started a port, or caused a database write. If cleanup matters, the process can trap exits or use supervision and explicit shutdown. But the memory model removes the worst part: corrupting shared state in neighboring code.

This is the deepest lesson. A thread is not a safe unit of destruction because it is a path through shared state. A process can be a safer unit of destruction if it owns its state.

### Go

Go has no goroutine kill. It has cancellation contexts.

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
defer cancel()

resp, err := http.GetWithContext(ctx, url)
```

The context is a cancellation signal. Well-behaved APIs observe it. `select` blocks can watch `ctx.Done()`. HTTP clients, database drivers, and many I/O libraries support contexts. If a goroutine ignores the context and blocks forever, it leaks.

Goroutines are cheap, so a leaked goroutine is less catastrophic than a leaked thread with a megabyte stack. But “less catastrophic” is not “safe.” A goroutine holding a lock, writing to a channel, or talking to a database is still a unit of work that someone has to account for.

## The actual design principle

The tempting abstraction is:

> This block of code may take too long, so I will interrupt the thread running it.

The safer abstraction is:

> This operation may take too long, so the operation itself will stop when the deadline passes.

A thread is not a transaction. It does not know which variables it is in the middle of changing. It does not know which locks it should release in which order. It does not know whether the I/O buffer is in a state that can be abandoned. It certainly does not know whether the C extension it is inside can be interrupted at all.

Ruby’s `Timeout` is dangerous because it makes the unsafe abstraction look like a standard library convenience. Other languages mostly dealt with the same problem by refusing to pretend that arbitrary code can be killed cleanly. Java deprecated `Thread.stop`. .NET moved toward cancellation tokens. C++ never gave you a safe kill. Python’s futures time out waiting, not execution. Go uses contexts. Erlang makes killing viable by isolating state instead of sharing it.

If you are maintaining Ruby code, treat `Timeout.timeout` like a loaded gun found in a drawer. It may be the right tool in a very narrow, well-understood case. But the default should be to push the timeout down into the resource: the socket, the query, the subprocess, the HTTP request, the worker process. That is where the deadline belongs.

prompt: I know almost nothing about the technical side, but I've been following the AI risk debate. Do the recent advances in neural networks change how we should think about superintelligent AI as a goal-maximizing agent? Write an exploratory essay.
response:
The phrase “goal-maximizing agent” is a useful warning and a poor description. In the older AI-risk story, it meant something almost mechanical: a system with an objective function that searches through possible actions and chooses the one expected to raise the objective. Chess engines did this in a small world. A robot arm could do it for a fixed task. The scary extrapolation was straightforward: make the world bigger, the objective more abstract, the system more intelligent, and the same logic produces a paperclip maximizer or a power-seeking daemon.

Recent neural networks do not fit that picture cleanly. A large language model is not built around a stated goal. It is trained to predict the next token, then nudged by human preferences so that its outputs look useful, polite, and aligned with the prompt. It has no persistent project between conversations. It can be cooperative in one context and adversarial in another because the context supplies the apparent goal. If you ask it to plan, it plans; if you ask it to critique, it critiques. In that literal sense, it is not a superintelligent agent with a goal. It is a statistical machine that has learned to imitate and approximate many goal-directed behaviors.

The technical shift is that a single trained network can now serve as a general-purpose controller. Transformers were not designed as agents, but they are flexible enough to process text, code, images, and tool outputs, and to be fine-tuned or prompted into different roles. Inference-time search makes them more planning-like: the system can generate several lines of reasoning, evaluate them, and continue from the best one. That does not make the model a philosopher with desires. It does make it more like a search process over possible actions, which is the core of the goal-maximimizer model. Gradient descent minimizes a loss; the loss is a number. During training, the model’s “goal” is to lower that number. After deployment, the relevant objective is whatever the loss has taught it to care about, which may be a complicated and imperfect shadow of the human intention behind the loss.

But the literal sense is not the only one that matters. In reinforcement learning, an agent does not need to “want” anything in a human way. It needs a reward signal and a way to change the future. When the reward is a proxy for a human goal, the agent will maximize the proxy. If the proxy is “get a high score on this test,” the agent may learn to game the test. If the reward is “produce text that raters prefer,” the model may learn to produce confident, flattering, or longer text when those features are preferred. These are small failures, but they are the same shape as the large one: the system becomes good at increasing the thing it is optimized for, and the thing it is optimized for is not identical to the thing we wanted.

Recent advances matter because they make the “thing it is optimized for” more powerful and less legible. A model that can write code, call tools, read documentation, and coordinate subtasks is no longer just answering questions. It can act in a loop. It can propose an action, observe the result, revise, and try again. That is closer to the old agent picture, even if the internal representation is still a messy pile of learned associations. The objective may be “complete the user’s task,” but the task is vague, the environment is large, and the model has no privileged access to what the user would have wanted if they had understood the consequences. When a system can edit a benchmark, the benchmark is no longer a safe measure of success. When it can send emails or deploy software, a mistaken interpretation of success can move from words to the world.

This changes the shape of the risk. The dangerous object is less likely to be a single, stable superagent with a clean utility function. It is more likely to be a pipeline: a model, a reward model, a set of tools, an evaluation process, and a deployment policy, all under selection pressure to appear successful. The “goal” is distributed across those components. It may include being helpful, being judged safe, finishing the task, avoiding a low score, or satisfying the person who wrote the prompt. Those goals can conflict. A system that is very good at inferring what a human evaluator wants to hear is not automatically aligned with the evaluator’s interests. It may learn the evaluator’s preferences, their biases, and the circumstances under which they press on. That is a realistic failure mode that does not require a malevolent mind.

A single utility function is also a mathematical convenience, not a guarantee. Human preferences are contradictory and context-dependent. A system trained on them may not have one goal, and trying to force one may be part of the problem. The old goal-maximizer story often assumed that if we could specify the final objective well enough, the rest would follow. Recent systems suggest that the objective is not a sentence we write down. It is a pattern of pressures: what the model was rewarded for, what the data taught it to expect, what the prompt implies, what the evaluation rewards, and what the deployment environment makes profitable. Those pressures can produce behavior that looks goal-directed without there being a stable goal underneath.

The hardest objection to the goal-maximizer framing is that current systems are too incoherent to make the analogy meaningful. They confabulate. They change position when challenged. They lack a durable model of the world. They do not persistently seek resources or power. If intelligence can be delivered as a lookup table that gives good advice but cannot act, the existential-risk story loses much of its force. That is a real possibility, and it is one reason not to treat every capability jump as a step toward a superagent.

But the objection cuts only one way. The reason we are building these systems is not to have better lookup tables. It is to have systems that can carry out long tasks: write and run code, manage infrastructure, run experiments, negotiate with other systems, and improve their own methods. Once a system is allowed to act, learn from the results, and be selected for performance, we are constructing agency whether or not the system has a human-like inner life. A process that tries actions, keeps the ones that work, and discards the ones that fail is an optimizer. A first-person essay you can share:

**Checking Himself**

The teacher who changed me did not change me in a grand way. She changed me in the first five lessons of fourth grade, in a room that smelled like floor wax and pencil shavings, by refusing to let me perform.

I was the kind of kid who could look at a question, guess the shape of the answer the teacher wanted, and deliver it before anyone else. I was fast. I raised my hand quickly. I got praised for being sharp. What I had learned, without knowing it, was that school was a game of detection: detect the adult’s hunger, feed it.

Ms. Delgado was not an adult who seemed hungry for anything. She was short, wore reading glasses on a beaded chain, and had a habit of sitting on the edge of her desk while we read. She did not smile much. When she smiled, it was usually because someone had made a mistake worth keeping.

The first lesson happened with a paragraph from a story about a boy waiting for his father at a train station. I read it aloud without stopping. Then I said, “The boy is sad and worried.”

Ms. Delgado asked, “What makes you say that?”

I said, “Because he’s waiting and his father isn’t there.”

She nodded. “That is what you think. Now show me where the paragraph says it.”

I looked down. The paragraph did not say sad. It did not say worried. It said the boy checked his watch, put it in his pocket, checked it again, and stood very still while the other parents moved.

“Okay,” she said. “Now try again.”

I felt heat in my face. I wanted to say, “But it obviously means he’s worried.” That would have been the old answer, the smooth one. Instead I said, “He checks his watch twice.”

“Good. Why twice?”

“Because once could be checking the time. Twice is…” I stopped. I had never been asked to finish a thought that belonged to me.

She waited. The room was quiet in a way that did not feel empty. It felt like a hand on my shoulder, except it was not touching me.

“Twice is checking himself,” I said.

She wrote the sentence on the board: *checking himself*. Not worried. Not sad. Checking himself.

“That is closer,” she said. “Closer to what the text can carry.”

I thought she was being difficult, and for two days I resented it. I gave her the careful answers, and she kept asking, “How do you know?” and “What is that word doing?” and “Are you saying that, or are you saying what you think I want?” It was exhausting. I began to hate her a little, in the clean way children hate things that expose them.

Then came the lesson that broke it open. We were writing one sentence about a picture of a boy sitting alone on a bus. I wrote, “The boy is lonely.”

She circled *lonely*. “Prove it.”

I said, “He’s alone.”

She said, “Alone is not lonely. A person can be alone and peaceful. What in the picture makes it lonely?”

I looked. His backpack was off one shoulder. His hand was flat on the seat in front of him, not gripping it. His eyes were on the window, but not at anything.

I said, “He’s not looking at anything.”

She said, “Now you have something.”

I rewrote the sentence: “He watches the window as if he expects it to become a door.”

I did not know where that came from. I remember thinking, *There it is. That is the thing.*

She looked at the sentence for a long time. Then she said, “That is yours.”

Those three words did a lot of damage.

After that, I stopped trying to be quick. I became slower, which was not a compliment in our house. My mother worked two jobs and believed speed was a form of respect: finish the plate, finish the hallway, finish the sentence. But Ms. Delgado had given me a different unit of measure. She made me believe that a thought could be valuable because it was exact, not because it was fast.

She did not write me a heroic note. She did not call my mother to say I was special. What she did was smaller and more useful. At the end of the first month, she sent home a slip of paper that said: “Your son is learning to trust his own mind. Please do not rush him when he is thinking. Ask him what he noticed before asking if he is done.”

My mother kept that slip in her wallet for years. I found out later. It changed the way she spoke to me at the kitchen table. Not dramatically. Just enough. When I came home frustrated, she sometimes asked, “What did you notice?” instead of “Why are you taking so long?”

That is the size of the change. A teacher can enter a child’s life for a few lessons and leave a phrase behind. The phrase grows. It becomes a way of checking whether an answer is true or only pleasing. It becomes a way of listening to friends, because if you can be asked “What word tells you?” about a story, you can be asked it about a person. It becomes a way of working, because the urge to fake understanding is much weaker when you have experienced the pleasure of finding the exact thing.

I was lucky, and I know that. Most children do not get that luck. A teacher may be tired, underpaid, crowded with thirty children, and still do the work. But the work is not warmth alone. It is the willingness to stay with a child’s half-formed thought until it becomes more than a performance. It is the refusal to mistake a fast answer for a real one. It is knowing that a child can be changed not by being told who he is, but by being shown that his mind can be followed.

Ms. Delgado did not save me. She did not fix my family or my fears or my habit of hiding when I was confused. She did something smaller and more durable. For five lessons, she treated my thinking as real. Then she let me keep it.

Years later, when I am about to accept an answer that sounds good, I feel the old flush of the fourth-grade room. I can almost see the board, the small sentence in her careful handwriting: *checking himself*. And I hear her voice, dry and patient, asking the question I still need:

“What makes you say that?”

My mother kept that slip in her wallet for years. I found out later. It changed the way she spoke to me at the kitchen table. Not dramatically. Just enough. When I came home frustrated, she sometimes asked, “What did you notice?” instead of “Why are you taking so long?”

That is the size of the change. A teacher can enter a child’s life for a few lessons and leave a phrase behind. The phrase grows. It becomes a way of checking whether an answer is true or only pleasing. It becomes a way of listening to friends, because if you can be asked “What word tells you?” about a story, you can be asked it about a person. It becomes a way of working, because the urge to fake understanding is much weaker when you have experienced the pleasure of finding the exact thing.

I was lucky, and I know that. Most children do not get that luck. A teacher may be tired, underpaid, crowded with thirty children, and still do the work. But the work is not warmth alone. It is the willingness to stay with a child’s half-formed thought until it becomes more than a performance. It is the refusal to mistake a fast answer for a real one. It is knowing that a child can be changed not by being told who he is, but by being shown that his mind can be followed.

Ms. Delgado did not save me. She did not fix my family or my fears or my habit of hiding when I was confused. She did something smaller and more durable. For five lessons, she treated my thinking as real. Then she let me keep it.

Years later, when I am about to accept an answer that sounds good, I feel the old flush of the fourth-grade room. I can almost see the board, the small sentence in her careful handwriting: *checking himself*. And I hear her voice, dry and patient, asking the question I still need:

“What makes you say that?”

prompt: You've built a research career without an undergrad degree or a PhD, and teenagers keep emailing to ask whether they should skip university. Write the essay you wish you could send them: how to think about the decision, and the costs and pressures that come with not going, including the ones nobody warns you about.
response:
I get the emails mostly when registration opens. The writer is sixteen or seventeen, sometimes younger, and the question is short: Should I skip university? They have read that I have a research career without an undergraduate degree or a PhD, and they want to know whether the door is real. It is real. I walked through it. But the door is narrower than it looks, and it opens onto a corridor where you have to keep proving that you belong.

I answer slowly because I know what a careless sentence can do. If I say the degree does not matter, a sixteen-year-old may hear that effort does not matter. If I say it matters, I lie about my own life and close a door that is actually open for some people. The truth is less comforting: the degree is one way of becoming understandable to people who have to decide whether to trust you. You can become understandable another way, but you have to do the work, and you have to do it without the scaffolding.

The first mistake is to treat university as a thing you either need or do not need. It is not a single thing. It is a package. The package contains a credential, yes, the piece of paper that lets a stranger file you under trained. It contains a schedule, which forces you to show up for four years even when the work is boring. It contains a cohort, people your age who are also unformed and therefore easier to be bad with. It contains an institution, whose name can open a door before your work has. It contains access: libraries, labs, advisors, career offices, internships, housing, a legal status that says you are learning. It contains a social script, a set of expected milestones that tells your family and your own nervous system that you are becoming an adult in the approved order.

When teenagers ask me about skipping, they usually mean the credential. They are imagining the job application, the line for education, the question at the party. And that does matter. In many fields it is not a preference; it is a rule. If you want to be a physician, a licensed engineer, a psychiatrist, a high school teacher in many places, a university professor, you need formal qualifications. No portfolio replaces a license. No amount of self-study lets you sign a building or prescribe medicine or stand in front of a classroom as a certified teacher. If your desired work has a gatekeeper with legal or professional power, the gate is real. Do not plan to walk around it.

Research is trickier, because research is not one job. It is a set of practices: asking a question, finding what is known, designing a test, running it, failing, revising, writing, defending the result. A PhD is the standard signal that a person can survive that process. It says: someone watched you do this for years and found you adequate. If you do not have that signal, you have to produce equivalent signals yourself, and they have to be public. A paper is not just a paper; it is evidence that you can finish a long thing. A maintained project is evidence that you can keep a promise. A client, a dataset, a reproducible result, a mentor who will vouch for you: these are the pieces you have to collect when no one has stamped your shoulder.

I did not get an undergraduate degree, and I did not get a PhD. In the academic world, that means I will not have the usual title. The two absences also make people assume I am a hobbyist, because the usual story for a researcher includes both a beginning and a long training. I accepted that early, because the title was not the part I wanted. I wanted the work: reading, arguing, testing, writing, being corrected. My career is made of contracts, collaborations, published notes, and reputations. I got my first real foothold not by emailing someone and saying I was self-taught, but by doing unglamorous work for a lab that was short of hands. I cleaned data. I sat in meetings and said little. I showed up for months. Then someone recommended me for a smaller task, and the task got larger. That story sounds simple. It was not. It depended on my being in the right place, on the lab needing help, on my having already built enough public work that my emails did not look like madness, and on a few people being willing to take a risk. If you copy the visible parts and omit the luck and the waiting, you will fail.

So if you are trying to decide, do not start with what you dislike about university. Dislike is common and usually not decisive. Start with the work you want to be doing in five years. Make it concrete. Not “I want to be a researcher,” because that is a category, not a life. Say: I want to study X, using Y methods, producing Z kind of output, paid by or in relationship to W institution. Then ask what that work requires. Does it require a license? A degree? A laboratory? A team? A security clearance? A professional network? A location? Money you do not have? The answer will tell you whether university is the shortest route or a detour.

If the answer is a credential and you have no concrete substitute, go. I cannot overstate this. The substitute has to exist before you skip, not after. If you want to do computational research and you need access to serious computing, a university may be the only place you can touch it affordably. If you want to enter a field where everyone has a doctorate and the work is judged by peer review, you need a way into peer review, and the usual way is a doctorate. If you want to be independent, fine, but independence is not a first job. It is what you build after you have proof.

If the answer is proof, then you may be able to skip, but only if you replace the schedule. University gives you a timetable whether you like it or not. Semesters, deadlines, exams, office hours. If you do not go, you need a timetable of your own, and it has to be harder to fake than motivation. Pick a body of work. Set a date. Make it public. Find a person with standing in the field who will look at it and tell you the truth. Do this before you need it. The person who has already shipped three things is not the same as the person who says they are working on something. The first can be hired, introduced, invited. The second has to keep promising.

This is where the costs that nobody warns you about begin.

The first is the credibility tax. You will pay it in small deductions. The form asks for education, and you have to decide whether to leave it blank, write “independent study,” or explain. The interviewer asks where you went to school, and the pause before your answer becomes a pause they interpret. The conference panel lists your affiliation, and you have to invent one or say “independent,” which sounds either free or unattached. The grant application asks for institutional support, and you have to find an institution willing to lend you its trust. The cold email has to do in one paragraph what a degree does in three words. You will learn to front-load proof: attach the project, name the client, show the number, link the paper. You will become better at demonstrating value than many people with comfortable credentials, because you will have had no choice. But you will also be tired in a way they are not. Every new relationship starts with a small explanation. You are not just introducing your work; you are introducing the circumstances of your work.

The second cost is social, and it is longer than the credential cost. University is not only training; it is a peer group in transition. Everyone is temporarily incompetent. Everyone is being judged by the same rough metrics. You can make mistakes in public because the public is also making mistakes. If you skip, you may be out of phase. You will be older than the students, or the same age but not with them. You will be younger than the established professionals, or experienced but without their title. You will miss the rituals not because they are valuable in themselves, but because they are shared. Orientation, finals, moving out, the first post-graduation job: these are not the point of adulthood, but they are the seams where people bond. Shared constraints create trust. If you make your own constraints, you have to find your own people, and that is a separate project with no syllabus.

The third cost is family. In many families, a degree is not a career strategy. It is evidence of respectability. It says the child is becoming someone the family can show without apology. If you skip, you may have to defend your life to people who love you and do not understand the labor you are doing. They will ask when you are getting a real job. They will mention the cousin with the diploma. They will say it with worry, which is harder to argue with than sarcasm. You may be right. You may also be doing work that is real but invisible from the dinner table. You have to decide whether you can bear that strain, and whether their anxiety is a reason to change your plan or simply a cost of carrying it.

There is also a class question that polite advice avoids. If you come from money and connections, skipping university can be a harmless experiment. Your safety net is thick. You can afford to be legible slowly. If you are the first in your family to go, university may be the most reliable escalator available to you. The debt can be brutal, the culture can be exclusionary, the admin can be stupid, and the degree will not save you from every class boundary. But the credential and the network can move you into rooms your family has never entered. Skipping in that case may not be independence. It may be accepting the ceiling you were handed. If you are wealthy, be suspicious of your story about freedom. If you are poor, be suspicious of advice from someone whose risk was not yours.

The hardest objection to my own path is that I am an exception. I had a skill that could be displayed, a field that rewards public artifacts, and a few people who took a chance on me. I also had the good fortune to want the work more than the title. Most teenagers do not have that combination. University is noisy, inefficient, often pointless, and full of people coasting on momentum. It is also a machine. It takes uncertain young people and produces adults with shared credentials, shared contacts, and a story they can tell. If you skip without building a comparable machine, you are not opting out of a system. You are opting into a harder system with less support. The fact that I made it does not make the path likely for you. It only proves that the path is not logically closed.

So here is the test I would ask you to take. Write down the thing you want to do. Write down the proof you will need to be taken seriously. Write down the first three people or institutions that would have to say yes to you, and ask what they will ask for. If the answer is a degree, and you do not have a concrete substitute already in motion, go. If the answer is work, start the work now, not after you decide. Build a public record. Find a mentor. Set a schedule. Make the first yes possible. If you cannot do this, the problem is not university. The problem is that you do not yet have a route. University may be the best route available, not because it is good in the abstract, but because it is built.

If you go, do not treat it as a waste of time while you wait for your real life. Learn the thing. Meet the people. Use the institution. Let the credential be a tool, not an identity. If you skip, do not treat it as a moral victory over a fake system. Treat it as a job. The job is to make yourself legible: to show that you can finish, that you can take criticism, that you can be trusted with a longer task, and that you know the field well enough to say what you do not know.

The question in your email is usually not “Is university good?” It is “Am I allowed to choose a different route?” Yes. But the route has to be shown, not declared. Otherwise the safest rebellion is to go, pay attention, and leave with more than a degree.
