prompt: I sell my small software product both as a downloadable desktop app and as a web app. Is it actually worth keeping the desktop version around?
response:
Probably not, unless the desktop version is doing a different job for a segment of customers who pay for that difference. For a small product, the default should be one product. A desktop app is not a second window; it is a second product: installers, OS versions, code signing, auto-updates, local file permissions, antivirus false positives, users who never update, and a support queue that says “works on my machine” in ways web tickets rarely do. If you are one person or a tiny team, that second product is where the schedule goes to die.

Put a number on it. Say maintaining desktop takes six hours a week: packaging, update bugs, OS regressions, answering version-specific questions. If your time is worth $50 an hour, that is about $1,200 a month. If the desktop version serves 100 paying customers at $10 a month, it brings in $1,000 before support. If those customers also generate more tickets than web users, the desktop version is not a revenue line; it is a cost center wearing a revenue line’s clothes. The threshold changes with your pricing and team, but the arithmetic is unforgiving.

Desktop earns its place when the job is local. Batch-processing files on disk, reading a database, watching folders, working offline, using global hotkeys, running in the background, keeping sensitive data off your server: these are real advantages. A tool for converting local video, analyzing code repositories, migrating files, or handling private documents may be primarily a desktop product. A shared project board, simple converter, content tool, or anything centered on an account is usually better as a web product. If the desktop app is mostly an icon that opens the same web experience, ask what the icon buys. If the answer is offline access and a launcher, an installable web app may cover enough.

Browsers have gotten better at local work. They can store data, request file access, use hardware security keys, and be installed. They still cannot do everything a native app can: arbitrary filesystem access, reliable background processing, system tray behavior, global shortcuts, deep OS integration, and some performance paths. But those capabilities matter only if your users need them. Do not carry a native client because it could do things; carry it because customers leave without them.

The strongest argument for keeping desktop is that desktop users are more serious. They downloaded an installer, maybe paid a one-time price, and they stay. That can be true. A small, loyal cohort can still be a bad business if it consumes disproportionate support. Ten percent of revenue that causes thirty percent of tickets is a tax. The relevant comparison is not web users versus no users; it is the incremental profit from desktop users versus the engineering hours they require. If desktop users have lower churn and higher lifetime value, the case improves. If they are just harder to serve, the case weakens.

If the desktop version is sold as a one-time license, be even stricter. You are selling perpetual support. The customer may keep using an old version for years, and you will still field questions about it. A subscription desktop client is easier to justify because the revenue continues while you maintain it. A one-time desktop client is a separate product with a long tail, and small companies often discover they are supporting software they no longer control.

I do not know your metrics, so I cannot say yes or no for your product. The way to find out is to stop pretending desktop and web are equal citizens. Freeze new desktop features. Keep security fixes, crash repairs, and critical bug fixes. Tell users that new capabilities will appear in the web app first. Then measure for a quarter. Compare cohorts: revenue per user, renewal or repeat purchase, support tickets, time to first value, and the reason people say they need desktop. If desktop is twenty percent of revenue and ten percent of effort, keep it. If it is ten percent of revenue and thirty percent of effort, retire it. If a meaningful group leaves because they need offline files or local privacy, you have found a real niche. If they leave because they wanted an icon, you have saved yourself a second product.

The middle path is often right: maintenance mode. A stable desktop app that receives fixes but no new features can preserve a useful segment without dragging the roadmap. That is better than either pretending desktop is a peer or deleting it abruptly. The practical test is simple: if you cannot explain in one sentence what the desktop version does that the web app does not, and the customers who want it do not clearly pay for that difference, let it stop growing.

prompt: honest question: why do you think so few women want to join early-stage startups?
response:
I don’t think the main reason is that women are less ambitious, less hungry, or less willing to take risk in some global sense. I think early-stage startups, as they are usually run, are a worse expected-value package for many women than they are for many men.

The first thing to qualify is the premise. If you include all small businesses, women are a large share of owners and employees. The striking gap is in venture-backed, high-growth, often software-heavy startups, especially in founder teams, technical roles, and senior operating roles. That is a specific world, not “work” in general.

And “want” is doing a lot of work in your question. People do not choose careers from a list of abstract preferences. They choose among offers, with incomplete information, under constraints, based on networks and signals. A woman who says no to an early startup may not be rejecting startups. She may be rejecting a specific package: lower cash, uncertain equity, long hours, a founder she has never met, a team with no parental policy, and a role whose scope is unclear.

Early-stage startups are not just jobs. They are risk bundles. They ask you to accept a lower probability of success, less predictable income, more ambiguity, more concentrated power, and less institutional support. For anyone, that is a high-variance bet. The question is why the bet is priced differently for different people.

A concrete example helps. Suppose a Series A startup offers a product manager $160k base, no bonus, and 0.2% equity. The comparable role at an established company pays $200k plus RSUs and has a clearer career path. Four years later, if the startup is acquired for $200M, the 0.2% may have been diluted to 0.1%, worth $200k before tax. If the company dies, the equity is zero and she has forgone well over $160k in cash. The upside is real, but it is not automatically life-changing. The mission, the team, or the network has to be strong just to make the risk worth it. If the startup is pre-seed, the equity slice may be larger, but the probability of success is lower and the pay cut may be bigger.

That calculation is not gendered. The gendered part is that the downside is not equally expensive for everyone. Women, on average, have less accumulated wealth, are more often the primary caregivers, and face a larger penalty for career gaps. A failed startup is a resume line for everyone, but if the person also had to absorb childcare costs, has less savings, or is trying to re-enter after a break, the same failure changes the next offer. Risk tolerance is not just personality. It is balance sheet.

Then there is information. Early-stage jobs are often not posted. They are filled by founders calling friends, alumni, engineers they trust, people from previous companies, people their investors know. If you are inside that network, you get the offer. If you are not, you may never see the role. Startups also inherit the gender composition of the fields they hire from. A lot of early-stage startups are software companies, and software has a gender gap that predates the startup. A male founder hiring his first product person may unconsciously look for someone who feels like the team: same humor, same references, same tolerance for chaos, same willingness to work late. That is not usually conscious exclusion. It is pattern matching. But pattern matching on a homogeneous sample produces a homogeneous team.

Culture matters more at early stage than at big companies, because there is less structure to absorb it. A 30-person startup has no real HR function. The founder is the culture. If the founder works late, the team works late. If meetings are aggressive, the team is aggressive. If there is no parental leave, there is no parental leave. For someone with caregiving responsibilities, those are not minor preferences; they are daily logistics.

There is also a safety calculation. In a small team, a bad manager is not a department you can avoid. The founder may be the only manager. Harassment, intimidation, or a toxic “grind” culture is harder to verify and harder to leave. Even if the probability of a bad actor is low, the cost of being stuck is high. People who have been through bad workplaces are often very good at reading early signals, and many early startups send signals that would make a cautious person say no.

Evaluation is another issue. Early-stage work is ambiguous. There is no job description, no promotion committee, no clear precedent. You have to make your value visible. There is a long-running pattern in which women are penalized more than men for the same self-promotion and rewarded less for the same assertiveness. If the first engineer is a man, later women engineers are compared to him. If the first growth marketer is a man, the role becomes coded that way. Being the only woman also creates a weird tax: you may be expected to represent all women while still being judged as an individual.

This creates a loop. Fewer women in early teams means fewer women become the operators, engineers, and investors who later recruit, fund, and vouch for other women. The startup world then looks, feels, and talks like a place where few women are. That is not evidence that few women want it. It is evidence that the place was built by a narrow set of people and keeps hiring from the same set.

The hardest objection to all this is that it may be a story about offers, not desires. If you gave women the same information, the same equity, the same pay, the same safe team, and the same network, maybe the gap would shrink dramatically. I think that is partly true. We do not have a clean experiment. I am less confident about the size of the residual preference gap after controlling for offers, stage, country, family status, and field. What I am confident about is that “want” is revealed under constraints. If a woman has not been recruited by a founder she trusts, has been offered a pay cut for a small equity slice, has heard that the company has no leave policy, and has no sponsor inside the company, her “no” is a rational response to that package. Calling it a preference can make the founder feel she simply is not hungry enough.

Also, “women” is too broad a category. A 24-year-old woman with high savings and no dependents may take a bigger risk than a 45-year-old man with a mortgage. A woman in a later-stage startup with revenue and a product may say yes where she would say no to a pre-revenue all-hands role. The average hides the fact that the relevant variables are often the specific offer and the specific person’s life, not gender alone.

What changes the calculation is concrete. Women join startups when the role is real, the pay is fair, the equity is meaningful, the founder is competent and safe, the team includes people they can talk to, the hours are human, and the career path is legible. They also join when the mission is strong enough to offset the risk. The fact that these conditions are not automatic is the point. Early-stage risk is often taken by people who can afford it, and the narrative calls that boldness.

So the honest answer is not that women want startups less. It is that many early-stage startups are a high-variance, low-information, high-power-concentration bet, and the costs of that bet are distributed unevenly. If a founder asks why so few women want to join, the useful next question is: what exactly am I offering, who am I asking, and what would have to be true for a smart woman to say yes without having to take a leap of faith?

prompt: You run an accelerator that picks companies after a short interview. Why do funding rounds take months to close, and does it really have to be that way?
response:
A short interview can tell you whether a founder is sharp, coachable, and likely to execute. It cannot tell you whether the business will survive the next 18 months. A funding round is not just a selection event; it is a transfer of a large, illiquid sum into a company with incomplete information and new control rights. The months are mostly the time needed to turn a good impression into a defensible bet.

There are three separate delays in a round: deciding, negotiating, and paying. The decision phase is diligence. The negotiating phase is terms, valuation, board seats, pro rata rights, information rights, drag-along, liquidation preference, and the legal documents that put all of that into enforceable form. The paying phase is signatures, board approvals, wire transfers, and sometimes tranched closings. People say “the round took four months” when really it was three different processes stacked together.

Diligence is real, even at early stage. Suppose a founder has 40 customers, $15,000 of monthly revenue, and a strong demo. Your interview can tell you if the founder will listen. It cannot tell you whether two of those customers are friends of the founder, whether the code lives in one person’s laptop, whether the cap table has an old angel with a 3x liquidation preference, or whether the main client can cancel in 30 days. A $2,000,000 investor needs those answers because the downside is large and the position will be held for years. The accelerator can afford to be wrong in a way the venture fund often cannot: the accelerator’s check is smaller, the batch provides immediate feedback, and the accelerator does not usually take the kind of control rights that make a bad round painful to manage.

Then there is the investor’s internal life. A fund is not one person making a decision. A partner may like the company, but the fund may need investment committee approval, a check against its allocation, a conversation about whether it is too concentrated in that sector, and a legal review of the documents. That is bureaucracy, but it is also the mechanism by which a fund avoids one partner’s enthusiasm becoming the fund’s bad quarter. The delay is not always stupidity. Sometimes it is the price of having a group make a large irreversible bet.

The negotiation phase is where months become easiest to see and hardest to justify. A lead investor sets terms, but the syndicate is not a clone of the lead. One investor may want a side letter. Another may have different outside counsel. The founder may be comparing two leads. The company may be trying to create a competitive process without signaling weakness. The lawyers work in batches. The founders are running the company and answering diligence questions between product meetings. Every party has a reason to wait a little longer.

Timing matters too. Startups are noisy. Revenue can jump in a quarter and fall in the next. Churn can look stable for two months and then reveal a problem. A founder may wait for one more cohort of customers, one more renewal, one more product metric. An investor may wait to avoid being the only one who believes the story. A round that drags becomes a signal: if it does not close, something may be wrong. That can be rational, but it can also become a self-fulfilling tax on uncertainty.

Does it have to take months? For a pre-seed or seed round, usually no. A fast round is possible when the company has a data room ready before it starts talking, when the investor is comfortable making small checks, when the terms are standard, when the process is run with a deadline, and when someone is willing to be the lead. A 30-day seed process is not fantasy: identify 10 to 15 plausible investors, give them the same materials, let them ask questions in parallel, get term sheets inside 10 days, use standard documents, and close in three to five weeks. Accelerators are good at this partly because they have already done the first screen and created the deadline.

But speed has a cost. If the process is too fast, investors may pay too much, miss a legal problem, or accept terms they later regret. If the founder is rushed, the company may take a lead whose money is not as good as it looked. Convertible instruments can remove pricing from the early step, but they do not remove diligence; they mostly postpone the hard conversation. For a $30,000,000 growth round, months are more defensible because the check is bigger, the board matters more, the documents are more complex, and the investor may need to understand the business model, contract structure, and integration risk in more depth.

The hardest objection to the whole thing is that a lot of round time is not discovery. It is commitment management. Investors need to feel they chose the company rather than were forced into it. Founders need to feel they had options. The process gives both sides cover. That cover is useful in a small way: it reduces regret and gives time for red flags to surface. But when it becomes ritual, it is just expensive waiting.

So the answer is not that rounds should be fast because accelerators are fast. They should be as fast as the risk can be verified. For early-stage companies, that is usually weeks, not months. For later-stage companies, it may be longer. The useful question is not whether the round is slow, but whether the time is being spent learning or merely waiting.

prompt: people always say 'greed is good' and it makes me cringe. is there any version of that claim that actually makes sense?
response:
The cringe is probably a useful signal. “Greed is good” sounds like someone announcing that taking from you is a civic virtue. That version does not make sense. But if you translate the phrase from moral praise into a claim about institutions, something survives: people will work, take risks, and pay attention to other people’s needs when they can profit from doing so, and systems that ignore that fact often become brittle, corrupt, or inefficient.

The first move is to separate “greed” from “self-interest.” Greed usually means wanting more without a stable limit. Self-interest is broader: a person wants to feed their children, keep a job, pay for medical care, avoid humiliation, build something they are proud of. The slogan collapses these. A parent working two jobs is not the same moral creature as a financier who engineers a bonus for destroying value. But both are acting on their own interests. The defensible claim is not that insatiable greed is admirable; it is that ordinary self-interest, under the right rules, can be directed toward useful ends.

Adam Smith’s famous point about the butcher, the brewer, and the baker was not that greed is noble. It was that you get dinner not because they love you, but because they understand that serving you serves them. That is a modest and important observation. Human beings are not angels. If a system depends on everyone doing the right thing for strangers out of pure goodwill, it will usually fail. People need reasons. Profit is one reason. So are wages, reputation, fear of punishment, pride, and love. The mistake is to assume that only the last four count, or that profit is the only reliable one.

A concrete case helps. Suppose a city needs groceries at 7 p.m. on a Friday. You could rely on the grocer’s love of community. Sometimes that exists. But the more dependable explanation for the stocked shelves, the open register, and the person restocking the cereal aisle is that the store wants revenue, the workers want pay, and the customers want convenience. The profit motive makes the store count costs, notice what people buy, and adjust when tastes change. If a new neighborhood appears, or if half the customers start buying different products, the store has a reason to find out. A system organized purely around benevolence lacks that feedback loop.

But the mechanism is not greed. It is competition. If many sellers want your money, they must serve you to get it. If one seller has power, the same self-interest turns into extraction. Imagine a town with one bus line. If the real cost of a ride is two dollars and the company can charge ten without losing all its riders, it may do so. Passengers have no alternative. Now imagine three bus lines competing for the same riders. The price is pushed down, service quality matters more, and the company has a stronger reason to listen to complaints. The underlying human motive—wanting revenue—has not changed. The institutional arrangement has.

That is why the slogan fails when it leaves out the conditions. “Greed is good” only sounds plausible when the greedy actor is also constrained: by rivals, by law, by reputation, by the need to repeat the transaction. Without those constraints, greed is just predation with better branding. A company that pollutes a river because cleanup is expensive is not doing the public a favor by maximizing profit. A lender that hides terms from borrowers may make money once, but if the market learns what it does, it becomes harder to do business. A monopoly that raises prices and lowers quality is not “serving demand”; it is taxing the people who cannot leave.

There is also the question of externalities, which is the technical name for costs that someone else bears. A factory may profit by dumping sludge into a creek instead of treating waste. The profit is real, but it is partly made from other people’s health, fishing, and property. The market transaction looks efficient from the factory’s ledger and catastrophic from the town’s. The sensible response is not to pretend greed is virtuous. It is to make the factory pay for the damage, enforce property rights, or regulate the harm. The profit motive can then work again, but only after the costs have been put where the decision-maker can see them.

Sometimes the high price that feels greedy is actually doing useful work. In a snowstorm, taxi fares may surge. That is easy to hate, especially if you are stranded. But if the fare stayed normal while demand spiked, many drivers would stay home, because the risk and effort would not be compensated. The high price is what calls cars onto the roads. It allocates scarce vehicles to the people who most need them at that moment. The policy lesson is not “greed is good.” It is that if you suppress a price signal, you need another way to allocate scarcity; otherwise you get queues, favoritism, or no supply at all.

As advice to an individual, though, “greed is good” is usually bad. Most valuable relationships are repeated games. A greedy partner, employer, supplier, or friend may win a few exchanges, but they become expensive to deal with. Trust is a form of capital. People pay less, cooperate more, and reveal more information when they believe the other side is not trying to skin them. A firm known for sharp practice often finds that good employees leave, customers defect, and investors demand a discount. The greedy move can pay in a one-shot encounter. In a long life, it often raises the price of everything.

The hardest objection is not that greed can lead to bad outcomes. That is obvious. The harder point is that if the defensible version is really just “incentives matter,” then “greed is good” is still the wrong sentence. It moralizes a structural fact. It turns a warning about human nature into a license for selfishness. It also underestimates the amount of good that comes from non-greedy motives: teachers who stay late, engineers who care about quality, parents who sacrifice, neighbors who help after a disaster. Those things do not fit neatly into a profit-and-loss statement, but they are not irrelevant to how well a society works.

So the claim can be saved only by shrinking it. In a competitive market with enforceable contracts, honest information, and rules that make people internalize the harms they cause, the pursuit of profit is often a powerful way to get people to do things that benefit others. They must anticipate needs, control waste, take responsibility for quality, and bear the consequences of failure. That is genuinely valuable. But it is not a reason to praise greed as a character trait. It is a reason to design institutions that can use self-interest without being ruled by it. Your cringe is the right response to the boast. The underlying idea survives if you stop calling it a virtue and start treating it as a force to be channeled.

prompt: We're an early-stage startup and I honestly don't know what number we should be tracking or what 'good' looks like. How should we think about growth?
response:
Track the number that tells you whether your next user is worth acquiring. If you are too early to know that, track the number that tells you whether the product is being used enough to become worth acquiring. That distinction matters because early-stage teams often pick a number that feels exciting, not a number that forces a decision.

Growth is not a single dial. It is a loop: someone discovers you, tries you, gets value, comes back, pays or tells someone else. If the loop is broken, the number that looks best will mislead you. A paid campaign can make signups grow while retention dies. A referral program can make invites grow while conversion dies. A founder can personally onboard 20 customers and make revenue look real while the process cannot scale. The useful metric is not the biggest number. It is the number at the weakest link.

Ask where users stop. If most people stop before doing the core action, track activation. If they do the core action but do not return, track retention. If they return but do not pay, track willingness to pay. If they pay but do not stay, track churn. If they stay but you cannot find more of them, track acquisition. Pick the first broken link, not the one that makes the dashboard look impressive.

For most early-stage products, the first number is not growth rate. It is cohort retention: of the users who arrived in week one, how many are still using the product in week two, week five, and week thirteen? Total users can hide a terrible business. If you start with 1,000 users and lose 500 a month, adding 600 new users makes the total grow, but the business is not compounding. Cohorts show whether the new water is staying in the bucket. If you can get 1,000 signups but only 50 are active after 30 days, the next 10,000 signups will produce 500 actives. That is not a growth engine. It is a churn machine.

If you are pre-revenue, the best early proxy for retention is activation. Define the action that means the user got real value. For a resume tool, it might be exporting a finished resume. For a habit app, it might be completing three habits. For a B2B project tool, it might be inviting a teammate or creating a project with actual content. Track the percentage of new users who do that action in the first session or first week. The exact percentage depends on the product, but the logic does not: if only a tiny slice of users reach value, you have a product or onboarding problem before you have a distribution problem. If 10% activate and 5% of those users come back next week, spending money on acquisition will mostly buy you a larger leak. If 50% activate and a meaningful share return without being nagged, you have something worth distributing.

Once retention exists, track the source of new users. The number I would watch closely is the fraction of new users who come from existing users: referrals, shared links, invites, word of mouth, community. If it is zero, you are renting every user. If it rises from 0% to 10% to 25%, the product is becoming easier to grow. This is often the earliest clean signal of product-market fit: not that people say they like it, but that their behavior brings others in.

If you are monetized, add the money number. The most useful one is CAC payback, not raw CAC. CAC payback tells you how many months of customer contribution it takes to recover the cost of acquiring that customer. Suppose a customer pays $100 per month and costs $20 per month to serve. Contribution is $80. If CAC is $800, payback is 10 months, before accounting for the fact that some customers will churn before you get paid back. If churn is 5% per month, the average customer lifetime is roughly 20 months, so 10-month payback is plausible but not luxurious. If CAC is $2,000, payback is 25 months, and you are financing growth with customers who may leave before you break even. This is why “our CAC is $300” is not an answer. It becomes an answer only when paired with contribution margin, churn, and expansion.

The other money number is net revenue retention by cohort. It asks whether existing customers are a stable base, a shrinking base, or an expanding base. If a cohort starts with $10,000 of monthly revenue and three months later produces $9,000 after churn and contraction, net revenue retention is 90%. That is a leak. If it produces $11,000, retention is 110%, and the business can grow from the base even before new sales. For early B2B software, I would be uncomfortable below 100% for long. Around 100 to 110% is healthy. Above 120% is strong, though category and pricing model matter.

The right metric changes with the model. If you are a marketplace, do not track total users as the main number. Track liquidity on the scarce side: the percentage of listings that receive a valid inquiry in seven days, the percentage of buyers who find what they want in the first session, the percentage of supply that transacts in a month. If you have 10,000 consumers and 50 drivers in a city, consumer growth may make the experience worse, not better. If you have 1,000 drivers and no demand, adding more drivers increases costs and disappointment. The growth problem is not “more users.” It is making one side useful enough that the other side stays.

If you are sales-led B2B, the early number is often not signups but conversion. Track meetings to opportunities, opportunities to pilots, pilots to paid contracts. If 50 qualified conversations produce one close, the problem may be product-market fit, pricing, buyer selection, or sales motion, not marketing. More meetings will not fix a broken close. If the close rate improves as you narrow the ideal customer profile, that is a strong signal you are finding the segment for whom the problem is urgent.

If you are consumer, track frequency and return, not just installs. A user who opens the app once is not a customer. Track day-one, day-seven, and day-thirty return, and sessions per week among retained users. The exact benchmarks vary wildly by category, but the pattern is the test: does a cohort settle into a habit, or does it decay to zero? If day-seven retention is low, a paid install campaign is just buying a larger graveyard.

What “good” looks like is less about a universal threshold and more about the shape of the curve. Bad growth is when every new user requires more founder effort: more personal onboarding, more manual support, more targeted outreach, more custom work. Good growth is when the time to go from 100 to 200 activated users falls while your hours per user fall. Bad growth is when retention is flat and you are buying your way upward. Good growth is when retention improves as you refine the audience and the first-run experience. Bad growth is when CAC falls only because you are reaching less qualified users. Good growth is when CAC is stable or rising while retention, contribution margin, or expansion improves.

A number is good when it makes the business more self-reinforcing. If you can predict next month’s active users from this month’s, you have some structure. If you can price an ad channel because you know what a retained customer is worth, you have leverage. If you can hire a marketer or salesperson because the process already works, you have a machine. If the metric only moves when you personally push it, you have a job, not a growth engine.

One caution: early numbers are noisy. With small cohorts, one or two users can move a percentage wildly. Do not make major decisions from a single week. Use four-week rolling cohorts, compare similar stages of the user journey, and treat the line as a direction until the sample gets bigger. If 3% of 200 users refer a friend, that is interesting, not truth. If 30% of 3,000 users return after 30 days, that is more likely real.

The hardest objection is that investors, founders, and momentum all point to growth rate, and retention feels slow. That is true, but growth rate can be a warning sign in disguise. Fifty percent monthly growth sounds great until you learn that 70% of users churn in the first month. The number is not growth. The number is growth that survives. A slower rate with improving retention and organic pull is usually more valuable than a fast rate that requires constant fuel.

For the next 30 days, build one simple table: cohort, new users, activated, active next week, active next month, paid, referred. Define activation concretely. Pick the first column where the percentage is too low. Make that your main metric until it improves. If you cannot instrument it, you are not ready to optimize it. If you can instrument it and it is bad, resist the urge to scale acquisition. Fix the link first.

prompt: Two senior people on our open source project keep arguing about whether a section of the docs is clear. Each thinks their rewrite is better. How do you actually settle that kind of thing?
response:
You settle it by turning the argument into a small experiment, because “clear” is not a property of prose. It is a relation between prose and a particular reader trying to do a particular thing.

First write one sentence about what the section is supposed to accomplish. Not “explain the feature,” but something like: “After reading this, a new user can enable retries with three attempts and one-second backoff,” or “After reading this, a maintainer can tell whether a failing test is caused by the cache or by the network layer.” If the two rewrites serve different versions of that sentence, the real disagreement is about audience or scope, and that should be decided first. A section in a quickstart should not be judged by the standards of a reference page.

Then test the two versions against that sentence with a few plausible readers. Do not ask them, “Which one is clearer?” People will hedge, split the difference, or praise the one written by the more senior person. Instead, give them a task. For a how-to section, ask them to do the thing. For a conceptual section, ask them to predict what happens in two or three cases. Record what they ask, where they get stuck, and what they get wrong. Three or five people is not enough to rank subtle differences in style, but it is often enough to show that one version consistently produces the wrong command, the wrong mental model, or the same confused question.

If you cannot recruit real readers, do the next best thing. Have each author write down the specific failure mode of the other’s version: “This wording makes people think the flag is optional,” “This example hides the default value,” “This uses a term we define three pages later.” Then have a third person, preferably not one of the two authors, check those claims against the text and, if possible, against one or two outside readers. This forces the argument to move from taste to consequences.

If both versions pass the test, stop trying to decide which is more beautiful. Choose the one that is easier to maintain: shorter, consistent with the terminology already used in the docs, less dependent on a private metaphor, and less likely to break when the feature changes. If both versions fail, the answer is not to pick the lesser evil; it is to rewrite both, because the section is probably missing an example, an assumption, or a distinction that neither author noticed.

The hard case is when the only available judges are the maintainers themselves, and they already know the system. Then their judgment is biased, because they can fill gaps that a newcomer cannot. In that situation, agree on a tie-breaker before looking at the prose: clarity for new contributors, consistency with the CLI, fewer moving parts, or fit with the surrounding pages. Ship the result with a short note in the issue: what was tested, what was unknown, and what evidence should reopen the decision. A documented, reversible decision is usually better than a long debate over two competent paragraphs.

prompt: I just found out there are already a few companies doing basically what I want to build. Am I too late? Should I drop the idea?
response:
No—finding a few competitors is not the same as being too late. It is the first useful piece of information. The question is no longer whether the idea exists; it is whether you can win a specific slice of it.

I don’t know what you are building, so I can’t tell you whether the market is full. But the existence of a few companies does not decide it by itself.

If nobody is doing it, that can mean you are early, or it can mean the job is not important enough for people to pay for. A few companies is often a better sign: someone has already shown that customers will pay, but the market has not been sorted out. In software especially, the first movers are frequently not the winners, because the product category is still being defined. The winner is often the one who makes it easier, cheaper, or more relevant to a particular buyer. But this is not automatic. A few companies can also mean the market is small, the product is hard, or the incumbents are already good enough.

The hardest case against you is simple: if they already do basically what you want to build, why would a customer choose you? “Basically” is where most side projects die. People do not switch because a new option is slightly better. They switch when the current option is painful, when the new one removes a specific risk, or when it reaches them through a channel they trust. If your answer is “mine will be cleaner” or “I just like the problem,” that is not a business. You need a wedge: a customer segment, a use case, a price point, a speed advantage, a distribution advantage, or a cost advantage that is concrete enough to state in one sentence.

For example, if existing tools are project management for 50-person agencies, you might build for two-person design studios that only need invoices, files, and client approvals. If existing vendors sell to hospitals with six-month implementations, you might sell to outpatient clinics that need it working before lunch. If existing products charge $200 per seat, you might win by charging $20 per user and making setup take 15 minutes. The wedge matters because it lets you ignore the parts where incumbents are strong and compete where they are weak or indifferent.

Then ask whether the competitors have real first-mover advantages. In many businesses, being early is not protective. If the product is a standalone tool, switching costs are low and the market is fragmented, a late entrant can win by being better at sales, support, or product fit. If the product is a marketplace, a social network, a platform with deep integrations, or a business with exclusive contracts, proprietary data, or regulatory barriers, then timing matters more. If the first companies have locked in the users, suppliers, or data that make the product valuable, you may indeed be late. If they merely have websites and a small customer base, you probably are not.

You also need to ask why you. Competition is not only about the product; it is about access. Do you know the buyers? Can you get in front of them? Do you understand the workflow well enough to avoid building the obvious wrong thing? Can you serve them cheaper or faster because of your background, location, cost structure, or audience? If not, you may be entering as an outsider with no reason for customers to take a chance on you. That is a stronger reason to drop the idea than the existence of competitors.

The practical test is not to compare features against competitors. It is to find a narrow group of potential customers and ask what they do today, what they pay, what they hate, and what would make them switch. Then watch behavior. “I would try it” is not enough. A useful signal is someone asking when it will be ready, offering to pay for a beta, or letting you do the job manually for them. If you can get a handful of customers to use a rough version, the idea is alive. If you cannot get attention, the problem may be the market, not the fact that others are already there.

Drop it if the market is too small for the outcome you want, if the people you talk to are polite but uninterested, if the incumbents have structural advantages you cannot touch, if you have no way to reach the first hundred customers, or if you need revenue soon and this will take years. Continue if you can name a specific customer, a specific pain, a specific reason they would choose you, and a realistic path to talking to them this week.

Too late is a real status, but it is usually earned by a lock-in, not by the mere presence of other companies. The fact that a few are doing it should make you sharper, not stop you.

They switch when the current option is painful, when the new one removes a specific risk, or when it reaches them through a channel they trust. If your answer is 'mine will be cleaner' or 'I just like the problem,' that is not a business. You need a wedge: a customer segment, a use case, a price point, a speed advantage, a distribution advantage, or a cost advantage that is concrete enough to state in one sentence.

For example... If existing tools are project management for 50-person agencies, you might build for two-person design studios that only need invoices, files, and client approvals. If existing vendors sell to hospitals with six-month implementations, you might sell to outpatient clinics that need it working before lunch. If existing products charge $200 per seat, you might win by charging $20 per user and making setup take 15 minutes. The wedge matters because it lets you ignore the parts where incumbents are strong and compete where they are weak or indifferent.

Then ask whether the competitors have real first-mover advantages. In many businesses, being early is not protective. If the product is a standalone tool, switching costs are low and the market is fragmented, a late entrant can win by being better at sales, support, or product fit. If the product is a marketplace, a social network, a platform with integrations, or a business with exclusive contracts, proprietary data, or regulatory barriers, then timing matters more. If the first companies have locked in the users, suppliers, or data that make the product valuable, you may indeed be late. If they merely have websites and a small customer base, you probably are not.

You also need to ask why you. Competition is not only about the product; it is about access. Do you know the buyers? Can you get in front of them? Do you understand the workflow well enough to avoid building the obvious wrong thing? Can you serve them cheaper or faster because of your background, location, cost structure, or audience? If not, you may be entering as an outsider with no reason for customers to take a chance on you. That is a stronger reason to drop the idea than the existence of competitors.

The practical test is not to look at competitors' features. It is to find a narrow group of potential customers and ask what they do today, what they pay, what they hate, and what would make them switch. Then watch behavior. 'I would try it' is not enough. A useful signal is someone asking when it will be ready, offering to pay for a beta, or letting you do the job manually for them. If you can get a handful of customers to use a rough version, the idea is alive. If you cannot get attention, the problem may be the market, not the fact that others are there.

Drop it if the market is too small for the life you want, if the people you talk to are polite but uninterested, if the incumbents have structural advantages you cannot touch, if you have no way to reach the first hundred customers, or if you need revenue soon and this will take years. Continue if you can name a specific customer, a specific pain, a specific reason they would choose you, and a realistic path to talking to them this week.

Too late is a real status, but it is usually earned by a lock-in, not by the mere presence of other companies. The fact that a few are doing it should make you sharper, not stop you."

prompt: if one country gets superintelligent AI a few months before its rival, why would that be dangerous? is there a historical analogy?
response:
Assume by superintelligent AI we mean a system that can do most cognitively demanding work in science, engineering, hacking, finance, and strategy better and faster than human teams. If it is only a very good assistant, a few months is not a crisis. The dangerous case is that the technology changes what a few months can accomplish. In ordinary strategic competition, ninety days is not enough to build a fleet, an army, or a nuclear arsenal. Physical bottlenecks remain. But much of what AI does is remove the human thinking bottleneck: finding software vulnerabilities, designing control systems, optimizing logistics, reading intercepted intelligence, modeling adversary decision-making, and perhaps designing harmful biological or chemical agents. If the human part of a project normally takes years and the AI cuts it to weeks, three months is not a small head start; it is enough to turn a technical lead into several deployable advantages.

The deeper problem is that the lead is not a fixed margin. It may decay as the rival catches up, or it may widen if the first country’s AI improves its own design. In the first case, the leading country is tempted to act before the margin disappears: coerce the rival into concessions, disable its infrastructure or development effort, steal its secrets, or attack the people and systems that would allow it to respond. In the second case, the rival may believe waiting is hopeless. Both calculations push toward early action. The danger is not simply that one country is stronger; it is that both may believe the window for acceptable action is closing.

This can undermine deterrence in a second way: verification. Nuclear stability depends partly on knowing that the other side can retaliate and on having enough time to confirm what is happening. AI capabilities are harder to observe than missiles. They can sit in data centers, cloud services, or ordinary networks, and they can be used without visible launch preparations. A cyberattack on power grids, financial systems, or command networks may look at first like an accident or a limited probe, but it may be the first phase of something larger. If leaders have less time to decide and less confidence in their information, the chance of miscalculation rises.

There is no clean historical analogy, because no previous technology was a general-purpose cognitive accelerator. The closest strategic analogy is the missile-gap panic of the late 1950s and early 1960s. The United States believed the Soviet Union had a large lead in intercontinental ballistic missiles, and the fear made first-strike planning and preemption much harder to dismiss. Later analysis showed the gap had been badly overstated. That makes the analogy useful rather than weak: even a suspected short lead in a decisive capability can destabilize a rivalry, because the threatened side may not want to gamble on finding out later whether the lead is real.

The 1945–1949 nuclear monopoly supplies the other half of the lesson. The United States did not have the atomic bomb for only a few months; it had it for four years. Even so, the temporary monopoly changed bargaining, encouraged coercive diplomacy, and made the Soviet Union treat closing the gap as an existential priority. If the monopoly had been shorter, the incentive to use the advantage before it vanished would have been stronger, not weaker.

July 1914 is the closest analogy to the timing problem. The great powers were not competing over a new machine in the way the question describes, but they were competing over short windows created by mobilization timetables. Once leaders believed that waiting would let the other side complete its preparations, diplomatic flexibility shrank. Deadlines were issued, ultimatums were accepted or rejected under pressure, and a regional crisis became a general war. A superintelligent AI would be like that same logic with a faster clock and less visible preparation: the advantage may be real or exaggerated, but if it is thought to be temporary, it can make war look like the cheaper option.

prompt: if I really can't model something, can't I just say I don't know and refuse to put a probability on it? like choosing between a safe grant and a wild long shot
response:
Yes, you can say “I don’t know.” That is often the honest answer. But if you are actually choosing, the answer does not let you avoid the decision. It only changes the form of the decision.

The key distinction is between two different uses of probability.

One use is epistemic: “I believe there is a 7% chance this works.” That is a claim about the world. If you have no good model, no reference class, no data, and no reliable intuition, then yes, you should refuse to make that claim with confidence. Pretending to know a precise probability is a bad idea.

The other use is decision-theoretic: “What odds would I need before I would forgo the sure thing?” That is not a claim that you know the true odds. It is a statement about your threshold. You can refuse to estimate the chance of success while still knowing the chance at which you would act.

Suppose the safe grant is worth $50,000. The wild long shot could be worth $500,000 if it works and $0 if it fails. If money is the only thing that matters and you are risk-neutral, the break-even probability is 10%. At 10%, the long shot has the same expected value as the safe grant: 0.10 × $500,000 = $50,000.

Now you do not need to say, “The real probability is 12.3%.” You can say, “I do not know the real probability, but I will not give up $50,000 for sure unless I think the chance is above 10%.” That is a coherent position. It is not false precision. It is a decision rule.

If you can place the unknown probability clearly on one side of the threshold, the decision is easy. If you think the chance is almost certainly below 10%, take the safe grant. If you think it is almost certainly above 10%, take the long shot. The trouble is the middle case: the probability might be 4% or 18%, and you do not know which. Then “I don’t know” is true, but you still have to choose by something.

At that point, several legitimate fallbacks appear.

You can choose by risk tolerance. If you need the safe grant to stay afloat, the safe option may dominate even if the long shot has a higher expected value. A $50,000 certainty can be worth much more to a person or organization near a cliff than its face value suggests. Conversely, if you are already secure and the long shot could change your trajectory, you may be willing to accept a much lower probability.

You can choose by option value. If taking the safe grant does not permanently kill the long shot, take the safe grant and keep the option open. If the long shot can be tested cheaply before the big commitment, spend a little to learn. If the decision is reversible, favor the option that leaves you more information. If it is irreversible, be more conservative.

You can choose by the cost of being wrong. Losing the safe grant may be painful but recoverable. Missing the long shot may be a once-in-a-decade opportunity. Or the reverse may be true. The “right” choice under ignorance depends on the asymmetry of the mistakes.

You can choose by a precommitted rule. For example: “When I cannot estimate the probability, I require a 3-to-1 payoff before I will forgo a sure thing.” Or: “When I cannot estimate the probability, I take the sure thing unless the upside is transformational.” These rules are not magic. They are explicit ways of handling the fact that you do not know.

The hardest objection is this: if I have no basis for a probability, isn’t any number I use just arbitrary? In a sense, yes. If you say “I assign it 12%” and your real reason is “12 felt right,” that is bad reasoning. But there is a difference between inventing a fake belief and using a transparent decision threshold. “I cannot estimate the probability, but I need at least 10% to make this trade” is defensible. “I estimate the probability at 10.4%” is not, unless you actually have grounds for that precision.

There is also a social and practical pressure against total refusal. If you repeatedly say “I don’t know” when choices force you to act, your actions will reveal your implicit odds anyway. If you take the long shot over the safe grant, you have effectively said the chance is high enough, or the upside is valuable enough, to justify it. If you take the safe grant, you have said the opposite. Denying that you are setting odds does not stop you from setting them.

In repeated decisions, this matters even more. If you never assign probabilities, you cannot tell whether your hunches are calibrated. You cannot compare a 2% chance of a huge win with a 50% chance of a moderate win. You cannot allocate resources across opportunities. You become someone who makes choices by mood, status quo, authority, or the option that felt most dramatic in the moment. That may be fine for low-stakes one-offs. It is a poor strategy for serious judgment.

So the answer is: you can refuse to give a probability as a factual claim. You should, if you do not have one. But you cannot refuse to have a stance. The best version of “I don’t know” in a decision is not bare silence. It is something like:

“I cannot reliably estimate the probability. The sure option is worth X. The risky option is worth Y if it succeeds. I would need at least Z% to switch. I do not currently believe the chance is above Z%, so I take the sure option. I would revise that if I learned A, B, or C.”

That is honest. It avoids fake precision. And it still makes the choice.

prompt: Should a company care more about its customers than about its own survival?
response:
A company should not be ranked as owing more to customers than to its own existence, but it should not be allowed to treat its own existence as a higher good than its service to customers. The distinction matters because a company’s survival is not an end. It is the condition that allows the company to deliver a product, honor a warranty, keep an employee, maintain a network, or provide a service tomorrow. If a firm is insolvent, its promises to customers are hollow. A bakery that gives away bread to be liked will close; an airline that cannot buy fuel cannot fly; a software company that cannot pay for servers cannot serve users. In that ordinary sense, caring about customers requires caring about viability.

But viability is a constraint, not a rival purpose. A company can be alive on paper and dead in the market. It can preserve its legal entity, its management, its current margins, or its existing revenue streams while losing the reason people choose it. That is the failure mode behind many well-known collapses. Blockbuster did not die for lack of a survival instinct. It spent years defending late fees, physical stores, and a rental-by-mail competitor while customers moved toward convenience and streaming. Kodak had digital imaging technology and still made choices that protected film, and eventually went bankrupt in 2012. In both cases, the company was trying to survive, but it attached survival to the wrong thing: the old business model rather than the customer problem it had once solved.

This is where the question becomes strategic. A company’s best chance of survival is usually to create value that customers are willing to pay for repeatedly. If a firm ignores customer needs to protect short-term earnings, it may survive a quarter, a year, or a decade, but it is borrowing legitimacy. The borrowing ends when customers find an alternative or when the harm becomes visible. Boeing’s 737 MAX episode is a severe example: pressure to deliver a product quickly and cheaply, with safety and certification problems, led to two crashes, 346 deaths, regulatory battles, losses, and a damaged reputation. The company was certainly trying to remain competitive, but the attempt showed that survival pursued through customers can destroy more value than it saves.

Legally, the answer is not that a company may simply choose to fail out of virtue. Officers and directors generally owe duties to the corporation and its owners, and they cannot squander assets or abandon a going concern because they dislike it. But those duties are not a command to maximize this quarter’s numbers at the expense of the firm’s future. In many jurisdictions, directors must consider the long-term consequences of decisions for employees, customers, suppliers, communities, and the company’s reputation. Even where the law is narrower, a board that preserves a company by deceiving or exploiting customers is creating legal, regulatory, and reputational risk. It is not protecting the company; it is postponing the bill.

There is a harder case, though. Sometimes a company is the only practical provider of something people need, and its survival is not just a private financial question. A utility, a hospital system, a regional bank, or a platform with network effects may be harder to replace than it looks. If it fails abruptly, customers and employees may be harmed even if the company was not serving them well. In such situations, a society may decide that continuity matters, and regulators may step in to keep the firm going while forcing it to change prices, service levels, ownership, or governance. That is not the company morally prioritizing customers over survival; it is the public deciding that the company’s survival is useful enough to manage. The company itself should not get to claim that “we must survive” excuses bad treatment of customers. If it needs public support to continue, it should accept public conditions.

Another hard case is when customers want to be harmed. A payday lender, a tobacco company, a data broker, or a company that sells people things they cannot afford has customers in the narrow sense: people who buy. But “caring about customers” cannot mean only satisfying every stated preference. If it did, the most customer-oriented company would be the one most willing to exploit people’s weakness, impatience, addiction, or ignorance. A company that says it puts customers first should mean their interests, not just their transactions. That sometimes means refusing a profitable sale, limiting a feature, raising a price to avoid debt, or exiting a market where the product does more harm than good.

This also changes what “survival” should mean. A company should survive if it can do so by earning trust: by being reliable, safe, transparent, and useful. It should not survive if it can do so only by extracting from customers faster than it is creating value, by deceiving them, by shifting risk onto them, or by depending on monopoly power that lets it ignore them. The first kind of survival compounds. The second kind may look like survival for a while, but it is fragile because it depends on the customers’ inability to leave or understand.

Employees and other stakeholders matter too, and customer focus can become a mask for bad behavior. A company can delight customers while underpaying workers, breaking contracts with suppliers, or externalizing costs onto communities. That is not a complete answer to the customer-survival question, but it prevents the answer from becoming a simple cult of the customer. A firm’s legitimacy comes from the whole set of promises it keeps. Customers are central because they are the reason the firm exists, but they are not the only people the firm affects.

The practical rule is therefore not “customers first, survival second” as a sentimental ranking. It is: remain viable enough to keep your promises, and be willing to change or stop when continuing means taking from people rather than serving them. A company that is too reckless with its finances cannot serve customers. A company that is too attached to its own existence will eventually either die or do harm. The better orientation is to treat survival as the means by which customer value is delivered over time, not as a separate good that outranks the customers themselves.

Potential final:

A company should not be ranked as owing more to customers than to its own existence, but it should not be allowed to treat its own existence as a higher good than its service to customers. The distinction matters because a company's survival is not an end. It is the condition that allows the company to deliver a product, honor a warranty, keep an employee, maintain a network, or provide a service tomorrow. If a firm is insolvent, its promises to customers are hollow. A bakery that gives away bread to be liked will close; an airline that cannot buy fuel cannot fly; a software company that cannot pay for servers cannot serve users. In that ordinary sense, caring about customers requires caring about viability.

But viability is a constraint, not a rival purpose. A company can be alive on paper and dead in the market. It can preserve its legal entity, its management, its current margins, or its existing revenue streams while losing the reason people choose it. That is the failure mode behind many well-known collapses. Blockbuster did not die for lack of a survival instinct. It spent years defending late fees, physical stores, and a rental-by-mail competitor while customers moved to convenience and streaming. Kodak had digital imaging technology and still made choices that protected film, and eventually went bankrupt in 2012. In both cases, the company was trying to survive, but it attached survival to the wrong thing: the old business model rather than the customer problem it had once solved.

This is where the question becomes strategic. A company's best chance of survival is usually to create value that customers are willing to pay for repeatedly. If a firm ignores customer needs to protect short-term earnings, it may survive a quarter, a year, or a decade, but it is borrowing legitimacy. The borrowing ends when customers find an alternative or when the harm becomes visible. Boeing's 737 MAX episode is a severe example: pressure to deliver a product quickly and cheaply, with safety and certification problems, led to two crashes, 346 deaths, regulatory battles, losses, and a damaged reputation. The company was certainly trying to remain competitive, but the attempt showed that survival pursued through customers can destroy more value than it saves.

There is a harder case, though. Sometimes a company is the only practical provider of something people need, and its survival is not just a private financial question. A utility, a hospital system, a regional bank, or a platform with network effects may be harder to replace than it looks. If it fails abruptly, customers and employees may be harmed even if the company was not serving them well. In such situations, a society may decide that continuity matters, and regulators may step in to keep the firm going while forcing it to change prices, service levels, ownership, or governance. That is not the company morally prioritizing customers over survival; it is the public deciding that the company's survival is useful enough to manage. The company itself should not get to claim that "we must survive" excuses bad treatment of customers. If it needs public support to continue, it should accept public conditions.

Another hard case is when customers want to be harmed. A payday lender, a tobacco company, a data broker, or a company that sells people things they cannot afford has customers in the narrow sense: people who buy. But "caring about customers" cannot mean only satisfying every stated preference. If it did, the most customer-oriented company would be the one most willing to exploit people's weakness, impatience, addiction, or ignorance. A company that says it puts customers first should mean their interests, not just their transactions. That sometimes means refusing a profitable sale, limiting a feature, raising a price to avoid debt, or exiting a market where the product does more harm than good.

This also changes what "survival" should mean. A company should survive if it can do so by earning trust: by being reliable, safe, transparent, and useful. It should not survive if it can do so only by extracting from customers faster than it is creating value, by deceiving them, by shifting risk onto them, or by depending on monopoly power that lets it ignore them. The first kind of survival compounds. The second kind may look like survival for a while, but it is fragile because it depends on the customers' inability to leave or understand.

Employees and other stakeholders matter too, and customer focus can become a mask for bad behavior. A company can delight customers while underpaying workers, breaking contracts with suppliers, or externalizing costs onto communities. That is not a complete answer to the customer-survival question, but it prevents the answer from becoming a simple cult of the customer. A firm's legitimacy comes from the whole set of promises it keeps. Customers are central because they are the reason the firm exists, but they are not the only people the firm affects.

The practical rule is therefore not "customers first, survival second" as a sentimental ranking. It is: remain viable enough to keep your promises, and be willing to change or stop when continuing means taking from people rather than serving them. A company that is too reckless with its finances cannot serve customers. A company that is too attached to its own existence will eventually either die or do harm. The better orientation is to treat survival as the means by which customer value is delivered over time, not as a separate good that outranks the customers themselves.

prompt: what's the deal with over-abstracting things? why do clever people end up building vague 'general' systems that miss the point?
response:
Over-abstracting is usually not a failure of intelligence but of evidence. A designer sees a few concrete cases, notices a common shape, and then builds the common shape as the system. The problem is that the common shape is a hypothesis, not a fact. The real question is which parts of the shape will still be common after the system is used by people who did not design it. If you get that wrong, you have not built a general solution; you have built a complicated way to do the original thing.

Cleverness helps produce the abstraction quickly. It also makes the abstraction feel authoritative, because it is easy to manipulate in one’s head. A clever person can imagine ten variations of the problem and see a pattern before the organization has actually had one. That is useful for spotting traps, but it is a bad substitute for knowing which variations actually exist. The mind likes to complete patterns; reality is messier and often less symmetric. Clever people are sometimes worse at stopping at the concrete answer precisely because they can see the general answer, and the general answer feels more satisfying.

A team needs three reports: daily sales, monthly invoices, and a regulatory export. They build a “reporting framework” with query builders, layout templates, a scheduler, a permission matrix, and a UI for defining fields. Six months later, changing a column in the daily report touches five modules, and the regulatory export still requires a special case in the code. The abstraction generalized over report structure, but the hard parts were deadlines, ownership, and what the numbers mean when they disagree. The framework made the system look larger than the problem.

This happens because concrete problems are expensive to understand. To know why a PDF needs a signature block, you have to talk to compliance, read the form, see the edge cases. To design a “renderer interface,” you only need a whiteboard. In many organizations, the whiteboard work is more rewarded because it looks architectural. It also has a future-oriented value: it promises reuse. A script that solves one problem looks throwaway even when it is correct. A platform looks durable even when it is wrong.

There is also an argumentative advantage. Abstractions let people coordinate on nouns. “The service should be pluggable” is easier to agree on than “the invoice must include VAT only when the customer is in the EU and the order total is below the threshold.” The general statement sounds wise because it avoids the details where disagreement lives. But the details are usually the point. A system that cannot represent the details cannot solve the problem.

The strongest case against this critique is that real systems do need generality. TCP is general; it does not know what application is sending data, and that is why the internet works. SQL is general; it expresses operations over relations, not one table. Interfaces, dependency injection, feature flags, and event buses exist because some variation is unavoidable. The answer is not “never abstract.” The answer is that successful abstractions are precise about what varies and what does not. TCP’s generality is constrained by checksums, sequencing, flow control, and a very hard problem: moving bits across unreliable networks. It is not a vague idea of “transport.” A bad “general” system is often the opposite: it is precise in the wrong places, with many knobs and extension points, while the core domain rules remain implicit, scattered, or wrong.

Good abstraction is usually discovered, not invented. You write the first version for the real case. You write the second. You see that three lines of logic are identical, or that a boundary keeps leaking, and you move only that repeated part into a smaller unit. The test is not elegance. The test is whether the next real case is cheaper to add, and whether the old cases remain understandable. If the abstraction makes the first three cases harder to trace, it has not paid rent.

The practical tell is that a vague general system usually needs a lot of explanation to say what it actually does. It has names like manager, engine, hub, framework, layer, or platform, and its main virtue is that it “can” do things. A useful concrete system can be described in terms of a real user, a real object, and a real failure mode. When people over-abstract, it is rarely because they are trying to be profound. It is because the abstract layer is easier to build, easier to defend, and easier to extend on paper than the concrete thing they were originally supposed to fix.

Let's outline:

Start: Over-abstraction happens when a designer replaces a known problem with a possible class of problems, and the possible class is not yet real. The system optimizes for imagined variations, not actual requirements.

Why clever people: They are good at seeing patterns, naming them, and manipulating symbols. That makes abstraction tempting. Abstraction feels like progress: it turns many concrete cases into one clean concept. But abstraction only earns its keep if it makes the next concrete case easier, not if it makes the current one harder.

Concrete example: Suppose you need to send 10 kinds of emails. You build a "notification engine" with templates, channels, user preferences, scheduling, retry policies, localization. You spent three weeks on machinery; now adding a new email is a config job but the original problem is buried. The abstraction missed point because the point was not to support 100 channels, it was to tell users their thing happened.

Another: ORM/data access layer. You want to avoid SQL. You build repository abstraction with generic CRUD, mapping, criteria builders. It works until queries need to be efficient, or domain rules need to live in SQL. The abstraction was based on the assumption all data access is the same; it wasn't.

Why: several mechanisms.
1. Specificity is expensive: to understand a real case you must learn its ugly details. Abstraction lets you stay in comfortable generality. Clever people can do it faster.
2. Generality is a status signal. A "framework" sounds better than "script for this thing." It claims future value.
3. Abstract interfaces are easier to argue about than concrete implementations. People can design around nouns.
4. Abstraction hides ignorance: if you don't know how the domain works, a general interface can look plausible. It defers hard questions.
5. Organizational incentives: platforms promise reuse; reuse is visible and defensible in budget meetings; solving one concrete problem is not.
6. The first abstraction is often a hypothesis. If not tested against actual use, it hardens.

Good abstraction is subtractive: it removes repetition without adding unknown unknowns.

Example: company needs to export CSV, PDF, email. They build a "document pipeline" with content providers, renderers, delivery handlers, approval workflows, metadata schemas, and a configuration UI. Six months later, the original three outputs still take days to change, and every new output is a project. The abstraction was general over a dimension that was not the hard part. The hard part was that each output had different legal requirements, different review paths, and different definitions of "done." The pipeline hid those differences behind interfaces, so they became integration problems instead of design decisions.

This happens because concrete problems are expensive to understand. To know why a PDF needs a signature block, you have to talk to compliance, read the form, see the edge cases. To design a "renderer interface," you only need a whiteboard. In many organizations, the whiteboard work is more rewarded because it looks architectural. It also has a future-oriented value: it promises reuse. A script that solves one problem looks throwaway even when it is correct. A platform looks durable even when it is wrong.

There is also an argumentative advantage. Abstractions let people coordinate on nouns. "The service should be pluggable" is easier to agree on than "the invoice must include VAT only when the customer is in the EU and the order total is below the threshold." The general statement sounds wise because it avoids the details where disagreement lives. But the details are usually the point. A system that cannot represent the details cannot solve the problem.

The strongest case against this critique is that real systems do need generality. TCP is general; it does not know what application is sending data, and that is why the internet works. SQL is general; it expresses operations over relations, not one table. Object-oriented interfaces, dependency injection, feature flags, and event buses exist because some variation is unavoidable. The answer is not "never abstract." The answer is that successful abstractions are precise about what varies and what does not. TCP's generality is constrained by checksums, sequencing, flow control, and a very hard problem: moving bits across unreliable networks. It is not a vague idea of "transport." A bad "general" system is often the opposite: it is precise in the wrong places, with many knobs and extension points, while the core domain rules remain implicit, scattered, or wrong.

Good abstraction is usually discovered, not invented. You write the first version for the real case. You write the second. You see that three lines of logic are identical, or that a boundary keeps leaking, and you move only that repeated part into a smaller unit. The test is not elegance. The test is whether the next real case is cheaper to add, and whether the old cases remain understandable. If the abstraction makes the first three cases harder to trace, it has not paid rent.

The practical tell is simple: a vague general system usually needs a lot of explanation to say what it actually does. It has names like manager, engine, hub, framework, layer, or platform, and its main virtue is that it "can" do things. A useful concrete system can be described in terms of a real user, a real object, and a real failure mode. When people over-abstract, it is rarely because they are trying to be profound. It is because the abstract layer is easier to build, easier to defend, and easier to extend on paper than the concrete thing they were originally supposed to fix.
