prompt: Should a small, very productive core team of a language like Julia slow down to add code review, tests and internal docs so outsiders can contribute more easily? Or is that not worth it?
response:
A small core team should do this only if the thing limiting the project is no longer the team’s ability to write code, but its ability to trust changes. If the team can keep shipping at the speed it wants and the outside world is mostly filing issues or sending small fixes, adding ceremony is a tax. If the team is already spending its time reviewing, debugging regressions, explaining why a PR is wrong, and covering for the one person who understands the compiler, then tests, review, and docs are not red tape. They are the only way to scale without turning every contribution into a core-team project.

The usual framing is “how do we make it easier for outsiders to contribute?” That is the wrong question, because outsider contributions are not uniformly valuable. Some are useful bug fixes. Some are documentation improvements. Some are tests that catch a real edge case. Others are half-designed features, style preferences, or changes that solve the contributor’s problem badly. A small core team does not want to accept more of everything. It wants to accept more of the things that reduce its own future burden: fixes that are correct, features that fit the design, and maintainers who can take ownership of a subsystem without asking the core for every decision.

That is where tests matter most. A contributor who changes a parser rule, a macro, a numerical routine, or a public API and provides a failing test before the fix has already done part of the reviewer’s job. The reviewer does not have to invent the regression, guess the intent, or spend an hour trying to reproduce the bug on three platforms. A PR with no test, by contrast, forces the core team to become the test writer, the risk manager, and the compatibility analyst. For a language, that is expensive because the blast radius is not one user’s script. It is every package that depends on the behavior.

Code review is different. It is not about catching every typo. It is about preserving design coherence. A small team can move fast partly because the same few people share an implicit model of what the language should be. If that model never leaves their heads, every outside contribution is suspicious by default. Review is how the model gets externalized: a reviewer explains not just “this is wrong,” but “this breaks the invariant we rely on in the compiler” or “this API will make the next three years of extensions harder.” The goal is not to make review slow; it is to make the reasons for rejection explicit so contributors can learn the design instead of guessing.

Internal docs are the least glamorous and probably the highest leverage. Public API docs help users, but internal docs help maintainers. A language codebase is full of decisions that are invisible in the code: why the parser is structured this way, why a particular optimization is disabled, why a function has that odd signature, why a certain edge case is undefined. Without notes, every new maintainer re-derives the history. Worse, every core member has to spend time explaining it again. If the core team finds itself repeatedly saying “because the compiler assumes X,” that is a document waiting to be written.

The hardest objection is that process can kill exactly the quality that made the small team effective. A small group can refactor across the compiler, standard library, and REPL in a week. It can change its mind when an early design choice turns out to be wrong. It can keep the language coherent because the people making the changes are the same people who live with the consequences. Add review queues, required tests, and documentation gates, and you may slow that feedback loop down enough to make the project feel bureaucratic. This is a real risk, especially early in a language’s life, when the design is still moving.

The answer is not to avoid process, but to scope it. Stable public behavior should be protected strictly: tests for changes, docs for exported functions, review for anything that affects compatibility or performance. Experimental areas should stay loose. If a feature is uncertain, put it in a package, behind a flag, or in a fork until it has been used. The core should not be the place where every idea is prototyped. In a language like Julia, much of the ecosystem already lives in packages, which is a good thing: it means the core team does not have to absorb every feature request. But the core still owns the parts where mistakes are most expensive: semantics, performance, compatibility, and the basic tools users build on.

A practical test is to look at where core time actually goes. If the team spends most of its time designing and implementing important work, and outside contributions are occasional and low-risk, do not add heavy process. If the team spends a large share of its time reviewing small PRs, chasing regressions, onboarding contributors, answering the same architecture questions, or cleaning up after changes that should have been easier to evaluate, then the project is already paying the cost of missing infrastructure. It is just paying it in hidden labor instead of upfront setup.

The threshold is lower for a language than for a library. A library can often change its API with a major version. A language’s core behavior is embedded in thousands of packages, examples, notebooks, and users’ mental models. Trust is part of the product. Tests and docs are how you maintain that trust without requiring every change to pass through the same two or three people. If the core team is the only place where trust exists, the project will stay small forever, not because it wants to, but because growth would make it less reliable.

So the short answer is: yes, but only as far as it stops the core team from becoming the bottleneck for trust. Add enough CI to make regressions visible, enough tests to make bug fixes verifiable, enough review to protect public behavior, and enough internal docs to make the design legible. Do not add approvals, rituals, or coverage requirements for their own sake. The point is not to let more people in. The point is to let the core team stop doing all the thinking by hand.

prompt: how come people say anti-rape poster campaigns are proven effective? what's the evidence and is it any good?
response:
People usually say “proven effective” because there are evaluations of anti-rape campaigns, but those evaluations usually measure the soft outcomes: awareness, knowledge, and short-term attitude change. That is a real result, but it is not the same as proof that the campaign reduced rape.

The first thing to separate is what “effective” means. A poster campaign might be effective at:

1. getting people to notice the message;
2. making people more likely to say rape is not the victim’s fault;
3. reducing agreement with rape myths, e.g. “she was asking for it,” “he couldn’t control himself,” “if she didn’t fight back it wasn’t really rape”;
4. increasing willingness to report or tell someone;
5. actually reducing the incidence of sexual assault.

The evidence for the first three is the strongest. The evidence for the fourth is patchier and highly context-dependent. The evidence for the fifth is, as far as I can tell, not good enough to support “proven.”

Most of the positive findings come from surveys or short experiments. People are exposed to a poster, PSA, or campaign message, then asked what they think. Compared with people who did not see it, they may be more likely to endorse the message and less likely to endorse rape myths. Those effects are usually modest and often fade over time. That is not nothing: changing public attitudes is a legitimate public-health goal, and reducing rape-myth acceptance can matter for how bystanders respond and how victims are treated afterward. But it is an intermediate outcome, not the final one.

The jump from “people agree less with rape myths” to “there will be fewer rapes” is where the argument gets weak. Rape is not a single kind of behavior that is stopped by a slogan. Much of it happens in relationships, often involving alcohol, often in private, often by someone the victim knows. A poster on a bus shelter, in a bar, or on a campus wall does not, by itself, create the conditions that would deter a specific person at a specific moment: it does not make detection feel certain, does not change the peer group’s norms in real time, and does not remove the opportunity. If the poster says “rape is never OK,” that is a moral statement. It may be true and important, but moral disapproval alone is a weak brake unless it is backed by credible social and institutional consequences.

The hardest case for these campaigns is that they may be part of a broader norm-shift. If posters are repeated, targeted at the right audience, and backed by real reporting procedures, real victim support, and real accountability for perpetrators, then they can make the wider system feel more credible. In that setting, the posters are not doing the work alone; they are the visible face of a policy. That is a plausible mechanism. But it is also exactly why the evidence for “posters” is hard to isolate. If a university puts up posters, trains staff, changes reporting rules, and gets media attention all at once, and then sees a change in attitudes or reports, it is difficult to know how much of the effect came from the posters.

There are also methodological problems. Many campaign evaluations are pre/post designs: measure attitudes before, measure them after. That can pick up the campaign, but it can also pick up other changes: a high-profile trial, a social-media moment, a new campus policy, a change in reporting rules. Some studies compare people who say they saw the campaign with people who did not, but self-reported exposure is biased: people who already care about the issue are more likely to notice and remember the message. Follow-up is often short. And official rape statistics are especially unreliable, because a campaign that makes victims more willing to report can increase recorded rape even if the underlying incidence does not fall.

So is the evidence any good? For “posters can shift some attitudes in some people for a while,” yes, it is reasonable. For “posters reduce rape,” no, not at the level of “proven.” I would treat anti-rape posters as the weakest link in a prevention package, not the engine. They can be useful if they are part of a sustained strategy: clear messages, repeated contact, audience-specific design, and institutional follow-through. They are much less convincing as a standalone claim that a few posters will change the rate of sexual violence.

The useful question is therefore: proven to do what? If the answer is “make people aware that rape is not the victim’s fault,” that may be defensible. If the answer is “fewer rapes,” that is a much stronger claim and, in my view, not supported.

prompt: Why does everyone complain about lag on tablets and VR headsets but nobody seems to care about keyboard-to-screen latency on a normal computer? Is keyboard input just inherently less sensitive to delay?
response:
Part of the premise is false. People do care about input-to-screen latency on ordinary computers; gamers measure monitor input lag, mouse polling, frame time, and “input lag” in games. What is rare is complaints about keyboards specifically. The reason is not that keyboard delay is invisible, but that it is usually small and, more importantly, it sits in a different kind of control loop.

A key press is a discrete event. You decide to press A, your finger moves, the switch closes, the operating system receives an event, the application inserts a character. You do not need to see the character before deciding the next key. Touch typing is largely a motor routine: the screen confirms the sequence, but it does not steer each finger. If the confirmation is late, the sentence feels sluggish; if it is a few tens of milliseconds late, most people do not notice.

Touch and VR are continuous. While your finger is on the glass, the system is supposed to tell you where the finger is and what is happening under it. If that answer is 50 ms old, you are looking at a highlight that is no longer under your finger, and your next micro-correction is based on the wrong place. The same is true of a mouse: the cursor is a moving object, and each new hand motion is partly a correction of where the cursor just was. Add delay and the cursor trails, overshoots, feels floaty. In VR the problem is worse because the inner ear reports head motion almost immediately; if the visual scene follows 30 or 50 ms behind, the brain gets two different stories and the result is discomfort.

Spatial coincidence makes the delay visible. On a tablet, the input and output are at the same place: finger, touch, highlight. A mismatch is easy to see. On a keyboard, the input is on your lap or desk and the output is a row of text. There is no continuous object to compare. A delayed key event does not create a visible gap between hand and effect; it only changes the tempo of an abstract sequence.

The thresholds differ, not by magic but by bandwidth and error cost. A USB keyboard sampled at 1000 Hz can report in about 1 ms; even a 125 Hz keyboard adds at most 8 ms. A 60 Hz display may wait up to 16.7 ms for the next frame; a 144 Hz display up to 6.9 ms. Those numbers are already near or below the level where discrete typing feels bad. In VR, the commonly quoted target for motion-to-photon latency is well under 20 ms because the vestibular system does not forgive it. For touch, tens of milliseconds can feel soft and a hundred feels laggy; for keyboard, a few tens is transparent and a couple of hundred makes typing feel dead, but you can still do it.

That does not mean keyboard latency is irrelevant. It is very relevant when the task is timing rather than tracking: typing at speed, rhythm games, competitive fighting games, remote desktops, virtual machines, or any setup where the OS or network adds a visible pause. prompt: can you build a startup hub like Silicon Valley in another city, or is it a one-off? what would it actually take?
response:
You can build a startup hub, but not by building a smaller Silicon Valley. Silicon Valley is a one-off as a historical object: it was made by a particular combination of American institutions, postwar technology waves, a huge domestic market, immigration, universities, defense spending, semiconductors, venture capital norms, and a culture that tolerated technical risk. You cannot reorder those events in another city.

But the thing people usually mean by “a hub” is not the specific valley. It is a dense system where founders, investors, engineers, lawyers, accountants, recruiters, operators, and customers form a network that repeatedly produces globally competitive companies. That kind of system is repeatable, though usually around a wedge, not as a full copy.

The hard part is not the startups. It is the second-order effects.

In a real hub, a failed company is a hiring pool for the next one. A CFO who ran a failed Series B company knows how to help the next founder avoid the same mistake. A lawyer has templates for stock options, data room requests, and customer contracts. An investor has seen enough local founders to know which red flags matter. A university lab has a pipeline of people who want to build, not just publish. A supplier knows what a hardware prototype needs. A media outlet covers deals because there are deals to cover.

That density lowers the cost of starting and scaling. A city can have two hundred startups and still not be a hub if the CTOs commute in from elsewhere, the investors sit in London, the lawyers are generalists, and the best engineers leave after two years. The hub is the labor market for startup roles, not the number of companies on a map.

This is why Silicon Valley looks unrepeatable. It became the default place because it crossed a threshold early. Once the best technical people, investors, and service providers concentrated there, the network effects became self-reinforcing. A founder comparing cities is not asking, “Which city has the best slogan?” The founder is asking where the hire will be faster, the round will close faster, the customer will trust the product faster, and the exit will be easier. Existing hubs win that comparison by default unless another city is clearly better at something specific.

Other places have built hubs by being better at something specific.

Tel Aviv shows how a small city can become a global node. It had a concentrated pool of mathematically strong people, defense and university research, a culture of building security and communications products, and access to U.S. customers and investors. It did not become a second Silicon Valley in scale. It became one of the world’s centers for cybersecurity and certain kinds of applied software. That is enough to make it a hub.

Bangalore shows a different route. It has enormous engineering talent, English-language fluency, low relative labor costs, and decades of IT services that produced managers, product people, and systems builders. Those people later founded companies selling to global customers. Bangalore’s ceiling has less to do with absence of founders and more to do with capital depth, governance, regulatory friction, and exit culture. It is a hub, but a hub with different constraints.

Shenzhen shows that a hub does not have to look like app-layer venture capital. Its advantage is hardware: components, factories, supply-chain speed, manufacturing talent, tooling, and a huge domestic market. It produces consumer electronics, drones, batteries, and hardware companies through a mix of state capital, private capital, and industrial networks. It is not Silicon Valley, but it is a real innovation system built around a different stack.

Singapore shows what law, tax, capital, and connectivity can do. It can become a place where funds, holding companies, regional headquarters, and wealthy families put money. But without a large native founder base and a deep local labor market, it produces fewer homegrown global product companies relative to its financial importance. It is a capital hub more than a founder hub.

Toronto, Berlin, London, and New York show that second hubs usually specialize. Toronto has had world-class AI research but a thinner record of turning that research into large global product companies. Berlin has talent, culture, and engineering skill, but has had to work harder for late-stage capital and exits. London has capital, finance talent, and global connections, which is why it became strong in fintech. New York has media, finance, consumers, and ambition, but its startup system is shaped by those industries rather than by the pure software scaling model of the valley.

The pattern is that a new hub rarely beats the existing center at everything. It wins by making one kind of company cheaper, faster, or more likely to succeed.

So what would it actually take?

First, a city needs a wedge. “We are going to build a tech ecosystem” is not a strategy. The wedge has to come from a real local advantage: a university lab with a strange capability, an industry with margins, a regulatory regime, a supply chain, a diaspora, a customer base, a legal regime, or a talent pool. Cybersecurity, fintech, developer tools, health data, energy software, agritech, robotics, space, gaming, and AI applications are all possible wedges, but only if the city has a reason to win in that area. The wedge matters because the first investors, first hires, and first customers are domain-specific. A person who has built a payment company understands payment companies. A person who has built a medical device understands regulatory pain. General “startup” expertise is useful, but domain expertise is what creates the first cluster.

Second, it needs a capital stack that can absorb failure. Venture capital is a portfolio business. Most early companies fail or stagnate; a few pay for the rest. If local investors need every company to succeed, they will fund safe expansions, not risky products. A hub needs angels who write first checks, seed funds that can close rounds quickly, growth capital that can follow companies beyond the early stage, and limited partners with long horizons: family offices, endowments, pensions, insurers, or sovereign funds willing to accept illiquidity.

It also needs exits. Investors need to know that a winner can be sold to a global strategic buyer or taken public. If the only exit is “we hope it grows,” early-stage capital dries up. A city does not need to produce a Google. It needs to produce enough winners that the local investor class can say, “We lost eight, but the ninth paid for the fund.”

Third, it needs talent inflow and mobility. Local universities are necessary but not sufficient. No city has enough native talent to build a global company by itself. Silicon Valley is a net immigrant economy in practice: it depends on people moving in from other U.S. states and other countries. A new hub needs visas, work permits, spousal work authorization, school access, housing, and a reason for outsiders to move. It also needs labor mobility. If employees cannot move between companies, the ecosystem becomes a set of fiefdoms. If failure is a permanent stigma, the best people choose banks, consultancies, or the civil service. If employment law makes hiring and firing agonizing, early companies hire too slowly and too few.

Fourth, it needs boring institutions. This is where most attempts fail. A founder should be able to incorporate, grant equity, sign a customer contract, protect intellectual property, hire foreign talent, raise from an investor, and enforce a deal without fearing arbitrary reversal. Contracts, bankruptcy, tax certainty, data rules, currency convertibility, and the absence of corrupt licensing matter more than co-working spaces. In places where access to permits depends on relationships, startups become small local firms. Rule of law is the difference between a business and a venture in the risky sense.

Fifth, it needs access to global demand. A city of two million people cannot support a global software company by buying from its own residents. The first meaningful customers often have to be outside. Public procurement can help as a testbed, especially in deep tech: government agencies can buy the first smart-grid system, the first hospital analytics platform, the first autonomous port pilot. But if the government becomes the main customer, the ecosystem learns to sell to the government. That produces a different kind of company, and it often cannot scale globally.

Sixth, it needs public goods, but not picked champions. Governments can help a lot by improving the commons: universities, basic research, datasets, test facilities, energy, compute access, broadband, transit, housing, and regulatory clarity. In AI, energy and compute access may matter more than a logo on a building. In biotech, wet labs, clinical trial infrastructure, and regulatory pathways matter. In hardware, supply-chain testbeds and manufacturing partners matter. The state should make the commons better, not sit on the board of the favorite company.

A government fund can be useful if it behaves like a limited partner: it writes checks, takes a minority position, stays out of daily operations, and accepts portfolio risk. It becomes harmful if it demands control, local job quotas, political loyalty, or guaranteed returns. Then founders learn that the state is a customer with strings, not a referee.

Seventh, it needs density and reputation, but those are symptoms, not causes. Conferences, media coverage, visible exits, and a local narrative reduce search costs. They help investors find founders, founders find talent, and customers find suppliers. But if a city builds the conference before it has the companies, it is wearing a costume. The reputation follows the proof: a company that reaches serious revenue, an acquisition by a global firm, a product that people outside the city use.

The hardest objection to building a hub is simple: if it can be done, why are there not more of them?

Because the pieces are interdependent, and existing hubs have inertia. A new city does not need to beat Silicon Valley at everything. It needs to be materially better at one wedge. If it is not, founders and capital will keep going to the place where the network is already dense. That is why second hubs specialize. They do not try to become the center of the universe. They become the best place to build a particular kind of company.

There is also a timing problem. The biggest prize of the last few decades was global internet: a U.S.-built consumer and enterprise platform that could be sold everywhere. That window has largely closed. New hubs are more likely to form around new layers: AI applications, energy, biotech, robotics, defense tech, space, advanced manufacturing, or regional platforms that serve large non-U.S. markets. A city that tries to build “the next internet company” without a specific advantage is chasing a wave that already passed.

The failure modes are predictable.

A city builds accelerators, but there is no local capital to fund the companies after the demo day. A city offers tax breaks, but the legal system is slow and contracts are uncertain. A city opens a government venture fund, but the fund picks companies politically. A city restricts immigration, so the talent pool stops growing. A city makes employment law so rigid that startups cannot reorganize. A city builds a shiny district, but housing becomes unaffordable before companies reach scale, so junior engineers and support staff cannot live there. A city brands itself as an “AI hub,” but it has no compute, no data, no domain talent, and no customers who need the products.

The realistic target is not to become the next Silicon Valley. It is to become the place where a particular kind of company is easiest to build.

The minimum proof looks like this: a city has twenty or thirty credible companies in a wedge, a handful of local investors who can write seed and Series A checks, a first exit or a company with serious global revenue, and a labor market where people can move between those companies without leaving. At that point, the ecosystem stops being a program and starts being a system.

That takes a decade or more. It cannot be announced. It cannot be imported as a brand. It is built by reducing friction, opening talent flows, making capital patient, improving the boring institutions, and waiting for the first local winner to show that the system works.

The sign that it is working is not the number of startups on a slide. It is whether the next competent founder chooses the city because the hire, the round, the customer, and the scale-up are easier there. If the answer is yes, the hub is real. If the answer is no, the city has only built a picture of one.

prompt: Do you think we actually understand deep learning yet, or is the field still pretty ad hoc? Write a few paragraphs on it.
response:
The fair answer depends on what you mean by understand. If you mean “can we build, scale, and debug large models with confidence?”, then yes, the field is no longer ad hoc in any crude sense. Backpropagation is chain-rule bookkeeping, convolutions impose locality and weight sharing, attention is a differentiable routing operation, and residual connections make deep stacks trainable by giving gradients a stable path. We also have partial theories that explain real behavior: very wide networks approximate kernel methods during training, loss tends to scale as power laws with parameters, data, and compute, and overparameterized models can reach low training error despite nonconvex losses.

What we lack is a predictive account of the hard parts. We can often prove that a large network will fit its training data, but fitting is not the mystery. The mystery is that it also performs well on new data, sometimes with surprisingly little task-specific supervision. A small net on MNIST is close to something we can analyze; a large transformer trained on the web is not. We have candidate explanations—feature learning, implicit regularization, composition of representations, data structure—but they do not tell us in advance which architecture will work, how much data is enough, or why a change that looks harmless in a small model matters in a large one. A lot of practice is still driven by measured heuristics: weight decay, dropout, label smoothing, learning-rate warmup, Adam versus SGD with momentum, data augmentation, and schedule changes. We can ablate them, but we usually cannot derive them.

The strongest objection to calling the field ad hoc is that many useful technologies outrun their theories. Early radio engineers built receivers without quantum mechanics, and aircraft are designed without a complete microscopic theory of turbulence. Deep learning may be in the same place: an engineering discipline with a partial scientific core. Scaling laws are not derived from first principles, yet they are useful for estimating how much more compute or data will improve a model. That kind of understanding is not nothing.

The field is past the stage where success looks like magic, but it is not yet a closed theory. We understand the components, many failure modes, and the economics of training. We do not yet understand the boundary between what scale enables and what it does not, or why the same ingredients produce different capabilities at different sizes. The result is a productive but still empirical field: we run the experiment, read the curve, and revise the heuristics.

prompt: How did Steven Pressfield finally manage to finish a book after years of calling himself a writer?
response:
Pressfield’s answer is unglamorous: he stopped letting the identity of “writer” stand in for the work.

By his own account, he had spent about thirty years calling himself a professional writer while producing screenplays and novels that never got produced or published. The habit, as he describes it, was not just bad luck; it was a form of self-protection. Calling himself a writer let him remain connected to the idea of writing without having to finish something real.

The change came when he made a fixed commitment to finish a book. He wrote *The Legend of Bagger Vance* in about twenty days, working toward a deadline instead of waiting for the right mood, the right idea, or a draft that already felt good. In his formulation, he “stopped being a writer and started working.”

So the finish was not a sudden burst of inspiration. It was the result of showing up daily, producing a draft, and refusing to let doubt decide the day’s output.

prompt: Why do some bloggers refuse to promote friends' projects? Explain it as if you were one of them.
response:
I’m not refusing because I dislike the person. I’m refusing because a recommendation is not a kindness I can spend on someone I know. It is a claim I make to readers.

When I write “try this,” I am saying: I looked at it, I can stand behind it, I think it is worth your time. My readers gave me something finite. If I use my credibility to move a friend’s product, I have to ask whether the product survives the standard I would apply to a stranger’s. Most of the time, I don’t know. I know the friend, not the thing. I know their intentions, their late nights, the way they explain the idea at dinner. That is evidence about them, not about the landing page, the pricing, the support, the retention, the actual experience of using it. If I say “check this out” and the thing is mediocre, the reader pays the price. They lose twenty minutes, or thirty dollars, or trust.

The hardest objection is that I’m just jealous. I’ll grant that it is sometimes true. It is painful to watch someone you like ship a thing you didn’t, especially if it is good. But if I let envy decide what I recommend, my audience gets a mood board, not a filter. Sometimes I don’t want to be the person who says “congrats” in public and then quietly seethes in private. If the project is genuinely good, I can say that. If it isn’t, I don’t get to hide my discomfort inside a shout-out.

There is also a simpler arithmetic. A blog is a small machine for attention. Every post I write about a friend’s launch is a post I don’t write about my own work, my own opinions, or something I actually need to process. If I become a clearinghouse for people I know, the blog stops being a place where I have a point of view. It becomes a bulletin board. Readers don’t follow bulletin boards.

And the friendship changes. Once I promote, the ask gets easier for them and harder for me. The next project arrives with the same smile: “You already did it once.” I stop being able to say no without sounding like the person who bailed. I also start editing my honest opinions in private. If I told their last idea it was overbuilt, will they still send me the next one? If I didn’t tell them, I have already lost a useful kind of friendship.

So I don’t promote by default. I promote when the thing is good enough that I would recommend it to a reader who dislikes me a little. If a friend’s project clears that bar, I will write about it and say their name. If it doesn’t, I will still help in ways that don’t require my readers: I will read it, I will tell them what is confusing, I will introduce them to one or two people who might actually care. That is not nothing. It is just not the same as asking strangers to give me their time on my friend’s behalf.

prompt: I'm stuck in silver in Overwatch and everyone says you have to play DPS to climb out of low ranks. Is that actually true?
response:
Mostly, but only as a default. In Silver, games are often decided by who can reliably hit shots, take good angles, and not die when their team is out of position. DPS is the role where those skills show up most directly, so a player who is mechanically better than the local average will usually climb faster on DPS. That is the real reason the advice exists.

If you are already playing DPS and still stuck, the role is not the problem. The problem is one of the usual things: missing shots, picking a hero that does not fit the map, standing in the open, chasing kills when your team is dead, or playing a comp that cannot survive a coordinated fight. Switching to another DPS hero will not fix that.

Where you are in Silver matters. Lower Silver often has players who do not understand peel, ult timers, or map control, so a mechanically strong DPS can look almost unfair. By upper Silver, you will meet enough players who know how to focus you, so the same Tracer or Reaper can become much less effective if your team is not set up to support the pick.

The strongest objection to “play DPS” is that low-rank games still have team composition. A 3-2 team can win if its DPS is better, but it can also lose badly if the enemy tank and support are disciplined. If you pick Tracer and miss every shot, you have not carried; you have just made your team’s damage worse. If you pick Reaper and flank into three people, you are not playing aggressively, you are dying. The advice assumes you can do the basic mechanical tasks that make DPS valuable: land enough shots to force trades, reposition when your tank or support is down, and back off before you become a free kill.

A concrete case makes the point. On a 2-2-2 map, your team has two DPS, a tank, and a support. If your DPS can hit the enemy tank’s face while your tank trades, you win space. If your DPS is standing in the middle and dies to the tank’s dash, the same comp loses. The composition did not change. The execution did. That is what people mean when they say DPS carries in low ranks.

Support can climb out of Silver too, but it usually asks a different thing. A support who stays behind the tank, lands utility, and tracks ults can keep a team alive long enough for the DPS to win. A support who steps out to chase a kill gets deleted, and then the tank dies ten seconds later. You can win with support by preventing losses rather than creating kills. That feels less satisfying, so fewer people recommend it, but it is real.

The same is true for tank. A Reinhardt who charges only when his team is in position can win Silver. A Reinhardt who charges whenever he sees a head loses. A Winston who forces the fight on his terms can make a bad team look competent. A Winston who dives into a full-health backline makes the team lose space. Tank can climb, but it is unforgiving: if your team cannot follow up, you die alone and the fight is over.

So the better question is not “DPS or not DPS” but “what can I do reliably?” If you can land shots and reposition, DPS is probably your fastest route. If you are better at reading fights and keeping people alive, support may be better even if your KDA looks worse. If you are good at choosing when to engage and protecting your team, tank can climb. In Silver, the role that lets you avoid depending on your teammates’ mistakes is the role that wins.

For a practical test, pick one role and two heroes for your next 20 games. If you try DPS, choose one hero that rewards steady aim and one that rewards positioning, and after each loss ask why you died: missed shot, bad angle, team dead, or bad pick? If the answer is mostly your shots or positioning, keep working at DPS. If the answer is mostly “my team died first and I had no answer,” you may be better suited to support or tank. DPS is the most common answer in Silver because it is the most common place where one player can change the outcome. But it is not a universal rule; it is a shortcut for players whose skills already match the demands of the role.

prompt: we can't match big-company salaries. what are some cheap ways to make employees feel valued and keep them from leaving?
response:
If you cannot match big-company salaries, the first thing to accept is that some people will leave for money, and no amount of recognition replaces a real offer. But many departures are not pure money. They are lower pay plus a worse manager, less autonomy, more busywork, slower growth, or feeling like a replaceable pair of hands. If you improve enough of those, the pay gap becomes easier to live with.

Before buying anything, look at where people actually leave. If your best performers leave within two years for noticeably more pay, you have a pay problem, and the cheap fixes are only a bandage. If people leave after a bad manager, after a missed promotion, after a crunch, or after six months of onboarding that made them feel foolish, you have a different problem. Exit interviews are useful, but patterns are more honest: tenure, team, manager, destination employer, and the event before the resignation.

Cheap usually means low cash cost, not zero effort. The effort is mostly managerial.

- **Give real control over the work.**  
  Not just “flexible hours” in a handbook. Let people choose how they get things done: order of tasks, tools, schedule, and where they work when possible. If you require in-office presence from 9 to 5 while also monitoring productivity, flexibility is theater. A concrete version: let an engineer pick one maintenance task, let a salesperson set their own call schedule within coverage rules, let an admin choose which recurring forms to digitize. Autonomy feels like pay because it returns time and dignity.

- **Make their contribution visible.**  
  Big companies can make people small; small companies can make people legible. Put their name on the result. In a client email: “Dana built the reporting layer that caught the billing error.” In a team meeting: show the metric their work moved. A specific public credit is cheaper than a plaque and more believable. People stay when they can point to what they made.

- **Fix the manager.**  
  Often the immediate trigger for leaving is not the company but the manager. Weekly one-on-ones should not be status updates. They should ask: What is slowing you down? What should I stop doing? What do you want to be better at? What would make next quarter easier? If a manager’s team keeps leaking people, retrain them or move them out of people management. This is one of the highest-return “cheap” moves available.

- **Be transparent about money and promotion.**  
  If you cannot pay market rates, at least do not be arbitrary. Publish salary bands, promotion criteria, and review dates. When you say no to a raise, say why and what would change the answer. Resentment often comes from not knowing the rules. A person can tolerate a lower number better than a mysterious one.

- **Cut the invisible work.**  
  Meetings, approvals, status updates, bad tools, waiting for access, duplicated reporting. Ask each team to kill one recurring meeting or simplify one process. If a 25-minute daily standup can be a written update, make it one. Time is compensation. A day returned to real work is worth more than a branded mug.

- **Make the job grow the person.**  
  If you cannot promote, broaden. Let a support person spend one day a week on product questions. Let an analyst shadow sales. Let a junior employee own a small project end to end. Pay for a certification or conference when it connects to the role. The question is not “Can we give them a corner office?” but “Will they be better at their trade here in a year than elsewhere?”

- **Respect the life outside work.**  
  Flexible start times, remote days, no 10 p.m. messages, realistic deadlines. If a parent can work around school without asking permission, that may be worth more than a gift card. If you genuinely need availability, say what you need, when you need it, and pay for it. Constant low-grade urgency is a retention tax.

- **Recognize with opportunities, not slogans.**  
  The best “thank you” is a better assignment, an introduction to a decision-maker, a chance to present, a title that matches responsibility, or a line in their performance review that they can use later. Recognition should be specific: “Your rewrite of the onboarding email reduced bounce-backs” beats “You’re a star.” Vague praise starts to sound like management decoration.

- **Make practical things easier.**  
  A better laptop, an ergonomic chair, a home internet stipend, a transit pass, a health plan that actually works. These are small individually, but they signal whether the company thinks about the person or only the output. They also remove small daily frictions that accumulate into quitting.

- **Spend small money where it changes a decision.**  
  A modest one-time bonus, extra paid time off, or a retention agreement for the person most likely to leave can be cheaper than replacement. If you have equity, a small meaningful grant can matter, but only if the company has a plausible future. Targeted money is not “cheap,” but it is sometimes cheaper than losing someone expensive to replace.

- **Be honest about what you cannot offer.**  
  If someone asks for a raise and you cannot match it, say so plainly. Offer what you can: a project, a title, a review date, a one-time bonus, remote days, or a path to more money later. A clear no with a plan beats a vague “we’ll see.” People can work for less if they believe the company is straight with them.

What does not work:

- Free food, casual Friday, ping-pong tables, and mandatory team-building days. People do not stay for snacks. They may tolerate them.
- Titles without pay or authority.
- Forced positivity and loyalty language.
- Keeping people busy to avoid thinking about compensation.
- Using “family” language to extract unpaid work.

The hard limit is this: you cannot simultaneously underpay, overwork, and expect loyalty. If you are losing your best people to higher salaries, the non-pay improvements are not enough. You can either pay more, accept higher churn, or hire for the tradeoff: earlier-career people, people less marketable in that exact role, people who need flexibility, people who want ownership, people who care more about the work than the badge.

When money is fixed, the question becomes whether the job is worth the difference. Make it worth the difference, or accept that it is not. The first step is to stop guessing: map who left, where they went, and what they said. Then fix the cluster, not the culture.

prompt: Should I quit my job and start a company? I've been asking successful people for advice but it's all contradictory. Why?
response:
I can’t tell you whether to quit, but I can tell you why the advice feels useless: you are asking people who have already survived a risky sequence of events to explain the rules. The successful founders you meet are the visible ones. The ones who quit, burned savings, and returned to a job are not giving talks, and if they do, their story often sounds like “I was wrong.” So when one person says “do it” and another says “don’t,” they are not necessarily contradicting each other. They are reporting from different survivor pools.

There is also an incentive problem. Not all successful people want the same thing. An investor may cheer you on because new founders mean new deals. A senior employee may counsel caution because leaving makes them lose a good colleague or exposes their own untested side project. A founder may romanticize the leap because it made their story dramatic. You are not getting advice; you are getting positions.

Many successful people are also giving you the advice they wish they had received, or the advice that fits the story they tell. “I should have quit earlier” and “I almost ruined my life by quitting too early” can both be true, often in the same person. Their sample size is one. Their circumstances are not yours. Their risk tolerance, savings, skills, network, family situation, and luck are all different.

The real question is not “Is starting a company a good idea?” It is: “Does my specific company have enough real demand that my job is now the constraint?”

If you cannot name the customer, the problem, and the first thing they would pay for, do not quit. If you can, run the smallest test that could prove you wrong: a landing page, a manual service, a prototype, a pre-order, a pilot. The number matters less than the commitment. Will ten target customers pay, sign a letter of intent, or give you a real introduction? If the answer is no, you have saved yourself a resignation. If the answer is yes and the business is growing fast enough that working on it eight hours a week is costing you customers, then quitting becomes rational.

Before you leave, set a trigger, not a hope. For example: “I will quit if I have $5,000 monthly recurring revenue and a 12-month runway,” or “I will quit if I lose a clear customer opportunity because I cannot respond during work hours.” Without a trigger, you will either quit too early or drift for years, telling yourself you are “close.”

The strongest case for quitting immediately is that some opportunities are time-sensitive: a market window, a team, a customer who will only talk now. That can be true. But if the opportunity is truly time-sensitive, the evidence should be visible now: someone is willing to pay, commit, or act this month. If it is mostly in your head, the urgency is a feeling, not a fact, and a feeling is a bad reason to give up salary, benefits, and optionality.

Your personal constraints are part of the business case. Debt, dependents, health, location, and how long you can survive without income change the answer. A startup is not just a product; it is also a financial plan and a stress test.

So the practical answer is usually no, not yet, unless your current business is already pulling you forward. Keep the job. Use it to fund the experiment. Quit when the company has customers and the job is demonstrably blocking growth, not before.

prompt: Do you ever notice how your friend group doesn't look like the general population at all, even though you never chose it that way?
response:
I don’t have a friend group, but the thing you’re describing is one of the clearest ways to see how social life gets organized. A person’s close friends rarely resemble a random sample of the people around them, let alone the national population. The obvious reason is that you meet people where you already are: school, workplace, neighborhood, gym, parent group, online community. Those places are already sorted by age, income, education, language, and life stage. A graduate student in Chicago, a line cook in Tucson, a new parent in a suburb, and a retiree in a small town are drawing from four different pools. The national census is not the relevant pool; the relevant pool is the set of people whose schedules and locations intersect with yours often enough for friendship to form.

The less obvious filtering happens after the first meeting. Friendship is expensive in time. It requires repeated, unforced contact, similar rhythms, and enough mutual interest to keep showing up. A group that meets after work in a certain neighborhood, goes to certain events, or travels on certain weekends will drift toward people who can absorb that time and cost. It will also drift toward people who find the conversation easy. That ease often tracks shared class, education, and assumptions, not just personality. So a friend group can become self-renewing: existing members bring in newcomers who are somewhat like them, and the group’s habits make it harder for outsiders to enter.

When you say “look,” the visible part is the easiest to see: age, bodies, clothes, race, the whole surface. But the same sorting is in the invisible part too—what people assume, how they spend money, what they find funny, what they consider a normal week. A group of friends may look similar because they were produced by similar conditions, and then they begin to think and behave similar because they keep spending unforced time together.

The “never chose it” part is both right and misleading. You did not choose a demographic profile. Nobody sits down and decides the age range, racial mix, income level, and political temperature of their close circle. But you did choose, or were placed in, the institutions that produce the profile: where to live, what job to take, whether to have kids, which hobby to pursue, which arguments to have, which friendships to keep investing in. Those choices are small and local, but they add up. If you move to a city, join a professional field, and spend Saturdays at a climbing gym, you have not selected a type of friend, but you have selected a type of life, and the friends arrive with it.

Sometimes the mismatch with the general population is just arithmetic. The general population includes children, very old people, people with disabilities, people in occupations you will never enter, and people living in places you will never visit. A group of thirty-something urban professionals is not supposed to look like that. The more striking case is when the friend group does not even resemble the local adult population. That is where the sorting shows up: in a diverse city, your close circle may still be narrow; in a small town, it may look like the town but not like the country. In both cases, the circle is a slice of a slice.

There is a harder question underneath: if the group is not chosen, is it accidental? Not entirely. Accidents bring people into the room; maintenance decides who stays. You can meet a wide range of people by chance, but you will keep close only those with whom contact is easy and rewarding. That is why friend groups often feel inevitable in retrospect. They look like a portrait of you, but they are also a portrait of the logistics of your life: the commute, the salary, the neighborhood, the hours, the institutions, and the small daily decisions about who gets called back.

prompt: I feel completely unmotivated today, nothing seems worth doing. What should I do with a day like this?
response:
The first thing not to do is turn the day into a moral problem. “Nothing seems worth doing” can sound like a verdict on you, but it is usually just a state: low energy, low reward, maybe too much input and too little movement. On a day like this, the goal is not to find meaning. It is to avoid becoming a lump of guilt and scrolling.

Do not try to motivate yourself. Motivation is unreliable, especially when you are already depleted. Instead, lower the task until it is almost absurdly small. Not “clean the kitchen,” but put one cup in the dishwasher. Not “get in shape,” but put on shoes. Not “have a productive day,” but sit up and drink water. The point is not the task. The point is to interrupt the loop where your body stays still and your mind keeps judging you for it.

Pick one physical change first. Get out of bed if you are in it. Open a window. Wash your face. Make tea, even if you do not drink it. Walk to the end of the street and back. These are not fixes. They are levers. They do not require you to feel like anything. They only require a small amount of movement, and movement can loosen the stuckness enough for the next choice to feel possible.

If you have obligations, do the minimum version. Reply to the message with one sentence. Do the smallest part of the work. Eat something bland but real. Take the medication if that is part of your life. Keep the floor under you. A bad day does not need to become a collapsed day.

Be careful with rest, though. Rest is useful when it actually restores you. Rumination is not rest. Lying there feeling worthless while the hours pass is not recovery; it is just suffering with the lights off. If you decide to rest, give it a shape. “I will lie down for forty minutes, then I will wash my face and make lunch.” Rest without a return time often becomes the whole day, and the whole day becomes heavier.

Also, do not make big decisions today. Do not quit, confess, rearrange your life, or decide that everything you have been doing is pointless. Low states distort judgment. They make the familiar feel dead and the dramatic feel clear. Let the day stay small.

If this is a one-day dip, the above may be enough. But if “nothing seems worth doing” is your weather for weeks, or if it comes with hopelessness, numbness, sleep problems, or thoughts that you would be better off gone, that is not a discipline issue. That is a signal to get help: a doctor, therapist, someone you trust, a crisis line if you feel unsafe. You do not have to white-knuckle a depressive state into evidence that you are fine.

For the next hour, do not ask whether life is worth doing. Ask only: what is the smallest physical action that would make the next ten minutes slightly less stuck? Do that. Then ask again.

prompt: Polls say a huge share of Americans would give a kidney to a stranger, yet almost nobody actually does. Why is the gap so enormous? Is everyone just lying?
response:
No, not in the simple sense. Some people are giving the answer that makes them look good, even to themselves. But most are not sitting there calculating a lie. They are answering a different question from the one the act actually asks.

When a poll asks, “Would you give a kidney to a stranger?” it is not asking, “Will you submit to major surgery, take weeks off work, recover in pain, and live for the rest of your life with one kidney?” It is asking, “Do you see yourself as the kind of person who would do that?” That is a question about identity, not a medical form. A person can sincerely believe they are the kind of person who sacrifices a body part for someone in need, and still not do it when the surgeon calls.

The numbers make the point. In the United States, thousands of living kidney transplants happen every year, but most donors are relatives, partners, friends, or otherwise connected to the recipient. Anonymous, non-directed donation to a stranger is a small sliver of living donation. If a poll suggests that tens of millions of Americans would do it, the actual number of people who make that anonymous leap is a tiny fraction of that pool. That is not a rounding error. It is a different phenomenon.

A little of the gap is social desirability. Saying no to a stranger who might die sounds bad. But social pressure alone does not explain it. People also overstate what they will do in many private, low-stakes contexts: they will exercise more, spend less, give more, be more patient, be braver. The pattern is not usually deception. It is that a survey presents the choice in the best possible light: no pain, no paperwork, no one waiting on you, no calendar, no body.

The real act is full of concrete frictions. Imagine the sequence. You say yes in principle. Months later, a coordinator calls. You need bloodwork. Then imaging. Then a urologist, a cardiologist, maybe a psychosocial interview. You need time off work. You may need to stop certain medications. You may have to discuss your health history with people you do not know. You will be anesthetized, cut into, and sent home with a plan for pain, activity limits, and follow-up visits. Your spouse or partner may be uneasy. Your employer may be vague. Your insurance may cover the donation but not every downstream worry the way you hoped. At each step, the person who answered a survey can say, “I need to think about it,” without being a monster. The poll never asked any of those questions.

There is also the problem of the stranger. Human generosity is much stronger when the recipient is visible. We give more to a named child, a neighbor, a friend, a person whose story we can hold in our heads. Anonymous donation removes the feedback loop. You will not meet the recipient. You will not get a thank-you card, a photo, a story about their recovery. Their life may be transformed, but you may never know the details. Some people are motivated by exactly that: the purity of giving without recognition. But most people are not built that way. We are more likely to act when the good deed returns something—gratitude, pride, social acknowledgment, a relationship. A stranger gives none of that.

The transplant system itself is a filter. To become a non-directed donor, you do not simply click a button. You enter an evaluation process. You must be medically suitable, matched, scheduled, and cleared by multiple professionals. Some people are genuinely unsuitable because of age, health, medications, or other risks. But many others are lost to the sheer weight of the process. The system is not designed as a simple opt-in. It is a funnel, and funnels discard people.

In the United States, there are also practical fears that a poll does not mention. Will an employer treat a kidney donation leave like any other medical leave? Will a complication be fully covered? Will a future job application involve a medical question that makes the missing kidney a problem? Will a family member make it difficult? These worries are not always justified, but they are real. A person can be morally willing and still rationally hesitate when the consequences touch their job, insurance, and household.

The people who actually donate to strangers are also not the average poll respondent. They often have a prior connection to dialysis or kidney disease. They may belong to a religious or community tradition that makes the act feel ordinary rather than heroic. They may have entered a paired exchange, where their donation helps unlock a chain of transplants, giving the act a traceable shape. The poll averages over everyone, including people for whom the idea of giving up an organ is so remote that the yes is almost automatic.

The hardest objection to this explanation is that the system may be suppressing a lot of real willingness. That is partly true. If donor protections were universal, if the process were simpler, if the social and medical infrastructure made the path less frightening, more people would follow through. The current system probably turns away some people who would otherwise donate. But even a frictionless system would not turn half the population into kidney donors. The central barrier is not just bureaucracy. It is that a person is being asked to convert a moral symbol into a body part.

So the gap is not mainly a gap between truth and falsehood. It is a gap between a word and a body. A poll answer is cheap. It costs nothing and commits nothing. It captures a preference under ideal conditions: no pain, no risk, no one watching, no recovery. The act removes those conditions. People are not all lying. They are just answering the easy version of the question.

prompt: Is the slippery slope argument ever a good reason to oppose something that seems reasonable on its own?
response:
Yes—but only when it is a real prediction about how institutions move, not a picture of a bad future.

A slippery slope is not a special kind of logic. It is a claim that A will make B more likely, B will make C more likely, and C is bad enough to matter. That claim can be true. The bad version of the argument is: “If we allow X, eventually we’ll allow Y, so we must stop X.” The good version is: “X removes a specific legal or social barrier; once removed, officials or markets have an incentive to cross it; similar cases have crossed it; the harm at the end is severe; and the first step’s benefits do not outweigh the risk.”

Four things make the argument credible. First, a mechanism: what exactly changes after the first step that makes the next step easier? Not just “people will push further,” but a change in law, budget, personnel, social permission, or market incentive. Second, a base rate: have comparable steps actually expanded? Third, magnitude: is the endpoint serious enough to justify blocking or conditioning the first step? Fourth, brakes: is there a realistic way to stop before the bottom?

A concrete case is flavored e-cigarettes. Letting adults use flavored e-cigarettes seemed reasonable on its own: many smokers are less likely to switch from cigarettes if the alternative tastes like a cigarette. But flavors also made the product easier for adolescents to try and keep using. U.S. high school e-cigarette use rose from about 5 percent in 2012 to about 20 percent by 2018. The slope was not magical. It ran through product design, marketing, social imitation, and weak regulation. Someone who opposed broad availability of flavored e-cigarettes in 2013 could have been using a good slope argument, even though the adult harm-reduction case was real.

Assisted dying shows the same pattern in a legal setting. A law allowing terminally ill adults to request physician-assisted death can look reasonable: it serves a small group, has procedural safeguards, and addresses a concrete suffering. But in some jurisdictions the initial authorization became a precedent. Belgium expanded its euthanasia law to minors in 2014, and the Netherlands has allowed euthanasia for adults with dementia. In Oregon, by contrast, the 1997 Death with Dignity Act has remained narrow: terminally ill adults with a prognosis of roughly six months. The difference is not whether the first step was “reasonable” in the abstract, but whether the legal culture treated it as a principle or a doorway. If a society has broad physician discretion, weak review, and a practice already underway, the slope is more likely. If it has bright-line rules, public reporting, and a political commitment to the limit, the slope is less likely. So the slope argument can be a good reason to oppose a particular law in a particular institutional setting, or at least to demand stricter limits.

Emergency powers show the same dynamic. After 2001, the U.S. government argued that it needed access to records relevant to terrorism investigations. That sounded reasonable. But the legal standard in FISA Section 215 was broad enough that the NSA collected bulk telephone metadata, a practice revealed in 2013 and later allowed to lapse in 2015. The slope occurred because the authorization was categorical, oversight was secret, and the political cost of using it was low. The fact that it was eventually stopped does not make the original fear silly; it shows that public revelation and political pressure can be the brake.

But not every feared slope arrives. Legalizing marijuana in many U.S. states did not produce the predicted hard-drug cascade; it mostly changed where and how marijuana is sold. Expanding marriage rights did not lead to polygamy. These failures matter. They mean that a slope argument without a mechanism is just anxiety. If the proposed step has a clear legal limit, a visible beneficiary, strong public scrutiny, and no obvious incentive for expansion, the expected probability of the bad endpoint may be too low to outweigh the present benefit.

The hardest objection is that slope arguments are often a status-quo shield. They can be used to keep terminally ill people from relief, keep groups from rights, or prevent urgent reforms by imagining a future abuse that may not come. This is real. A fear of “the next group” can be a way of refusing to take the current group’s suffering seriously.

The check is not to ban slope reasoning, but to demand the same evidence for it as for any other consequence claim. If the fear is that assisted dying will be used on disabled or depressed people, the argument needs a mechanism: who would request it, under what legal standard, with what oversight, and what historical cases show? If the fear is that a right will be abused, ask who has the incentive and the power to abuse it. If the answer is “people are bad,” that is not a reason.

Inaction also has its own slope. If a reasonable step would reduce severe suffering now, delaying it because of a small chance of future misuse may itself cause harm. The question is not whether the future is risk-free, but whether the expected cost of acting is less than the expected cost of waiting.

So a useful test is: can the objector name the first rung after A, not just the bottom? What changes in law, budget, personnel, social permission, or market incentive? Has that change happened in comparable cases? How bad is the endpoint, and who bears it? Is there a credible stopping rule? If the objector cannot get past the bottom, the argument is weak. If they can, it deserves weight.

The slippery slope is a good reason to oppose something when the slope is part of the expected consequence, not when the objector has simply chosen a frightening endpoint. Policies should be judged by the world they make, and sometimes the world they make is the problem.

prompt: why are corporations so hard to regulate? they always seem to find a loophole
response:
Corporations are hard to regulate for a boring reason: law is a slow, general technology, and corporations are fast, specific, and resource-rich. A loophole is not usually a magic trick. It is the space left open when a legislature had to write a rule that could be applied to thousands of situations, enforced by courts, and defended against challenges. The more precise the rule, the easier it is to step around it; the vaguer the rule, the harder it is to enforce fairly.

They do not always evade. Many firms comply because the cost of violation, including lost reputation and customer trust, exceeds the gain. But when evasion happens, it happens for structural reasons.

Take tax. If a law taxes profit where the business is managed, a corporation can argue that a decision was made elsewhere. If it taxes income earned in a country, the firm can locate the legal owner of a patent, trademark, or financing arrangement in a lower-tax jurisdiction. In 2016 Apple said it held most of its $252 billion cash hoard abroad and that repatriating it would trigger a large U.S. tax bill. That was not a secret scheme; it was the result of a tax code that distinguished places and legal forms. Sometimes what looks like a loophole is ordinary legal planning: the company is not breaking a rule, it is using the rule’s categories. That makes the conduct harder to condemn and harder to close without rewriting broad policy.

Finance shows the same problem. Before the 2008 crisis, bank capital rules focused heavily on assets on the balance sheet. Banks could move risk into special purpose vehicles, securitizations, and over-the-counter derivatives such as credit default swaps. The economic exposure was real, but the legal packaging made it harder for supervisors to see. Regulators were not blind; they were dealing with instruments whose terms were private, customized, and changing.

Then there is information. A regulator usually learns about a firm through filings, audits, complaints, site visits, and data the firm chooses to report. The firm knows more. It knows which product is failing, which customer segment is being overcharged, which chemical is leaking, which algorithm is making biased decisions. If the harm is visible—smoke, speed, spoiled milk—regulation can work. If the harm is delayed, statistical, or buried in code and contracts, the regulator is partly dependent on the regulated firm’s cooperation.

Enforcement matters too. I would not put a precise number on corporate lobbying, because definitions and years vary, but the scale is billions of dollars annually in the United States alone, before counting in-house lawyers, economists, consultants, and campaign contacts. Agencies are small by comparison. The SEC has a few thousand employees for a market with thousands of reporting companies. A large corporation can spend months on one regulatory issue; an agency may have one team. That does not mean every rule is bought. It means the marginal rule is often shaped by the people who must live with it.

Corporations also understand expected value. Suppose a violation can earn $50 million. If the chance of detection is 10 percent and the average fine is $20 million, the expected cost is $2 million. Even a firm with a genuine compliance culture may accept that risk if the business unit is measured on profit. Fines can be huge and still not eliminate the incentive. BP paid $20.8 billion over the Deepwater Horizon disaster, one of the largest environmental penalties in history, and remained a major global energy company. The penalty punished the event; it did not make every shortcut impossible.

Legal form gives corporations another advantage: they can reorganize. If a subsidiary is fined, the parent may sell it. If a brand is tainted, the firm can rebrand. If a jurisdiction becomes expensive, the firm can move headquarters, incorporation, data storage, or customer contracts. Limited liability means the people who approve the risk usually do not pay the full social cost. The corporation is a machine for separating decision from consequence.

Political economy matters. Regulators need budgets, technical data, and legislative support. Industry can offer all three, or threaten jobs and investment if rules are too strict. The people who leave agencies often go into industry, and industry people often go into agencies. That revolving door is not proof of corruption; it is a labor market for expertise. But it means regulators often share assumptions with the firms they regulate, and rules tend to be written in ways that are administrable, familiar, and defensible.

The hardest objection is that governments should simply make penalties severe enough. Sometimes they do. But severe penalties require proof, and proof is hard. Corporate wrongdoing is often diffuse: a product is approved by engineers, reviewed by lawyers, sold by managers, priced by a committee. To convict, prosecutors must show who knew what and that the law was clear. If lawmakers instead write broad rules against “deceptive” or “reckless” conduct, companies can challenge them as vague, and regulators lose the ability to enforce consistently. The legal system that protects citizens from arbitrary power also protects firms from overreach. That protection is worth having, but it makes perfect regulation impossible.

Regulation works best when the harm is observable, the rule is simple, the regulator has independent data, and the firm cannot easily move. Speed limits, food inspections, emission monitors, and basic accounting rules work reasonably well because violations can be measured and the actor is tied to a place. Regulation struggles with financial risk, data practices, environmental damage that appears decades later, and global platforms that can serve customers from many jurisdictions at once.

So corporations are not hard to regulate because they are uniquely cunning. They are hard to regulate because they are adaptive, well-funded, and organized to persist, while law must be general, public, and constrained. Loopholes are the visible sign of that mismatch. The best regulation does not try to write a rule with no gaps. It tries to make the gaps visible, make the price of crossing them high enough, and keep the regulator from being starved of information by the very firms it is supposed to watch.

prompt: I've felt guilty for years about something I did when I was young. How reliable is my memory of it, really, and can I do anything about the past?
response:
Your memory is probably less reliable than its clarity suggests. Memory is not a stored recording; it is rebuilt each time from surviving fragments—emotional tone, partial images, later explanations, current beliefs. People can be led to remember events that never happened, and confidence in the memory is a poor guide to accuracy. A childhood memory has fewer anchors: you were younger, your understanding of motives was thinner, and the event may have been compressed into a scene you have revisited for years. That rehearsal changes the memory. The exact words, the sequence, the degree of blame, the other person’s reaction: these are the parts most likely to be distorted by the guilt itself.

That does not mean the guilt is imaginary. A persistent moral feeling usually has a source, even if the story around it has become inflated. You may have done something smaller than you now imagine, or you may have judged a child’s action by an adult standard. You also have some advantage over an outside witness: you remember your intention, your body’s involvement, and the feeling of the moment. The broad outline may be more trustworthy than the details. The task is to separate layers: what you directly remember, what you infer, what someone else told you, and what you assume because it fits the person you fear you were. The first layer may be thin. The feeling may still be true.

Age matters. A seven-year-old’s shove, a fourteen-year-old’s cruel joke, a teenager’s reckless choice are not the same moral facts as the same acts done by a settled adult. Young people often lack the perspective to foresee harm, the skill to regulate impulse, or the language to repair things on the spot. That does not make their actions harmless. It means the moral weight should be measured with the knowledge and capacities they had then, not with the full hindsight you now possess. If you judge a child by the standards of a person with decades of experience, you will almost always find the child guilty.

What you can do depends on whether there is a living person to whom repair is owed. If there is, ask whether contacting them would serve their needs or yours. An apology can be a genuine attempt to acknowledge harm, but it can also be a way of making yourself feel better while asking the other person to process your past. If you reach out, make it short, take responsibility without excuses, offer something concrete if appropriate, and accept that you may get no answer or a bad one. If the person is vulnerable, if the contact would reopen an injury, or if you cannot be sure it is safe, do not do it. Then make amends in the only available way: by not repeating the pattern, by recognizing it in others, and by giving your attention to the kind of harm you once did.

If there is no identifiable person, or the harm was minor, the work is mostly internal. Decide what you actually regret. Is it that you caused pain, that you were cowardly, that you missed a chance, or that you are ashamed of what the act says about you? Guilt, shame, regret, and anxiety are not the same. Guilt can be corrected by repair. Shame often needs evidence that you are not a fixed bad thing. Regret needs acceptance. Anxiety needs exposure to the fact that you can bear the memory without acting on it. If you can, write the event down as plainly as you can, mark the parts you are unsure of, and ask what a fair-minded person would say about a young person in that situation. If the memory resists that and keeps returning with the force of a command, it may be less a moral question than a wound, and a therapist who works with intrusive memories can help.

The hardest part is that uncertainty remains. You may never know whether the scene is exactly true. But the practical question is not whether you can recover the original file. It is what the memory is doing to you now, and whether your response to it is proportionate. If the remembered act was real, the best use of the guilt is to make the future different. If the remembered act has been exaggerated by years of rehearsal, the best use of the doubt is to stop punishing yourself for a wrong your own mind has embellished.
