prompt: why do non-programmers think software is almost done when the interface looks polished, or terrible when it looks plain?
response:
Because the interface is the only part of the software they can inspect.

A non-programmer cannot see the database, the background jobs, the error handling, the migrations, the race conditions, the test suite, or the places where the system quietly fails under load. They can see whether the buttons line up, whether the colors feel intentional, whether the app tells them what is happening. So when the interface looks polished, they infer that a lot of work has already happened. When it looks plain, they infer that the work has not happened yet.

That inference is not irrational. In physical products, finish is usually a reliable signal. A chair with smooth joints, even paint, and no splinters has probably passed through more stages than one that is rough and uneven. A house with trimmed edges, sealed windows, and painted trim feels closer to habitable than one with exposed studs. The visible surface is correlated with the hidden work because both come from the same process of making something presentable.

Software breaks that correlation, but only partly. In many products, the interface really is one of the last things to be done. An early version may be a command-line tool, a spreadsheet, a set of internal scripts, or a bare HTML page. Once there is a real design pass, the product often moves toward release. Rounded corners, consistent spacing, loading states, error messages, empty states, and brand colors are not just decoration; they are evidence that someone has thought about what the user will see in situations other than the happy path. So a polished interface often means: this thing has an opinion about itself, and it is close to being handed to people.

A plain interface often means the opposite, or at least it fails to prove the opposite. If a page has an input box and a button labeled “Run,” it can look like a test harness even if the button calls a working API that writes to a database and sends a notification. The user cannot tell the difference from the surface. They see a form. They do not see the system behind it. The plainness reads as incompleteness because it offers no reassurance. There is no hover state, no spinner, no confirmation, no indication of what will happen if the data is bad. The interface has not answered the basic question: what is this thing?

That is the key point. “Plain” is not experienced as neutral. It is experienced as absence. A polished interface communicates affordances: this can be clicked, this is disabled, this is selected, this is loading, this is an error. A plain interface may contain all the same functions, but it does not advertise them. The user has to guess. Guessing feels like friction, and friction feels like low quality. Even when the software is doing exactly what it should, the lack of visual feedback makes it feel unstable, as if it might be doing nothing at all.

There is also a social signal. A polished interface suggests that people with different skills have touched the product: an engineer, a designer, maybe a product manager, maybe a writer. It suggests that the team cared enough to make the thing presentable. A plain interface suggests a single author, a prototype, a hack, or a project that has not yet been judged by anyone outside its builder. That may be false, but it is a reasonable guess from the outside. In consumer contexts especially, aesthetics are a proxy for professionalism. If the surface looks careless, the user assumes the rest is too.

The hard objection is that this judgment is easily fooled. A startup can show a beautiful onboarding flow while the core feature is a fragile script behind the scenes. A design system can make a broken product look coherent. A demo can be reskinned in a weekend while the hard problems remain. Conversely, a terminal, a command-line tool, an enterprise dashboard, or a scientific application can be mature, powerful, and reliable while looking dated to an outsider. If the visible layer is cheap to fake, then judging software by its looks is a bad rule.

But the rule is not meant to measure the whole product. It is a first-pass estimate of readiness. A polished interface is not proof that the software is good; it is evidence that the software has reached a stage where it can be shown. That matters because many software failures are not only technical. A product that works but cannot be understood is not ready. A product that handles edge cases in the backend but gives the user a blank screen on failure is not ready. The interface is where the product makes its promises, and a polished interface makes more promises: I know what I am, I will tell you when I am working, I will tell you when I fail, I will not leave you guessing.

Plain software can overcome this, but it has to do it by behavior. If a tool is predictable, fast, and trusted by its users, the plainness stops mattering. Developers do not think of `curl` or `git` as terrible because they are not visually inviting; they know what the tools can do and have learned the cues. The problem is that non-programmers, and even experienced users in a new domain, do not have that history. They meet the software first as a surface. If the surface does not establish competence, they assume there is none.

So non-programmers think software is almost done when it looks polished because polish is often a late-stage signal and because it makes the product legible. They think it is terrible when it looks plain because plainness can mean missing affordances, missing feedback, and missing intention. The heuristic is rational from the outside, but it is calibrated to the wrong layer of the work. It mistakes the painted front door for the foundation, while still being right that a house without a front door is probably not ready for guests.

prompt: Is depression actually a real disease the way the flu is? Psychiatric diagnoses always seem kind of arbitrary to me, with everything overlapping with everything else.
response:
The short answer is: depression is real, but not in the way influenza is. The flu is caused by a virus. You can isolate the virus, and the illness usually begins, peaks, and resolves around a clear biological event, even though people experience flu differently. Major depression has no equivalent. There is no test that says “depression” and no single necessary cause. If you want a category with one pathogen and a clean boundary, depression does not qualify.

What it is instead is a syndrome: a set of symptoms that occur together more often than chance. A person may be irritable rather than sad, sleep too much or too little, lose or gain appetite, feel slowed down or keyed up, have trouble concentrating, feel worthless, or think about dying. The DSM draws a box around a certain number of these symptoms lasting a certain amount of time, with impairment. The box is partly conventional. Two weeks is a practical cutoff, not a law of nature. But the contents of the box are not random. Those symptoms cluster, they predict who will get worse, who will recover, and who is at risk of suicide.

The overlap you notice is real. Depression coexists with anxiety, ADHD, substance problems, chronic pain, thyroid disease, sleep disorders, personality patterns, and normal grief. That makes the labels feel slippery. But medicine is full of such categories. Diabetes is not one disease; type 1 and type 2 are different. Cancer is not one thing either. High blood pressure has a threshold that looks arbitrary until you see the curve of stroke and heart attack risk. A diagnostic category does not have to be a perfect natural kind to be useful. It has to carve reality at joints that matter for treatment and prognosis.

The overlap is also a clue that the cleanest divisions may be dimensions rather than boxes: negative mood, anxiety, sleep disruption, low reward sensitivity, psychomotor slowing. Psychiatric manuals cut these dimensions into named syndromes because that is how clinicians communicate and choose treatments. The cuts are imperfect. They are not meaningless.

Depression is also more real than “bad mood” in a less glamorous way. It runs in families, often without anyone having suffered the same event. Severe stress, trauma, poverty, and social isolation raise risk, but many depressed people have not had an obvious catastrophe. The brain and body are involved, though not as a single broken switch: depressed people frequently show differences in stress-response systems, reward circuitry, sleep, and sometimes inflammation, all of which interact with the immune and metabolic systems. Treatments help in many cases—therapy, antidepressants, ECT in severe cases—and they can change a person’s state even when their external life remains the same. That is not proof of a clean biological entity, but it is evidence that the syndrome is not merely a voluntary state.

The strongest case against taking the diagnosis too literally is that psychiatric categories are made by committees, and language can shape what people think they feel. If a person is told they are “depressed” after a breakup, the label may expand their self-description. That happens. But the same is true of many diagnoses: a person told they have chronic fatigue or irritable bowel syndrome may organize their life around the label. The problem is real, but it does not make the underlying suffering invented. A map is not the territory, and a bad map is not no territory. The question is whether the map tracks something.

It tracks something when the same cluster of symptoms appears across very different people and circumstances, when it raises objective risks, and when interventions aimed at it reduce those risks. Depression does all three. It increases suicide risk. It worsens adherence to treatment for heart disease and diabetes. It is associated with earlier death, partly through suicide and partly through its effects on behavior and physiology. Those are not just subjective reports. They are events that happen to people.

None of this means every sad person is sick. A person who loses a job and feels miserable for a while is not automatically depressed. Clinical depression is distinguished by persistence, severity, loss of pleasure, functional collapse, and often a quality of self-loathing or an inability to imagine improvement. The boundary is fuzzy, but the difference between grief and a chronic disabling syndrome is not nothing. A clinician can miss it, and a label can be misapplied, but the distinction has real consequences: one person may need support and time; the other may need treatment now.

So I would not call depression a disease “the way the flu is.” That comparison sets the bar at a single identifiable cause and a sharp boundary, and depression fails it. I would call it a real medical and psychological disorder: a heterogeneous cluster of states that are biologically grounded, clinically recognizable, often chronic, and sometimes dangerous. The arbitrariness is mostly at the edges, where categories meet normal emotion and each other. The center is not arbitrary. People are disabled, they stop functioning, they die, and some get better with specific help. That is not the flu. It is real enough to treat.

prompt: if you want to claim a rare disaster isn't a real risk because the yearly average death toll is low, how much does it matter where you start counting?
response:
A great deal. The yearly average death toll over a chosen period is not a property of the risk itself; it is a property of the period you happened to choose. For a rare disaster, that distinction is not a technicality. It is the whole argument.

Suppose a particular kind of disaster kills 10,000 people once every 500 years. The long-run expected toll is 20 deaths per year. But if you count 100 years in which it does not happen, the average is zero. If you count 100 years in which it does happen, the average is 100. If you start counting the year after a big event, you may get zero for the next four centuries and then a sudden enormous number. Same world, same underlying danger, wildly different “yearly average,” depending only on the starting point.

That is the problem. A rare disaster is not like a steady leak. It is mostly silence with occasional spikes. The average over a short or conveniently bounded window is therefore often binary: either the window contains the spike or it does not. The start date decides which case you get. If you are allowed to move the start until the average looks small, you have not measured the risk; you have selected a favorable sample.

There are conditions under which the starting point matters less. If the hazard has been stable for a very long time, and your counting window is long compared with the recurrence interval, then the average will tend toward the true rate. If you have several independent windows and they all give similar averages, that is also reassuring. But those conditions are exactly the ones rare disasters tend to fail. The recurrence interval may be centuries or millennia; the historical record may be shorter than that; the population exposed may have changed; the infrastructure may have changed; the climate or land use may have changed. In such cases, a low average since some arbitrary date may say more about the date than about the danger.

The start point also matters when the risk has changed. A floodplain may have been empty in 1800 and crowded in 2000. A bridge may have been replaced. A dam may have been built. A warning system may have reduced deaths without reducing the event. If you start counting after those changes, the average can be low even though the underlying hazard is still there. That low average may be real, but it is conditional: it is the average while the levee holds, while the city remains small, while the warning system is maintained. It does not show that the risk has disappeared.

So what can a low yearly average legitimately support? It can support a claim that the expected number of deaths per year is small, if the average is calculated sensibly over a relevant horizon and with a stable baseline. That may matter for priorities. If a disaster is expected to kill one person per year on average, and another risk kills a thousand, the first is less important in expected-value terms. It may also support a claim that a proposed mitigation is not worth its cost, if the cost is large and the expected loss is small.

It does not support the claim that the disaster is not a real risk. A risk is real if there is a possible bad outcome and uncertainty about whether it will occur. A low expected toll can coexist with a serious risk. A 1-in-10,000 chance of 10,000 deaths has an expected toll of one death per year, but the outcome, if it happens, is catastrophic. The average hides the shape of the distribution: many years of zero, then a year of enormous loss.

The deepest issue is that “where you start counting” is often a substitute for the actual question. The actual question is: what is the current annual probability of the event, given current exposure, current conditions, and the best available evidence? The average since 1950, or since the last eruption, or since the reform that reduced deaths, is only a rough clue to that question. If the clue can be made to point anywhere by moving the start date, it is not doing much work.

In short: if the claim is “this risk is small in expected deaths per year,” the starting point matters, and the claim is only as good as the interval. If the claim is “this risk is not real,” the starting point matters more: a low average can be produced by counting a quiet stretch, and a quiet stretch is not the same thing as safety.

prompt: why do colleges pay a few star professors a lot and the people who actually teach most of the classes so little? it doesn't seem like greed alone explains it
response:
The cleanest way to see it is to separate two jobs that often get hidden under the same title: producing the university’s reputation, and delivering the credit hours that keep students enrolled. Star professors are paid like assets. The people teaching most of the introductory sections are paid like labor. The gap between those two prices is not mainly greed. It comes from scarcity, revenue, measurement, and bargaining power.

A star professor is expensive because the institution can plausibly connect that person to money. In business, law, medicine, engineering, computer science, and economics, a famous professor may bring grants, patents, consulting clients, corporate relationships, donations, and applicants. A business-school professor with a strong industry network may earn a salary that is already high and then add consulting income on top. A law professor with a substantial practice can do the same. Even in fields where outside money is thinner, a well-known scholar can improve a department’s standing in peer surveys, attract better doctoral students, make the school look stronger in rankings, and give donors a reason to care. The university is not just paying for a classroom appearance. It is paying for a signal that the degree is worth more.

That signal has value because students and families usually choose institutions, not individual teachers. A family comparing colleges rarely knows who will teach introductory chemistry or microeconomics. They know the name, the selectivity, the location, the career outcomes, the price, and the general prestige. Once the student is enrolled, the instructor is assigned. So the demand for a particular teacher is weak, while the demand for the brand is strong. A university can lose an unremarkable part-time lecturer and replace that section next semester with almost no external consequence. It can lose a star and feel the difference in applications, faculty recruitment, and reputation for years.

The teaching side is cheap partly because of simple arithmetic. A large university needs thousands of course sections. If a part-time course can be bought for a few thousand dollars, the institution can expand enrollment without creating a matching number of permanent jobs. In many American four-year schools, a part-time course pays roughly in the range of a few thousand dollars, often around the mid-$3,000s to low-$4,000s, depending on the institution and the instructor’s rank. A full-time faculty line may pay more than that for a year, with benefits and job security, and the professor may teach only two or three courses a semester. If every section were taught that way, the fixed cost would be much higher, and the university would have to pay it even when enrollment fell. Part-time teachers are a shock absorber. They appear when sections are needed and disappear when they are not.

That is why the star salaries are often made possible by the low teaching salaries. The budget is a portfolio. A university can afford a few very expensive research hires because it has kept the cost of routine instruction low. The two are not unrelated extravagance and thrift. They are two sides of the same financial structure.

The low pay is also a labor-market outcome. Many people who teach part-time have doctorates, especially in the humanities and social sciences, but there are not enough tenure-track jobs for all of them. Some teach at several institutions. Some hold other jobs. Some want the flexibility. Some are underemployed but value the academic title or the connection to a field. That supply of willing instructors keeps the price down. It is not that nobody notices the pay; it is that enough people can live with it, or at least accept it for a while, that institutions do not face the same competitive pressure as they do for stars. Where adjuncts have organized and struck, course fees have risen in some places, which is a reminder that the low number is a bargaining outcome, not a natural law.

The strongest objection to this explanation is that students are the customers, and if teaching quality mattered, the market should bid it up. It does matter, but the market is not organized around individual teachers. Student evaluations exist, but they are noisy and easy to game. A professor who is rigorous may get lower scores than one who is lenient. A professor who teaches a popular subject may get high scores for reasons unrelated to quality. Colleges do not want to pay large premiums for ease, nor do they have a reliable way to measure long-term learning at the level of one section of one intro course. Research output, by contrast, is much easier to count: publications, citations, grants, awards, patents, named positions, invitations. The institution can see the star’s value in documents. It can only infer the teacher’s value from aggregate outcomes that many other things also affect.

So colleges monitor teaching in a coarse way. They care if completion rates collapse, if accreditation becomes a problem, if a program becomes notorious, or if sections cannot be filled. But they do not usually have a fine-grained price signal for the difference between a good instructor and a great one. That makes it hard to justify paying the great one much more. The star’s excellence is visible and marketable. The teacher’s excellence is real, but diffuse and hard to contract.

This is also why the pattern is strongest at institutions that are trying to be both prestigious and large. A small teaching college may pay its faculty more uniformly because teaching is the product. A community college may have less star-driven pay, but often lower overall compensation. A research university, however, wants the brand of the first and the scale of the second. The star-and-adjunct model lets it do that: a visible research elite supports the name, while inexpensive part-time labor carries the mass of introductory instruction. At research universities, the same logic extends even lower, to graduate teaching assistants who teach sections for stipends and tuition remission. The brand hire supports a system of cheap instructional labor.

Greed is not a useful explanation because it suggests that the main actors are simply taking money they do not need to. Most of the time, the institution is doing something more boring: competing for students, trying to keep costs flexible, investing where it can see a return, and underpaying where it can get away with it. The result can still be exploitative, but it is produced by incentives, not just character. The star can threaten to leave for a rival school. The adjunct can be replaced next term. The student has already chosen the school and now has to finish the degree. Those differences in power show up in pay.

So the people who teach most of the classes are paid little because their work is treated as replaceable delivery. The star professors are paid a lot because their work is treated as reputation-generating capital. The university sells a degree, a name, and a network. Classes are the delivery mechanism. When the delivery mechanism can be bought cheaply, and the brand cannot, the prices follow that difference.

prompt: what's the actual pitch for genetic testing to choose antidepressants? like why would knowing my genes help me pick one
response:
The actual pitch is narrower than the marketing usually implies. It is not: “your DNA tells you which antidepressant will make you feel better.” That would be a fantasy. The defensible version is: “your genes tell you how fast your body will clear a few common antidepressants, so your prescriber can avoid a drug that will accumulate, or a dose that will be cleared too fast.”

Most of the useful information comes from two genes: **CYP2C19** and **CYP2D6**. They code for liver enzymes that break down many psychiatric drugs. People have variants that make those enzymes slow, normal, intermediate, or fast. The slow end is usually called a *poor metabolizer*; the fast end is *ultrarapid metabolizer*.

Here is the concrete logic.

Citalopram and escitalopram are heavily dependent on CYP2C19. If you are a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer, a standard dose can leave you with higher blood levels than someone with normal enzyme activity. That can mean more nausea, drowsiness, sexual side effects, or, for citalopram specifically, more concern about dose-related QT prolongation. Citalopram’s FDA label explicitly says poor metabolizers should use a lower starting dose, around 10 mg rather than 20 mg. So if you were about to try citalopram and the test says you are a poor metabolizer, the rational move is not “take a different magic pill,” but “start lower, go slower, or pick a drug less dependent on that enzyme.”

The same idea works in the other direction. If you are an ultrarapid metabolizer, a normal dose may be cleared before it reaches a useful level. You might take sertraline or escitalopram for four or six weeks, feel nothing, and your doctor might conclude the drug “didn’t work.” In reality, you may have been underdosed relative to your metabolism. The test can reframe that: maybe the dose was too low for you, or maybe you should choose a drug metabolized by a different route.

CYP2D6 matters for a different set of antidepressants: paroxetine, fluoxetine, venlafaxine, nortriptyline, and to a lesser extent sertraline. Poor metabolizers of CYP2D6 can accumulate drug and get side effects; ultrarapid metabolizers may clear it too quickly and get poor response. Tricyclics like nortriptyline are a classic example because their blood levels have long been monitored clinically. Knowing your CYP2D6 status can help set the starting dose before you wait for toxicity or failure.

So the pitch is: **fewer obvious bad fits.**

It helps by doing three things:

1. **Avoiding accumulation.** If you are a poor metabolizer, a drug that is usually fine at 20 mg may act like 40 mg in you.  
2. **Avoiding subtherapeutic exposure.** If you are ultrarapid, a “normal” dose may not be normal for you.  
3. **Interpreting interactions better.** Some drugs inhibit these same enzymes. Omeprazole affects CYP2C19; fluoxetine and paroxetine inhibit CYP2D6. If your own enzyme is already slow, an inhibitor can push levels higher than expected.

That is real. It is not magic.

The big limitation is that antidepressant response is not mostly about metabolism. Whether an SSRI, SNRI, mirtazapine, bupropion, or TCA improves depression depends on the illness, your symptoms, sleep, pain, stress, bipolarity, thyroid issues, prior medication response, family response, side-effect tolerance, and a lot of noise. Metabolism affects how much drug reaches your system, not whether the drug’s mechanism fits your particular depression.

This is why a test that says “you are a normal metabolizer” is not very useful. That is the most common result, and it basically means: “no special metabolic warning; proceed with usual clinical judgment.”

The part of genetic testing that is weak is the “brain chemistry” part. Some panels also look at serotonin, dopamine, BDNF, COMT, or other candidate genes and imply they can tell you whether you need an SSRI versus an SNRI or whether you will respond better to one class than another. That part is mostly not clinically reliable. The actionable core is CYP2C19 and CYP2D6, especially for a handful of antidepressants with known metabolism.

The evidence is also modest. There are pharmacogenomic guidelines from groups like CPIC, and some drug labels mention CYP2C19 or CYP2D6 status. Observational studies suggest that prescribing in line with these genes may reduce side effects and sometimes improve response or time to response. But the evidence is not so strong that most major guidelines say every new depression patient should get tested first. It is more like a tie-breaker: useful when usual choices are unclear, previous trials were problematic, you are taking multiple interacting drugs, you have heart issues, or you are considering a drug where exposure matters.

So if someone asks, “why would knowing my genes help me pick one?” the honest answer is:

It may help you avoid a drug that will make you feel awful, or recognize that a drug that seemed ineffective was probably underdosed for your metabolism. It does not tell you which drug will lift your mood. It tells you which standard drugs are likely to be handled unusually by your body.

If I had to summarize the whole thing plainly: **the test is a dosing and safety filter, not a mood predictor.**

prompt: Why do big companies care so much about where job applicants went to college, if it's such a weak signal?
response:
A college name is a weak signal for a particular person and a useful one for a large hiring process. Those are different questions. I can’t say how much weight a particular recruiter consciously assigns, but the scale of the problem explains a lot. If a manager is trying to decide whether one candidate can do the job, the diploma tells her little: there are brilliant state-school grads and underperforming elite-school grads. But if the company has 15,000 applications for 80 early-career jobs, it cannot deeply evaluate everyone. It needs a first cut that is cheap, standardized, and good enough to shrink the pile.

Suppose 8% of all applicants would turn out to be acceptable hires. If applicants from a handful of schools have a 12% acceptable-hire rate, that is not a reliable test of any one person. It is still a useful filter. The company can interview the smaller group and spend its scarce manager time where the odds are better. The signal does not need to be accurate enough to identify a genius; it only needs to be accurate enough to make the funnel cheaper. In an applicant tracking system, “school” is also a neat field: a few clicks can produce a shortlist.

Big companies can use this filter in a way smaller ones cannot. A startup that ignored all non-local candidates might not get enough resumes. A large firm with a known brand gets enough applicants that it can afford to be choosy. It can say, in effect, “We will look carefully at people from schools where we have had good experiences, and we will look less carefully at everyone else.” That is not efficient from the perspective of any excluded applicant. It is efficient for a company that must process thousands of files without interviewing each one.

What the college actually signals is not a single skill. It is a bundle: the candidate passed a selective admissions process, survived a demanding peer environment, had access to career services and internships, and probably developed a certain polish. For experienced hires, that bundle matters less because the work history carries the weight. For new graduates, there is little work history, so employers lean on whatever correlated traits are visible. A school name is one of the few fields on a resume that can be compared quickly across candidates from different backgrounds.

There is also a channel effect. A college is not just a label; it is a place where a company can meet many candidates at low cost. A firm can send recruiters to a campus, host a presentation, and interview dozens of students in a day. If those students turn out reasonably well, the firm returns next year. The school becomes a pipeline, not merely a credential. Alumni then refer classmates, and hiring managers develop informal trust in candidates from institutions they know. The practice reinforces itself because the firms that use it get a steady supply of candidates who already resemble the people they have hired.

This matters more in some industries than others. In finance, consulting, and corporate trainee programs, early-career hires are often selected before they have much job-specific expertise. The firm is betting on general aptitude, stamina, client presence, and the likelihood that the person will move through the ranks. A recognizable school reduces uncertainty about all of those things, and it also carries network value: the employee may later bring referrals, contacts, or even business. In software engineering, by contrast, a portfolio or coding test may dominate the diploma, though even there a known school can get a resume read.

The obvious objection is that if college is only a noisy proxy, companies should replace it with better measures: work samples, trials, structured interviews, skills tests. They sometimes do, and for some roles those measures are clearly superior. But better measures are often more expensive, harder to administer at scale, and more legally sensitive. A take-home assignment can be gamed or unfair to people with caregiving responsibilities; a trial project takes time; an interview is noisy and biased. A college name is not good, but it is cheap, familiar, and socially acceptable. It also has the advantage of being common knowledge: recruiters know other recruiters use it, candidates know it, and hiring committees can point to a shared norm when explaining a decision.

That last point matters because hiring is not just a statistical problem. It is an institutional one. A hiring manager who rejects a strong candidate from an unknown school can be challenged; a hiring manager who favors a candidate from a school with a long alumni network can hide behind convention. Big firms are not trying to find the single most talented person in the world. They are trying to build a low-risk machine that produces acceptable employees repeatedly. A weak signal that is cheap and socially legible can be worth more than a strong signal that is expensive and contestable.

They care because the alternative is not “perfect judgment.” The alternative is a larger pile of resumes, more uncertain interviews, and no obvious reason to choose one early-career candidate over another. The college name does not reveal who the person is. It tells the company where the person has already been sorted, what group of people they have been around, and how much additional scrutiny the firm can afford to skip. That is why it survives even when everyone, including the recruiters, knows it is blunt.

The short answer is that a college name is a weak signal for a particular person and a useful one for a large hiring process. Those are different questions. If a manager is trying to decide whether one candidate can do the job, the diploma tells her little: there are brilliant state-school grads and underperforming elite-school grads. But if the company has 15,000 applications for 80 early-career jobs, it cannot deeply evaluate everyone. It needs a first cut that is cheap, standardized, and good enough to shrink the pile.

Suppose 8% of all applicants would turn out to be strong hires. If applicants from a handful of schools have a 12% strong-hire rate, that is not a reliable test of any one person. It is still a useful filter. The company can interview the smaller group and spend its scarce manager time where the odds are better. The signal does not need to be accurate enough to identify a genius; it only needs to be accurate enough to make the funnel cheaper.

Big companies can use this filter in a way smaller ones cannot. A startup that ignored all non-local candidates might not get enough resumes. A large firm with a known brand gets enough applicants that it can afford to be choosy. It can say, in effect, “We will look carefully at people from schools where we have had good experiences, and we will look less carefully at everyone else.” That is not efficient from the perspective of any excluded applicant. It is efficient for a company that must process thousands of files without interviewing each one.

What the college actually signals is not a single skill. It is a bundle: the candidate passed a selective admissions process, survived a demanding peer environment, had access to career services and internships, and probably developed a certain polish. For experienced hires, that bundle matters less because the work history carries the weight. For new graduates, there is little work history, so employers lean on whatever correlated traits are visible. A school name is one of the few fields on a resume that can be compared quickly across candidates from different backgrounds.

There is also a channel effect. A college is not just a label; it is a place where a company can meet many candidates at low cost. A firm can send recruiters to a campus, host a presentation, and interview dozens of students in a day. If those students turn out reasonably well, the firm returns next year. The school becomes a pipeline, not merely a credential. Alumni then refer classmates, and hiring managers develop informal trust in candidates from institutions they know. The practice reinforces itself because the firms that use it get a steady supply of candidates who already resemble the people they have hired.

This matters more in some industries than others. In finance, consulting, and corporate trainee programs, early-career hires are often selected before they have much job-specific expertise. The firm is betting on general aptitude, stamina, client presence, and the likelihood that the person will move through the ranks. A recognizable school reduces uncertainty about all of those things, and it also carries network value: the employee may later bring referrals, contacts, or even business. In software engineering, by contrast, a portfolio or coding test may dominate the diploma, though even there a known school can get a resume read.

The obvious objection is that if college is only a noisy proxy, companies should replace it with better measures: work samples, trials, structured interviews, skills tests. They sometimes do, and for some roles those measures are clearly superior. But better measures are often more expensive, harder to administer at scale, and more legally sensitive. A take-home assignment can be gamed or unfair to people with caregiving responsibilities; a trial project takes time; an interview is noisy and biased. A college name is not good, but it is cheap, familiar, and socially acceptable. It also has the advantage of being a common knowledge: recruiters know other recruiters use it, candidates know it, and hiring committees can point to a shared norm when explaining a decision.

That last point matters because hiring is not just a statistical problem. It is an institutional one. A hiring manager who rejects a strong candidate from an unknown school can be challenged; a hiring manager who favors a candidate from a school with a long alumni network can hide behind convention. Big firms are not trying to find the single most talented person in the world. They are trying to build a low-risk machine that produces acceptable employees repeatedly. A weak signal that is cheap and socially legible can be worth more than a strong signal that is expensive and contestable.

So they care because the alternative is not “perfect judgment.” The alternative is a larger pile of resumes, more uncertain interviews, and no obvious reason to choose one early-career candidate over another. The college name does not reveal who the person is. It tells the company where the person has already been sorted, what group of people he or she has been around, and how much additional scrutiny the firm can afford to skip. That is why it survives even when everyone, including the recruiters, knows it is blunt.

prompt: I heard that for years nearly every top Chinese official was an engineer. Is that real? Does it mean China was run by technocrats?
response:
The claim is a half-remembered fact. It is true that, for a stretch of the reform era, a striking number of China’s senior leaders had engineering or technical training. It is not true that “nearly every” top official was an engineer, and it does not follow that China was “run by technocrats” in any clean sense.

The easiest way to see the pattern is to look at the Politburo Standing Committee, the inner circle of seven or eight people. In 1997, four of its seven members had technical backgrounds: Jiang Zemin, who had studied electrical engineering; Hu Jintao, a water-conservancy engineer; Wen Jiabao, trained in geology; and Zhou Yongkang, who had worked in the petroleum industry. That is a high concentration. By the 2000s the number was lower, and by the 2010s most Standing Committee members had careers in Party organization, propaganda, law, security, the military, or general administration. Xi Jinping has an engineering degree, but even counting him, only a small minority of the 2022 Standing Committee were engineers. If you widen “top official” to the 25-member Politburo, or to provincial party secretaries and ministry heads, the proportion falls further.

The historical shift matters. Mao’s top circle was made of soldiers, party organizers, and political operators, not engineers. After 1978, the Communist Party needed people who could rebuild the economy, manage factories, plan infrastructure, and deal with foreign technology. Deng Xiaoping was not an engineer, but he made technical competence a political virtue. The gaokao was restored, technical cadres were rehabilitated, and the Party began recruiting more heavily from universities, research institutes, state-owned enterprises, and engineering ministries. In that context, an engineering degree was not just a personal credential; it was a sign that a cadre could do nation-building.

But “many leaders had engineering degrees” is not the same as “the country was governed by engineers.” A technocracy, in the ordinary sense, means that decisions are authorized by technical expertise: the expert’s judgment is final because it is technically correct. China’s system works differently. Leaders are selected by the Party, promoted through cadre evaluations, and judged on political reliability, local performance, administrative control, and loyalty to the center. Technical competence is one input, not the rule of decision. A water engineer can become a general secretary of the Party; that does not make water policy the product of engineering consultation any more than a lawyer’s presidency makes a country a legal technocracy.

Where the technocratic label has some truth is in the state’s style, not in the leaders’ degrees. China has a strong planning apparatus, a habit of large physical investment, and a central government that can mobilize resources for railways, power grids, ports, factories, and industrial upgrades. Local officials have long competed on growth and investment metrics. That produces real capabilities: fast infrastructure construction, large-scale industrial policy, and rapid supply-chain coordination. It also produces the familiar costs: overbuilding, local debt, environmental damage, displacement, and policy choices that favor measurable output over harder-to-measure social welfare. The Three Gorges project is a good example. It was a massive engineering undertaking, but its costs and benefits were not decided by engineers alone; they were political choices made by a Party state.

The hardest objection to the “technocrats” story is simple: if engineers were running the country, why did political priorities so often override technical or economic caution? Debt, real-estate risk, environmental degradation, and uneven development are not what one expects from a government whose decisions are settled by engineering judgment. The better description is a one-party developmental state with a strong technocratic apparatus and a leadership that frequently includes technically trained officials. The engineers were party officials first.

prompt: Why do mathematicians bother defining abstract structures like groups or rings instead of just studying numbers and sets directly?
response:
The point of the definition is to identify the exact properties a proof uses. A group is a set with a binary operation that is associative, has an identity, and in which every element has an inverse. Those conditions are precisely what make undoing legitimate. If \(ax=b\) in a group, then \(x=a^{-1}b\); in additive notation, if \(a+x=b\), then \(x=b-a\). That fact is true for the integers under addition, for the nonzero rationals under multiplication, for the symmetries of a polygon, and for invertible matrices. The abstraction says that the same short proof covers all of them.

The transfer is not just economical; it is diagnostic. Suppose a symmetry group has elements \(A, X, Y\) and you know that doing \(A\) then \(X\) is the same as doing \(A\) then \(Y\). You can cancel \(A\) by applying its inverse. In matrix algebra, \(AX=AY\) implies \(X=Y\) after multiplying by \(A^{-1}\). In integer arithmetic under addition, \(a+x=a+y\) implies \(x=y\) after subtracting \(a\). The group theorem packages the argument once. More importantly, it tells you that the argument cannot secretly depend on the elements being numbers, polynomials, or matrices. It depends only on the existence of inverses.

If one “studies sets directly,” one can indeed write a group as a set \(G\) together with a binary operation \(*:G\times G\to G\). But that description is complete only in a formal sense. A bare set has no addition, no multiplication, no composition; all it supports is counting and subset relations. The interesting questions begin with the operation. Defining “group” is not a retreat from sets; it is the step of saying which set-theoretic attachments matter. A set is the material; the operation and its laws are the structure.

Numbers also are not a single subject. The natural numbers, integers, rationals, reals, complex numbers, and residue classes modulo \(n\) behave differently. Abstract algebra sorts them by the laws they satisfy. The integers form a group under addition and a ring under addition and multiplication, but they are not a field, because \(2\) has no multiplicative inverse inside \(\mathbb Z\). The rationals form a field. The residue classes modulo \(6\) form a ring, but not an integral domain, because \(2\cdot 3=0\) in \(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\). That distinction is not cosmetic: in any integral domain, a nonzero polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) roots, but in \(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\) the polynomial \(x^2-x\) has four roots: \(0,1,3,4\). Knowing the structure tells you which theorem applies.

The same idea marks the boundary of familiar formulas. In a commutative ring,
\[
(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2.
\]
In a noncommutative ring, the expansion is
\[
(a+b)^2=a^2+ab+ba+b^2.
\]
Matrices give concrete cases where \(ab\neq ba\). If algebra were learned only from real numbers, one might mistake commutativity for a universal law. The definitions “ring” and “commutative ring” separate the cases in which the familiar manipulation is valid from the cases in which it silently fails.

Rings are useful for the same reason, but with two operations instead of one. They let one construction produce many familiar systems. Take a ring and quotient it by an ideal: you are declaring some elements to be zero. Quotienting \(\mathbb Z\) by the ideal \((6)\) gives \(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\). Quotienting the real polynomial ring \(\mathbb R[x]\) by \((x^2+1)\) gives a ring isomorphic to the complex numbers, because the class of \(x\) behaves like a square root of \(-1\). The operation of “modding out” is one operation, and theorems about ideals and quotients apply to all of these examples without reproof.

The most striking use of abstraction is when it makes a hidden object visible. The roots of a polynomial may be permuted in ways that preserve all algebraic relations among them; those permutations form a group, the Galois group. Galois theory says that the problem of solving a polynomial equation by radicals is, at bottom, a problem about that group. The general quintic has Galois group \(S_5\), which is not solvable in the group-theoretic sense, so no formula using only arithmetic operations and roots can solve quintic equations in general. The polynomial and its coefficients are concrete; the group is the structure that explains the obstruction.

The hardest objection to all this is that abstraction can be cheap. A definition of a group is easy; the difficult work is showing that a particular object really is a group, and a theorem stated for all groups may be too weak to compute with. If you want to factor \(15\), you do not need Sylow theorems. If you want the actual rotations of a cube, knowing that its symmetry group has order \(24\) does not by itself tell you where the rotation axes are. Abstraction pays when the same mechanism appears in several places, or when the question is about the mechanism itself: classification, solvability, existence, transfer. It is a compression device, not a magic solver.

So mathematicians define groups and rings because the right level of description is often not “elements” but “operations and laws.” At that level, one proof can serve many domains, one failure reveals a missing hypothesis, and new domains can be recognized when they appear. Numbers and sets remain the material; the structures are the patterns that make the material usable.

prompt: ok dumb question but what actually is a kernel? like what does it do while I'm just browsing the web
response:
Not a dumb question. The kernel is the part of the operating system that sits between your apps and your actual hardware. Your web browser can’t directly talk to the network card, disk, keyboard, or GPU. It asks the kernel to do those things, and the kernel is the only thing allowed to touch them.

While you’re browsing, the kernel is mostly waiting, but it jumps in constantly when something happens.

You type a URL. Your browser wants to send an HTTP request. It doesn’t put bytes on the wire itself. It calls into the kernel, roughly: “send this data on this network connection.” The kernel’s networking stack takes that, manages the TCP connection, breaks it into packets, asks the network driver to transmit them, and keeps track of what’s been sent, what’s been acknowledged, what needs retransmitting.

Then the response starts coming back. The network card receives packets. That generates an interrupt. The kernel wakes up, identifies which packet it is, checks the TCP state, copies the data into a buffer, and eventually tells your browser: “hey, you asked for bytes, here they are.”

Meanwhile, the kernel is also handling the boring stuff underneath all of that. It decides which program gets to run on the CPU next. Chrome has many processes and threads; the kernel schedules them. It keeps their memory separate so one tab crashing doesn’t let another tab scribble over it. If Chrome wants to read a cached image from disk, it asks the kernel. The kernel checks permissions, finds the file, maybe reads it from the page cache, maybe from the actual disk, and gives the bytes back.

When you click a link, the mouse event goes through the kernel’s input system before your browser even knows you clicked. When a new tab renders, the kernel is involved in memory allocation, possibly GPU driver calls, and scheduling the rendering process. When your laptop’s Wi-Fi card does anything, the kernel’s driver is translating between that hardware and the generic networking layer.

A useful mental model: your apps live in “user space.” The kernel lives in “kernel space,” with more privileges. Apps can’t just read arbitrary memory, talk directly to hardware, or mess with other processes. They make system calls. The kernel checks whether the request is allowed and performs the operation.

So while you’re “just browsing,” the kernel is doing the plumbing: scheduling CPU time, moving memory around, talking to drivers, handling interrupts, managing files and sockets, enforcing permissions, and waking your browser when something is ready. If your browser misbehaves, it can usually die. If the kernel misbehaves, the whole system goes down.

prompt: Why did societies stop trying to kill or legislate away their religious enemies? Explain how things like the First Amendment came about, in simple terms.
response:
The short answer is that the old method stopped working. For centuries, a government that wanted religious uniformity could try to enforce it with courts, prisons, exile, and execution. That worked only so long as the state controlled most of the information about people’s beliefs and the population was relatively uniform. When societies became more mixed, more mobile, more literate, and more divided by powerful sects, trying to make everyone worship the same way became expensive, unreliable, and dangerous to the state itself. The First Amendment came out of that process, especially in America, where no single church could command a stable national majority and where the new government had to be built without choosing an official religion.

A useful way to start is to notice that religious enemies were not just spiritual enemies. In early modern Europe, being Catholic or Protestant was also a matter of which king, law, army, and international alliance you belonged to. Heresy looked like treason. A Catholic subject who secretly became a Calvinist was not merely mistaken about grace; he might be a spy for a rival prince. So when states killed or banished religious dissenters, they were often defending political order, not only doctrine.

That explains why the change began with exhaustion. The Thirty Years’ War, fought mostly between 1618 and 1648, left large parts of Germany devastated. It was not a single religious war in a clean sense; it was a mix of confession, dynasty, land, money, and imperial power. But after it, the practical lesson was hard to ignore: trying to settle Europe’s religious disputes by force could destroy the states trying to settle them. The Peace of Westphalia did not create modern tolerance in any full sense. It did something more limited: it made religion more of a state matter and less of a universal demand. A ruler could still choose the religion of his territory, but the idea that all Christendom should be brought under one confession by sword or statute lost force.

A concrete case helps. France had the Edict of Nantes in 1598, which gave Huguenots, French Protestants, a degree of legal protection and military security. In 1685 Louis XIV revoked it. The usual story is that he believed religious uniformity would strengthen France. In one sense he was right: uniformity simplified rule. In another sense he was wrong. Huguenots were not merely “the false religion.” They were artisans, soldiers, merchants, shipbuilders, and skilled workers. When the edict was revoked, tens of thousands left France, and their absence hurt France while benefiting rival states. The lesson was not that conscience was sacred in a modern philosophical way. It was that persecution could be bad economics and bad statecraft.

That does not mean Europe became tolerant quickly. The Toleration Act of 1689 in England allowed many Protestants to worship publicly, but it excluded Catholics, Jews, and anyone who denied the Trinity. Toleration was often a matter of which minorities were useful or harmless. For a long time, “tolerated” meant “not worth exterminating,” not “equal in right.” Still, the direction was clear: the state’s job was to keep the peace, not to save every soul. Once that shift happened, religious belief began to move from public crime to private preference.

The Enlightenment helped supply the language for that shift, but it did not cause it. Many Enlightenment writers were not warm supporters of religious freedom. Voltaire famously argued for toleration, but often because he hated the power of clerical factions, not because he thought all religions were equally true. The deeper change was administrative and political. A state that could no longer inspect everyone’s prayer book, that had to compete for workers and soldiers, and that derived its power from law rather than from a single sacred hierarchy had less use for official creeds. Religion became one of many ways people organized their lives, rather than the only public identity that mattered.

America developed the same general trend in a different setting. The colonies were not born as free churches. Several had established churches. Massachusetts had a Congregational establishment for generations. Some colonies punished Quakers, Baptists, or Catholics. The story of American religious freedom is not a story of pure principle from the beginning. It is a story of pluralism making establishment unstable.

The colonies had many sects. There were Anglicans, Puritans, Quakers, Baptists, Presbyterians, Catholics, Jews, and various smaller groups. No one denomination could safely claim to be “the” church of a whole nation without creating a large class of resentful subjects. In a new country where people had already moved, argued, and formed new congregations, the old idea of a single national church looked artificial. It also looked corrupting: if the government chose the official religion, then church office became a political prize, and religious doctrine became a campaign issue.

This is where the First Amendment fits. The Constitution of 1787 did not mention religion, which alarmed some people. Anti-Federalists and religious minorities feared that the new national government might establish a church or interfere with state-established churches. James Madison, who had watched Virginia struggle with religious tests and establishments, proposed amendments. Virginia’s earlier Statute for Religious Freedom, largely written by Thomas Jefferson, had already argued against giving the state power over religion. Madison’s Memorial and Remonstrance against religious assessments made a key point: even if the established religion were true, state support would make it a political office and degrade it into a matter of law and patronage. If it were false, state support would be worse.

The First Amendment says: “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.” In simple terms, it meant that the national government would not set up a church, favor one sect over another, or pass laws that punished people for their worship. It also meant that religious belief would not be a qualification for federal office. At first, the amendment mostly limited the federal government. Some states still had established churches or religious tests for office. Massachusetts, for example, did not fully end its establishment until 1833. The amendment became a rule for the whole country later, in the twentieth century, when the Fourteenth Amendment was interpreted to apply the First Amendment’s religious clauses to state governments as well.

There is a harder objection here: if the First Amendment was only a political compromise, why did it stick? Because it matched a new way of forming the state. A modern state does not need its citizens to share a creed in order to obey the law. It needs them to accept the same courts, pay the same taxes, and submit to the same police. Once citizenship was defined by residence, loyalty, and legal consent rather than by baptism or confession, the state’s interest in religious conformity shrank. It still cared about public order, but it could protect that with general laws against fraud, violence, breach of the peace, and so on, without deciding which prayers were true.

That is why the line became: the government may not pick religious winners, but it may regulate conduct through neutral rules. You cannot be punished for believing something, but you can be punished for burning a building, defrauding people, or using religious practice to evade ordinary law. This line was not obvious at the time. It had to be worked out through cases: could a state require church attendance? Could it tax churches? Could it refuse a job to someone because of his religion? Could it fund religious schools? The First Amendment did not answer all of these neatly. It created the framework that made the questions manageable.

So the move away from killing or legislating away religious enemies was not mainly a moral awakening. It was a combination of war-weariness, state interest, pluralism, and new political theory. Europe learned that religious uniformity could bankrupt a state and give its enemies a cause. America learned that a nation made of many sects could not survive by making one of them official. The First Amendment came about because the founders needed to build a government that would not choose a religious side, while still allowing religion to flourish in civil society. Once citizenship stopped being a confession, the state no longer needed to know which god you prayed to, only whether you obeyed the same law as everyone else.

prompt: When people argue about whether X 'causes' Y, there's always some philosophical way the statement is imperfect. How should I decide whether a causal claim is fair to make?
response:
The philosophical imperfection is real: almost nothing causes anything by itself. A match needs oxygen, fuel, and temperature. A gene needs a body. A policy needs institutions. If “X causes Y” meant “X alone, in a vacuum, makes Y happen,” almost every ordinary causal claim would be false.

But we do not use the word that way. We use it as a compressed description of a causal model: some variables, some background conditions, and some change we could make. The question is not whether the claim is metaphysically perfect. It is whether the compression is legitimate for the purpose.

A practical test is to translate the claim into an intervention:

> If we changed X from its usual value to another value, in the kind of cases under discussion, Y would change in the direction and amount implied.

If you can defend that sentence, the causal claim is probably fair. If you cannot, the claim is too vague, too broad, or confounded.

The hidden work in any causal claim is the set of conditions you are leaving unsaid. The claim is fair when those omitted conditions are not material to the point being made.

### 1. Identify the contrast

“X causes Y” only means something relative to a comparison. “Smoking causes lung cancer” means smoking compared with not smoking, or heavy smoking compared with light smoking. “Exercise causes weight loss” means exercise compared with less exercise, with diet and other factors held comparable.

If the contrast is unclear, the claim is not yet evaluable. “Stress causes bad health” could mean stress compared with no stress, high stress compared with low stress, or acute stress compared with chronic stress. Those are different claims with different evidence.

A claim can also be unfair because the contrast is misleading. “Vaccines cause illness” may be true in a narrow sense: vaccines can cause sore arms, fever, or rare adverse events. But if the intended contrast is “vaccines versus no vaccines” and the intended outcome is serious long-term disease, the claim may be false or at least misleading. The contrast and the outcome have to match the point.

### 2. Specify the population and baseline

A cause can be strong in one subgroup and absent in another. A drug may work only in people with a particular biomarker. A social policy may help in one institutional setting and do nothing in another. A causal claim without a population is often just a mood.

Baseline matters too. If X raises the chance of Y from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000, “X causes Y” may be technically true but practically misleading. If X raises the chance from 10 percent to 40 percent, the claim is much more salient. If X raises the chance from 0.1 percent to 0.2 percent but almost everyone is exposed, X may still be responsible for many cases in the population. Absolute risk and prevalence both matter.

This is why “causes” is often too blunt. “Risk factor,” “contributes to,” “increases the probability of,” and “is associated with” do different jobs.

### 3. Separate association from intervention

A correlation can arise in at least four ways:

- X really affects Y.
- Y affects X.
- A third variable affects both.
- The comparison is selected in a biased way.

Ice cream sales and drownings rise together in summer. Heat is the common cause. Giving people more ice cream would not, by itself, produce many extra drownings.

Another example: people who pray may live longer, but the effect may come from social connection, discipline, medical care, or community support rather than prayer as such. If changing the prayer behavior would not change longevity after those other factors are held fixed, the causal claim is unfair.

The gold standard is randomization, because it balances known and unknown confounders. But randomized trials are not always possible, and they only estimate the effect in the studied population under the studied conditions. Outside trials, look for natural experiments, strong controls, time order, dose-response patterns, replication, and plausible mechanisms. No single observational argument is perfect; the fair move is to triangulate and say what assumptions are doing the work.

### 4. Check the confounders that matter

You rarely need to control every variable in the universe. You need to control the variables that could plausibly produce the observed association or change the effect of the intervention.

If you are asking whether a teaching method causes learning, you may need to control for student ability, prior knowledge, motivation, class size, and teacher quality. You probably do not need to control for the color of the classroom walls unless there is reason to think it matters.

When you are unsure which confounders matter, the honest thing is to say so. “The evidence suggests X causes Y, assuming that Z and W are not major confounders” is often better than a bare causal claim.

### 5. Distinguish kinds of causes

Many causal arguments go wrong because people silently switch between different notions of cause.

- **Necessary cause:** no X, no Y.
- **Sufficient cause:** X guarantees Y.
- **Probabilistic cause:** X raises the chance of Y.
- **Contributing cause:** X is part of a set that produces Y.
- **Enabling cause:** X makes the system responsive to another cause.

Most real-world causes are probabilistic and contributory. A single cigarette does not cause lung cancer. Smoking, over time, in a body with certain susceptibilities, raises the risk. A spark may cause an explosion, but only given fuel, oxygen, and confinement. Stress may worsen ulcers, but it is not the only or always the main cause.

If someone says “X causes Y” and means “X is sufficient,” the claim is probably too strong. If they mean “X is part of a causal process that can produce Y,” it may be fair.

### 6. Be careful with individual cases

Population-level causation does not automatically identify individual causation.

Suppose smoking raises the lifetime risk of lung cancer from 2 percent to 25 percent. A smoker who develops lung cancer has had their risk greatly increased, but not all of their cancer is “due to” smoking in a simple arithmetic sense. A nonsmoker who develops lung cancer has a case where smoking is not the cause, even though smoking causes many lung cancers in the population.

For an individual case, the relevant question is counterfactual: would this person, in this history, have had Y without X? That is often unobservable. You can estimate probabilities, but you usually cannot declare the individual cause with certainty.

This is why medical and legal language often uses softer terms: “likely contributed,” “more probable than not,” “a substantial factor,” “population attributable risk.”

### 7. Overdetermination complicates “but for”

Sometimes removing X would not have prevented Y, because another cause would have produced Y anyway. Two independent fires meet and burn a house. Each fire is a cause, even though the house would have burned if one had not occurred.

The simple test “Y would not have happened without X” can fail in such cases. A better question is whether X was part of a sufficient causal process and whether it was relevant under the background conditions. In ordinary language, we can still say “a cause,” just not “the cause,” unless the claim is justified.

### 8. Mechanism helps, but it is not decisive

A known mechanism makes a causal claim more credible and helps define its scope. If X affects Y through a known biological pathway, we know what to look for: dose, latency, side effects, interactions, resistance. If the mechanism is social, the “mechanism” may be incentives, norms, information flows, or institutional constraints.

But mechanism is not proof. A plausible story can be wrong, and a real effect can exist before we understand the mechanism. Conversely, a known mechanism may be too weak to matter in the population. A substance can be biologically active at laboratory doses and irrelevant at ordinary exposures.

Mechanism is especially useful for checking scope. If X causes Y only when Z is present, the bare claim “X causes Y” is incomplete.

### 9. Ask what the claim is being used for

The same evidence may support different conclusions depending on the job.

If the claim is for prediction, average effects and covariates matter. If it is for intervention, you need evidence that changing X would change Y. If it is for explanation, you need a process, not just a correlation. If it is for blame, you need more still: duty, foreseeability, contribution, and perhaps moral or legal proximity.

A variable can predict Y without being a lever for changing Y. Ice cream sales may predict drownings, but reducing ice cream sales is not a drowning-prevention strategy. A trait may be associated with success because of discrimination, not because the trait produces success. Punishing the trait may not improve the outcome and may deepen the harm.

### 10. The hardest objection

Even a good randomized trial does not give you a pure, context-free fact. It estimates an average effect in a particular population, under particular conditions, for a particular outcome, over a particular time. There may be effect modifiers. The effect may not generalize. The intervention may have worked because of attention, placebo, or implementation, not because of the active ingredient.

So every causal claim is incomplete. But that does not make causal language useless. It makes scope conditions necessary.

If the omitted conditions are not material, the shorthand is fair. “The button caused the light to turn on” is fair even though the claim leaves out wiring, electricity, and the power plant. If the omitted conditions are material, the shorthand is unfair. “The CEO’s confidence caused the stock to rise” may be unfair if the stock rose because of earnings, macro news, or market-wide buying. “Poverty causes crime” is unfair as a sufficient-cause claim; it may be fairer as “poverty increases the rate of some crimes through reduced opportunity, stress, policing, and other mechanisms.”

A useful decision procedure:

1. Rewrite the claim as an intervention: “If we changed X, Y would change by A in population P.”
2. Identify the contrast: X versus what?
3. Identify the background: what are you assuming held constant?
4. Ask what would make it false: confounding, reverse causation, selection, no effect after intervention, subgroup reversal.

prompt: when I run git stash, where do my changes actually go?
response:
`git stash` does not move your files into a special stash folder. It writes them into Git’s normal object database as a commit, trees, and blobs, then makes a reflog entry under `refs/stash` point to that commit.

Concretely, after you run:

```bash
git stash
```

Git has done roughly this:

1. It took the contents of your modified tracked files.
2. It stored those contents as blob objects under `.git/objects/`.
3. It built tree objects describing the stashed working tree.
4. It created a commit object pointing to that tree.
5. It made `refs/stash` and the stash reflog point to that commit.
6. It reset your tracked working tree and index back to `HEAD`.

So your “changes” are not saved as a patch file. They are saved as full file contents in Git’s content-addressed object store. Git can show diffs later, but the storage is snapshot-like, like a normal commit.

You can see the stash commit like this:

```bash
git stash list
git log -g --oneline refs/stash
git cat-file -p stash@{0}
```

The last command will show something like:

```text
commit <sha>
tree <tree-sha>
parent <HEAD-sha>
author ...
committer ...

WIP on main: <HEAD-sha> <commit subject>
```

That commit is the stash. Its tree contains the stashed file states. Its blobs contain the actual file bytes.

The ref is usually in:

```text
.git/refs/stash
```

or in `.git/packed-refs` if your refs are packed.

The history of stashes is in:

```text
.git/logs/refs/stash
```

That reflog is why `stash@{0}`, `stash@{1}`, etc. work. `stash@{0}` means “the newest entry in the stash reflog.” `refs/stash` itself points to the newest stash; older stashes are reached through the reflog.

The object files themselves live under:

```text
.git/objects/
```

For example, a loose object might be at:

```text
.git/objects/ab/cdef0123...
```

But after garbage collection or repacking, the same object may be inside:

```text
.git/objects/pack/*.pack
```

So you should not expect to find a visible file named after your branch or your stash message. The name is the object’s hash.

A useful way to inspect what is in a stash:

```bash
git show stash@{0}
git show stash@{0} -- path/to/file
git ls-tree -r stash@{0}^{tree}
git diff stash@{0}^ stash@{0}
```

`stash@{0}^` is the commit that was `HEAD` when you stashed, usually. The diff between that and the stash commit is the change you stashed.

One important detail: `git stash` by default only stashes tracked files. Untracked files stay in your working directory unless you use:

```bash
git stash -u
```

or, including ignored files:

```bash
git stash -a
```

If you include untracked files, Git stores them in a separate commit reachable from the stash. You can inspect them with:

```bash
git stash show -p --include-untracked stash@{0}
```

The reason `git log` does not show your stash is that `git log` follows `HEAD` by default. Your stash commit is not an ancestor of your current branch. It is reachable through `refs/stash` and its reflog, not through your branch history.

If you drop a stash:

```bash
git stash drop stash@{0}
```

Git removes that reflog entry. The commit and its objects may become unreachable. They can still be recovered for a while using tools like:

```bash
git fsck --lost-found
```

but eventually `git gc` may prune them. If you want to keep a stash permanently, make it reachable from a normal ref:

```bash
git branch stashed-work stash@{0}
```

or:

```bash
git tag saved-stash-1 stash@{0}
```

So the short answer is: your changes go into `.git/objects/` as normal Git objects, and `.git/refs/stash` plus `.git/logs/refs/stash` remember where that stash commit is.

prompt: why do we even get nightmares? is it just stress or is there more to it
response:
Nightmares are not one thing. They are the point where a dream becomes emotionally loud enough to break through sleep. Most happen during REM sleep, when the brain is active, the body is switched off, and memory circuits are replaying recent and older experiences. In that state the brain can build a scenario with almost no outside input. The emotional system is strong; the parts that normally fact-check and put things in perspective are quieter. So a dream can feel terrifying even if it is nonsense. Most people have nightmares occasionally; the problem starts when they become regular.

They are also different from night terrors, where a person wakes briefly from deep sleep, looks panicked or confused, and remembers little. A nightmare is a remembered disturbing dream, usually one that leaves you awake and thinking.

Stress matters because it does two jobs at once: it supplies material and it destabilizes sleep. A worried brain has more threat-like content to work on, and stressed sleep is lighter and more fragmented, which makes it easier to wake with the dream still attached. That is why bad weeks often produce bad dreams. But stress is a trigger, not the whole mechanism.

The cases that break the stress-only story are not rare. Young children get nightmares long before they have adult pressures; the content often tracks ordinary developmental fears—monsters, separation, the dark, being lost. People with no recent stress can get nightmares after a fever, a night of pain, alcohol withdrawal, or a medication that changes REM sleep. Sleep debt and REM rebound do the same: if you have been suppressing deep or REM sleep, the brain overcompensates, and the dreams come back stronger. And trauma survivors may have nightmares that replay a specific event, not just general tension. If nightmares were only stress noise, they would not line up so neatly with what happened, what the body is doing, and what treatment changes.

The hardest version of the “just noise” view is that the brain is a prediction machine running random scenarios while offline, and nightmares are simply the scary end of the distribution. Some of that is true. A lot of dream content is bizarre, incoherent, or pulled from unrelated fragments. But the patterns show that the content is not free-floating. The brain preferentially rehearses emotionally marked experiences, especially threat and loss. The same machinery that makes you remember a threat well enough to avoid it can stage a version of it at night. One plausible function is threat simulation: you practice being afraid and coping without real consequences. Another is emotional memory consolidation: the brain tags what mattered and files it. Nightmares are what happens when the tag is too hot. They are not a secret message, but they are not random either. They are emotional memory work gone too loud.

There is also a feedback problem. Once nightmares start, sleep itself becomes the threat. You lie awake half waiting for the next one, the brain stays more alert, REM becomes more intense, and the cycle gets worse. That is why occasional nightmares are normal and chronic ones can become a disorder. They can also be a symptom: PTSD, sleep apnea, fever, pain, substance use, or medications can all contribute.

That distinction changes what to do. If they are occasional, treat them as the brain doing messy housekeeping. If they are frequent, look at the levers: sleep schedule, alcohol and caffeine, medications, stress, trauma, and whether you are waking with panic or gasping. For trauma-related nightmares, the best-studied behavioral treatment is imagery rehearsal therapy: you write down the nightmare, rewrite the ending, and rehearse the new version while awake, which gradually weakens the fear script. CBT-I helps when the main problem has become dread of sleep. Prazosin, a blood-pressure drug that lowers norepinephrine activity, helps some people, especially with PTSD, but it is not a universal fix.

Stress often starts them, but they are built on the normal machinery of dreaming: a brain that can stage threats, replay emotional memories, and sometimes fail to keep them asleep.
